Namely, the dual stack $T^{\ast}(2j)\mathbf{A}^{2}(2i,0)$ in our table corresponds to $L(\mathrm{std},\tfrac{i}{2})L(\mathrm{std},\tfrac{2j-i}{2})$ in [Sak2, Table 1], and similarly $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(2j-2j\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}})$ in our table corresponds to $L(\mathrm{ad},j)$ in [Sak2, Table 1]. In fact, the numbers $i$ and $j$ can be read off entirely from the rational homotopy type of $X$ .*

#### Remark 1.1.11.

In the real and $p$ -adic settings, the analogue of Theorem 1.1.10 was studied in [GG2, Theorem 1] and [Sak2]. In proving Theorem 1.1.10, the work of Sakellaridis (especially [Sak2]) was very influential.

#### Remark 1.1.12 (Why rank $1$ ?).

Most of this article does not restrict attention to affine spherical varieties of rank $1$ ; this assumption is only imposed in Section 4 for doing computations. The restriction to rank $1$ here is not for any particularly deep reason: these varieties have very simple equivariant cell structures, which makes them more amenable to calculations. These examples also capture many interesting phenomena expected in [BZSV], and for these examples, the resulting homotopy-theoretic explanations for these phenomena become easier to understand.

#### Remark 1.1.13.

The reader might notice a conspicuous absence of loop-rotation equivariance in this article, which, under Langlands duality, conspires to a deformation quantization of the spectral/coherent side of Theorem 1.1.10. We have chosen to separate this topic into a different article [Dev5], in order to give it the detailed treatment it deserves (as well as for the purposes of length).

In the remainder of this introduction, we will:

- (a) explain the meaning of the terms in, and the proof of, the above theorem, and illustrate it in the example of the spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . When applied to the spherical $G\times G$ -variety $G$ , this discussion recovers the derived geometric Satake equivalence (even when $G$ is not of rank $1$ ).

- (b) explain the generalization of the derived geometric Satake equivalence to coefficients in connective complex K-theory, and some limited analogues of the above theorem on relative rank $1$ spherical varieties.

- (c) discuss some conjectures and expectations about a further generalization to coefficients in the sphere spectrum.

The homotopically-minded reader is suggested to skip to (b) and return to (a) as needed, and the conjecturally-minded reader is suggested to skip to (c).

### 1.2. The proof of Theorem 1.1.10

The basic strategy to prove Theorem 1.1.10 is discussed in Theorem 3.6.4. Let us give a high-level summary of this argument. Assume throughout that $H\subseteq G$ is a connected closed subgroup of a connected reductive algebraic group (we will sometimes identify this with the inclusion of their maximal compact subgroups).

#### Strategy 1.2.1.

- (a) First, Theorem 1.1.10 reduces to a question in homotopy theory under Hypothesis 3.5.2; this reduction relies on Theorem 3.6.4, which relies heavily on Hypothesis 3.5.2. This step does not require assuming that $G_{\mathbf{C}}/H_{\mathbf{C}}$ is rank $1$ .

- (b) On the Langlands dual side, recall (as mentioned before 1.3) that Ben-Zvi–Sakellaridis–Venkatesh construct the dual Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space ${\check{{M}}}$ using the spherical geometry of the quotient $G/H$ . One important observation we make is that the conjectures of [BZSV] in particular suggest that there is an isomorphism ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ of invariant-theoretic quotients, compatible with the natural maps to ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ , as well as a closed immersion $\kappa:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ called the Kostant section whose image “generates” $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{M}}}}$ under the ${\check{{G}}}$ -action; see Conjecture 3.5.11. We will implicitly assume the existence of the map $\kappa$ in the remainder of this introduction. In the case of affine homogeneous rank $1$ spherical varieties, we construct the Kostant section case-by-case. This idea, however, works in much more generality. For instance, in [Dev4], we study the dual of the spherical $\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{PSO}_{4}$ -variety $(\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{PSO}_{4})/\mathrm{SO}_{3}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ , in which case the above expectations boil down essentially to the existence of the Cayley hyperdeterminant.

- (c) Using a compact generation argument, Theorem 1.1.10 is reduced to proving that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}} $$

of graded group schemes over ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ . In other words, $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ is the stabilizer of the image of the Kostant section. It turns out that $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ is a commutative group scheme over ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ . It is a bit of a miracle, therefore, that the above isomorphism predicts that the fiber product ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ should be a commutative group scheme for every ${\check{{M}}}$ as in [BZSV] which is dual to an affine homogeneous spherical variety. Dually, it also might seem like a bit of a miracle that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ is a commutative ring (after all, the Pontryagin product on the homology of a $1$ -fold loop space such as $\Omega(S^{i}\vee S^{j})$ will not be commutative!); but this, at least, has a nice explanation coming from the Deligne conjecture. See Corollary 3.5.12. The nonequivariant homology of $\Omega(G/H)$ has been studied by many authors using Morse theory, at least in the case of symmetric spaces; see, e.g., [BS, Zil].

Together, the properties (b) and (c) of $\kappa$ imply that one can recover ${\check{{M}}}$ from the $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ -action on ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ , which ultimately leads to the proof of Theorem 1.1.10.

It is the isomorphism of (c) which we will establish in the rank $1$ case through case-by-case analysis, since the spaces $S^{n}$ , ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n}$ , $\mathbf{H}P^{n}$ , and $\mathbf{O}P^{2}$ form a finite list of such affine homogeneous spherical varieties up to finite covers (see [Akh1]). Although most of the rank $1$ cases behave quite similarly to each other, each case showcases some interesting basic homotopy-theoretic facts (see Table 3). In fact, we will establish the isomorphism of (c) even for homology with coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}[1/2]$ , and in some cases with coefficients in $\mathrm{ku}$ (see the next section).

#### Example 1.2.2 ((Spherical) geometrized spherical harmonics for $G/H=\mathrm{SO}_{3}/\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ ).

Let us illustrate (c) in the case of the spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (so $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ and $H=\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ ). The Hopf fibration gives a homotopy equivalence $(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m})(\mathbf{C})\simeq S^{2}$ , so (c) reduces to computing $\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})$ . The Borel-equivariant analogue of this computation is quite simple: there is a homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(BS^{1};\mathbf{C})\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}C_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})^{hS^{1}}, $$

with a single $d_{2}$ -differential. This spectral sequence degenerates on the $E_{3}$ -page, and gives an isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}C_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})^{hS^{1}}\cong\mathbf{C}[\![x]\!][b]/bx, $$

where $|b|=2$ and $|x|=-2$ . Replacing the left-hand side by $\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})$ simply has the effect of making $x$ into a polynomial (as opposed to power series) variable.

Ignoring degrees for a moment, write $\mathbf{A}^{1}=\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{S^{1}}(\ast;\mathbf{C})$ , and let $\kappa:\mathbf{A}^{1}\to T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ denote the map sending $x$ to the point $(x,1)$ in the cotangent fiber over $(1,0)\in\mathbf{A}^{2}$ . If we equip $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ with its natural $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action (coming from the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -action on $\mathbf{A}^{2}$ ), one can compute that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathbf{A}^{1}\times_{T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{A}^{1}\cong\spec\mathbf{C}[x,b]/bx, $$

and hence an (ungraded) isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2};\mathbf{C})\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\times_{T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\mathbf{A}^{1}. $$

The right-hand side can be equipped with a grading such that the above isomorphism is one of graded schemes, which gives (c). In the case of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , this leads to an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\!(t)\!)/\mathbf{G}_{m}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{C})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T^{\ast}[2](\mathbf{A}^{2}[2,0])/\mathrm{SL}_{2}[-2\rho]). $$

Before proceeding to the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic generalization, let us mention that many aspects of the Ben-Zvi–Sakellaridis–Venkatesh conjecture can be understood from the perspective of Hochschild (co)homology. For the purposes of the introduction, it will be convenient to Borel-complete, i.e., to work with the ring $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ .

#### Remark 1.2.3.

The process of Borel-completion above amounts to replacing equivariant cochains $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{C})$ with the Borel-equivariant cochains $\mathbf{C}^{hG}=C^{\ast}(BG;\mathbf{C})$ (given by the homotopy fixed points of $G$ acting trivially on $\mathbf{C}$ ). Just as there is an isomorphism $\spec C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{C})\cong{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ , there is an isomorphism $\spf\mathbf{C}^{hG}\cong\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ . This might seem like a minor distinction, but it is in fact a crucial one (which becomes much more significant with $\mathrm{ku}$ -coefficients).

#### Proposition (Corollary 3.5.8, Corollary 3.5.12).

The $\mathbf{C}$ -algebra $\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ can be identified with the relative Hochschild cohomology $\mathrm{HC}(\mathbf{C}^{hH}/\mathbf{C}^{hG})$ of the map $\mathbf{C}^{hG}\to\mathbf{C}^{hH}$ (this was already observed in [Dev2, Remark A.6]). In particular, the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem implies that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spf\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathcal{L}(G/H)_{hG};\mathbf{C})\cong T[-1]((\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})/(\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}), $$

where the right-hand side is the $1$ -shifted relative tangent bundle of the map $\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ , and the hats denote completion at the origin. Moreover, the Deligne conjecture equips $\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathbf{C}^{hG}$ -algebra.

#### Remark 1.2.4.

In Strategy 1.2.1, we said that Conjecture 3.4.12 often reduces to proving an isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}, $$

where we are ignoring gradings. The right-hand side is a group scheme over ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ , which we denote by ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ ; it is an analogue for ${\check{{M}}}$ of the regular centralizer group scheme.88 8 Perhaps it is better denoted by ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}}$ ; but we are going to be viewing ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ as an object constructed from $X$ , and then it is nontrivial that there is any relationship between ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ and ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ . Hence the notation ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ . If the left-hand side in the above isomorphism is replaced by $\spf\pi_{\ast}C^{\ast}_{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})^{\ast}$ , i.e., the dual of equivariant cohomology, the preceding proposition says that the right-hand side must be replaced by $T^{\ast}[1](({{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})/({{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}))$ ; this is simply the Lie algebra of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ . In other words, the dual of equivariant cohomology allows one to access the Lie algebra of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ ; to understand ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ itself involves a “decompletion”, which in homotopy theory is given by working with equivariant homology itself (since this is a predual of equivariant cohomology).

Summarizing, the various completions appearing in this article can, roughly speaking, be interpreted as follows:

- • There is an isomorphism between $\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ and the ring of functions on ${\check{{J}}}_{X}={\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ .

- • The $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{H}(\ast;\mathbf{C})$ -linear dual of $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{H}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})$ can be identified with the ring of functions on the completion of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ at the fibers of the map ${\check{{J}}}_{X}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ ; or equivalently, with the Lie algebra of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ .

- • The Borel-equivariant homology $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ can be identified with the ring of functions on the completion of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ at the origin of ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ .

The above result can be viewed as a relative version of [BF1, Theorem 1]. In a sense, most of this article can be regarded as an attempt to understand the decompletion of this Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg isomorphism. As a perhaps helpful guide, a general principle about equivalences of the form conjectured in [BZSV] lead to some analogies between topology and algebra, a limited collection of which we have recorded in Table 2.

| A-side/topology | B-side/algebra |
|---|---|
| Spherical $G$ -variety $X$ | ${\check{{G}}}$ -scheme ${\check{{X}}}$ |
| Free loop space $\mathcal{L}X$ | (Twisted) cotangent bundle $T^{\ast}_{\psi}({\check{{X}}})$ |
| Based loop space $\Omega X$ | Cotangent fiber |
| Sheaves on $X(\!(t)\!)/G[\![t]\!]$ with $\mathbf{Q}$ -coefficients | Perfect complexes on $T^{\ast}_{\psi}({\check{{X}}})/{\check{{G}}}$ |

*Table 2. Analogies between topology and algebra. Passing from the left-hand to the right-hand column is roughly implemented by (rational) cohomology and the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem.*

The above relationship to Hochschild cohomology allows us to make a basic observation about the structure of a Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space on ${\check{{M}}}$ . First, we note the following, which is closely related to [Tel, Section 5.2] and [Sak3, Section 5.1.5]. We have ignored homological shifts/gradings for notational simplicity.

#### Proposition (Proposition 3.6.16).

Let ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}$ denote the group scheme of regular centralizers of ${\check{{G}}}$ , so that

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}, $$

and similarly, let ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{H}}}}$ denote the group scheme of regular centralizers of ${\check{{H}}}$ . Then, there is a Lagrangian correspondence (interpreted in a derived sense):

$$ \textstyle{{\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{H}}}}} \textstyle{{\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}.} $$

Furthermore, there is an isomorphism

$$ ({\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})\times_{J_{{\check{{H}}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}. $$

This has an interesting consequence; let us state its “morally correct” form (but see Corollary 3.6.20 for a precise statement):

#### Corollary (Corollary 3.6.20).

Let ${\check{{M}}}$ denote the Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space dual to $G/H$ , and assume that there is a “Kostant slice” $\kappa_{{\check{{M}}}}:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ . Let ${\check{{M}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of this Kostant slice. Similarly, let ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}$ denote the Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}$ -space dual to $(G\times H)/H^{\mathrm{diag}}$ . Again assume that there is a Kostant slice $\kappa_{{\check{{M}}}}:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to{\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}$ , and let ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote its ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}$ -orbit. Then there is an isomorphism

$$ {\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{H}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}, $$

and a Lagrangian correspondence

$$ \textstyle{{\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}/({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{H}}}} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}},} $$

as well as a Cartesian square

$$ \textstyle{{\check{{M}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa} \textstyle{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast,\mathrm{reg}}.} $$

The Lagrangian correspondence of the preceding proposition, i.e., the Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}$ -space ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}$ , “controls” transfer for $H\subseteq G$ , in the sense that it can be thought of as a morphism from ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{H}}}$ to ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/{\check{{G}}}$ in the algebraic (and $1$ -shifted) avatar of Weinstein’s category of symplectic varieties and Lagrangian correspondences between them. As explained in Remark 3.6.22, the Cartesian square of the above result follows more generally from the perspective of Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions being swapped under Langlands duality.

#### Example 1.2.5.

In Example 3.6.24, we describe a curious calculation involving explicit descriptions of the regular centralizer group schemes for groups in the Gan-Gross-Prasad period. Namely, if $H\subseteq G$ is the inclusion $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ , so that ${\check{{H}}}=\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ and ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ , then ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ can be identified with $\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n})$ .

A result of Safronov’s from [Saf1] can be used to translate the desired Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -structure on ${\check{{M}}}$ into the language of shifted symplectic geometry (à la [PTVV]). This translation in turn predicts that equipping ${\check{{M}}}$ with the structure of a Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space should, in particular, imply that the map

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}[2-2\rho]/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]}{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}} $$

is Lagrangian, hence coisotropic (in an appropriate derived sense). It turns out that both Proposition 3.6.16 and the above coisotropicity are extremely general facts which have clean homotopy-theoretic explanations in terms of (higher) Hochschild cohomology.

#### Example 1.2.6.

In the special case when $G$ is replaced by $G\times G$ and $H$ is replaced by the diagonal embedding of $G$ (so that the associated homogeneous variety is just $(G\times G)/G^{\mathrm{diag}}\cong G$ ), the Hochschild cohomology $\mathrm{HC}(\mathbf{C}^{hG}/\mathbf{C}^{h(G\times G)})$ can be identified with the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -center $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}(\mathbf{C}^{hG}/\mathbf{C})$ . The Deligne conjecture equips $\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}\simeq\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}(\mathbf{C}^{hG}/\mathbf{C})$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ - $\mathbf{C}$ -algebra; this ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra structure is closely related to the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -monoidality of the derived geometric Satake equivalence.

Note that $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}$ is equipped with the structure of a (graded) Poisson algebra whose Poisson bracket has weight $2$ ; this structure exists on the homotopy of any ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra. It turns out that this Poisson structure in fact comes from a symplectic form (of weight $2$ ) on $\spf\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}$ . Moreover, Strategy 1.2.1 says, in particular, that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spf\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}\cong\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\times_{\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2-2\rho]/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]}\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}. $$

Returning to relative Langlands, one can also show that if $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup, $\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ admits the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}$ -algebra. The coisotropicity of 1.4 translates into the requirement that the natural map

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})\to\spec\mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{C}) $$

is coisotropic. One can directly prove its Borel-completed analogue:

#### Proposition (Observation 5.2.11 and Remark 5.2.13).

The natural map

$$ \spf\mathrm{H}_{H}^{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{C})^{\vee}\to\spf\mathrm{H}_{G}^{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{C})^{\vee} $$

is coisotropic (in an appropriate derived sense).

This result turns out to be a simple consequence of the fact that $\mathbf{C}[\Omega(G/H)]^{hH}$ admits the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathbf{C}[\Omega G]^{hG}$ -algebra, and a general property of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -centers as established in [Fra, Theorem 1.1]. We hope that further study of the relative Langlands program from the perspective of Hochschild (co)homology might shed more light into some of the structures predicted in [BZSV].

### 1.3. $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic aberrations

In the course of proving Theorem 1.1.10, or even the derived geometric Satake equivalence, the reader will likely observe that many components of the proof do not depend very heavily on the particular choice of coefficient ring for the $\infty$ -category of constructible sheaves. In particular, calculations such as that of $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{G}(\Omega G;\mathbf{C})$ (to construct the homomorphism 1.2) work equally well with $G$ -equivariant $\mathbf{C}$ -(co)homology replaced by any well-behaved equivariant generalized cohomology theory. Motivated by this observation, our second goal in this article is to suggest that the (geometric) Langlands program should admit a generalization to sheaves with coefficients in more “exotic” rings, such as the sphere spectrum or complex cobordism. We will discuss the conceptual role of these coefficients in the next section.

Establishing this generalized form of the Langlands program is rather tricky, and so our focus in this article will be on the simpler example of connective complex K-theory. Our focus is on this particular example for at least two reasons: first, it is a general principle in homotopy theory that statements about ordinary rational/integral cohomology which admit analogues for connective K-theory will likely admit generalizations to other complex-oriented spectra; second, it is mostly psychological, in that proving analogues for equivariant elliptic cohomology, etc., would requires further technical setup, and distracts from the main features of Langlands duality.99 9 A third reason, in keeping with the epigraph of our previous article [Dev2], is yet another quote of J. F. Adams $\mathrm{E}_{8}$ from [Ada]: “[To] consider the question [of torsion in the cohomology of $\mathrm{E}_{8}$ ] at all reveals a certain preoccupation with ordinary cohomology. Any impartial observer must marvel at your obsession with this obscure and unhelpful invariant. The author, like all respectable Lie groups, is much concerned to present a decorous and seemly appearance to the eyes of K-theory…” (It should be said immediately that we do not study $\mathrm{E}_{8}$ in this article.) I do not have such strong feelings against ordinary cohomology, but the general thrust of this quote still applies: going from ordinary cohomology to K-theory should reveal deeper structures under Langlands duality. An analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in periodic complex K-theory and elliptic cohomology was proved in [Dev2].

If $G$ is a compact Lie group, Atiyah and Segal defined $G$ -equivariant complex K-theory $\mathrm{KU}_{G}$ in [Seg, AS]: this is a generalized cohomology theory, viewed as a spectrum in the sense of homotopy theory, which classifies $G$ -equivariant vector bundles on finite $G$ -spaces. Direct sum and tensor products of $G$ -equivariant vector bundles equips $\mathrm{KU}_{G}$ with the structure of a ring spectrum; in fact, it is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring, meaning (for instance) that the multiplication on cohomology can be refined by Adams operations. Despite its definition, the geometric interpretation of cocycles for equivariant K-theory as equivariant vector bundles will play no role below. Two examples will play an important conceptual role:

#### Example 1.3.1.

When $G$ is the trivial group, $\mathrm{KU}_{G}$ is simply periodic complex K-theory $\mathrm{KU}$ , and Bott periodicity gives a graded isomorphism $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{KU}\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ with the Bott class $\beta$ in weight $2$ . On the other hand, when $G$ is a connected compact Lie group with complex representation ring $R_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ , the coefficient ring $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{KU}_{G}$ is the tensor product $R_{\mathbf{C}}(G)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ . In particular, if $G$ is a torus $T$ , then $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{KU}_{T}$ is the corresponding algebraic torus $T_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]}$ over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ .

Nonequivariant complex K-theory is in some sense the simplest generalized cohomology theory which is not just ordinary integral cohomology. In fact, the oft-cited analogies between them are more than coincidental:

#### Recollection 1.3.2.

There is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $\mathrm{ku}$ called connective complex K-theory such that there is a graded isomorphism $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ . If we set $\beta=0$ , this ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring simply degenerates to the Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum $\mathbf{Z}$ representing ordinary integral cohomology; and if we invert $\beta$ , it recovers periodic complex K-theory. In other words, $\mathrm{ku}$ interpolates between $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\mathrm{KU}$ , and can be viewed as a one-parameter deformation of the ring $\mathbf{Z}$ in a homotopy-theoretic direction (namely, along the Bott class $\beta$ ).

If $G$ is a compact Lie group, one can also construct an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ called $G$ -equivariant connective K-theory which interpolates between $G$ -equivariant integral cohomology and $G$ -equivariant (periodic) complex K-theory. In a precise sense (known in the homotopy-theoretic literature as complex-oriented/abelian descent), the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ is determined by the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings $\mathrm{ku}_{T}$ for compact abelian Lie groups $T$ , which are in turn determined by the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $\mathrm{ku}_{S^{1}}$ .

#### Example 1.3.3.

Since $\mathrm{ku}_{S^{1}}$ interpolates between $S^{1}$ -equivariant integral cohomology and $\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}$ , and there are isomorphisms $\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{S^{1}}(\ast;\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathbf{G}_{a}(2)$ (with coordinate in weight $-2$ ) and $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{KU}_{S^{1}}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]}$ , one expects $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{S^{1}}$ to interpolate between $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ . In fact, equivariant connective K-theory is concocted so that $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{S^{1}}$ is the canonical degeneration from $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ to $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ :

$$ \spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{S^{1}}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x}], $$

where $x$ is in weight $-2$ . We will denote this group scheme (where the group structure makes $1+\beta x$ into a grouplike element) by $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ . The case of a general compact abelian Lie group $T$ is a straightforward generalization:

$$ \spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}\cong\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T),\mathbf{G}_{\beta})=:T_{\beta}. $$

Note that when $\beta=0$ , this group scheme is just $\mathfrak{t}(2)$ ; and when $\beta$ is inverted, this group scheme is $T_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]}$ . This story is discussed further in Section 2.

Very simply, the effect of studying derived geometric Satake with coefficients in $\mathrm{ku}$ (instead of coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}$ ) is that the dual group remains unchanged, and every appearance/consequence of the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{t}$ in the “classical” story is replaced by the group scheme $T_{\beta}$ over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ . In order to make this more precise, let us explain a $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence as proved in Theorem 3.7.18.

#### Setup 1.3.4.

Write $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ to denote the polynomial ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathbf{Z}$ -algebra where $\beta$ lives in homological degree $2$ , so that it is obtained as a shearing of the graded ring $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku})$ .

- • There is a $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ of “ $G[\![t]\!]\times G[\![t]\!]$ -equivariant sheaves of $\mathrm{ku}$ -modules on $G(\!(t)\!)$ ”. The definition of this $\infty$ -category is given in Construction 3.7.15. However, this definition is extremely ad hoc; hence the “faux”. This $\infty$ -category is essentially defined by playing around with the subcategory of locally constant sheaves. We hope it will agree with a “correct” definition (see Remark 3.7.17 for a little more on this point).

- • Suppose ${\check{{G}}}$ is a group scheme defined over $\mathbf{Z}$ . Let $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ denote the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ , and let ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ denote the group scheme over $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{ku})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ given by $\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee},G_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]})$ . We will view ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ as a $\beta$ -deformation of ${\check{{G}}}$ . The quotient stack ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ is related to the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg filtration for the quotient stack $B{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Theorem 1.3.5 (Derived geometric Satake with $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic coefficients; Theorem 3.7.18).

Let $G$ be a simply-laced and connected Lie group, and invert the order of the Weyl group $W$ (for simplicity). Then there is a $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[1/|W|,\beta]$ -linear equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)), $$

where $G$ is the Chevalley split form of $G$ over $\mathbf{Z}[1/|W|]$ , and ${\check{{G}}}$ acts on $G$ by conjugation1010 10 That this makes sense is thanks to the simply-laced assumption on $G$ ..

#### Remark 1.3.6.

Upon setting $\beta=0$ , we have

$$ G(-2\rho)_{\beta}|_{\beta=0}=\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\vee}(2),G(-2\rho))=\Hom(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}^{\sharp}(2),G(-2\rho))=\mathfrak{g}(2-2\rho); $$

here, $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}^{\sharp}$ denotes the divided power hull of the origin in $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ , further completed at the divided power filtration. Because $G$ is simply-laced, there is an ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant isomorphism $\mathfrak{g}(2-2\rho)\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}(2-2\rho)$ . It follows that upon setting $\beta=0$ , the left-hand side of Theorem 1.3.5 becomes $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Z}[1/N])$ , and the right-hand side becomes ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}[2-2\rho]/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]$ . In other words, Theorem 1.3.5 just reduces to the derived geometric Satake equivalence (in the simply-laced and connected case).

On the other hand, upon inverting $\beta$ , Theorem 1.3.5 is related to the $\mathrm{KU}$ -theoretic derived geometric Satake equivalence of [Dev2], since

$$ G(-2\rho)_{\beta}|_{\beta^{-1}}=\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\vee},G)=\Hom(\underline{\mathbf{Z}},G)=G. $$

All objects on the right hand sides of the above displayed isomorphisms are to be understood as base-changed from $\mathbf{Z}$ to $\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ (we omitted this from the notation for readability): since $\beta$ lives in weight $2$ and is invertible, we may ignore the $-2\rho$ -shift. In particular, Theorem 1.3.5 implies that the $\beta$ -adic filtration on $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]/Z(G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{KU})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ corresponds to the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg filtration on the free loop space of the quotient stack $B{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Example 1.3.7.

Let us illustrate Theorem 1.3.5 in the case when $G$ is a torus $T$ . Identifying $\mathcal{L}T$ with $T\times\Omega T$ , we see that the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ is just $\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{T}(\Omega T;\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ . However, $\Omega T$ is simply the discrete set $\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)$ of cocharacters of $T$ , so that $\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{T}(\Omega T;\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\bigoplus_{\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)}\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{T}(\ast;\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ . Almost by construction, there is an equivalence $\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{T}(\ast;\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}T_{\beta})$ . On the other hand, there is an equivalence $\bigoplus_{\mathbb{X}_{\ast}(T)}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(B{\check{{T}}})$ . Together, we obtain an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{T}(\Omega T;\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}T_{\beta}\times B{\check{{T}}}), $$

which is the right-hand side of Theorem 1.3.5.

Since the group scheme $G_{\beta}$ may seem somewhat mysterious, let us mention that it has an extremely concrete interpretation if, for instance, ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{n}$ .

#### Example 1.3.8.

When $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ , and $G_{\beta}=\mathrm{SL}_{n,\beta}$ is the group scheme whose $R$ -points (for $R$ being a graded $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -algebra) consists of those $n\times n$ -matrices $A$ such that

$$ \frac{\mathrm{det}(I+\beta A)-1}{\beta}=0. $$

Since the derivative of the determinant is the trace, the specialization of this condition to $\beta=0$ is simply the condition that $A$ is traceless. When $\beta$ is not required to be zero, the above equation should be thought of as a $\beta$ -deformation of the equation $\Tr(A)=0$ : for example, when $n=2$ , it says that $\Tr(A)+\beta\mathrm{det}(A)=0$ . In particular, generically in $\beta$ (that is, when $\beta$ is invertible), $\mathrm{SL}_{n,\beta}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_{n}\times\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ via the map $A\mapsto I+\beta A$ .

More conceptually, $G_{\beta}$ is a variant of $G$ whose Cartan subgroup is replaced by its $\beta$ -deformation, but whose unipotent parts remain unchanged. For instance, there is an analogue of the Bruhat decomposition for $G_{\beta}$ where the big cell is $N^{-}\times T_{\beta}\times N$ .

As mentioned before Theorem 1.3.5, the definition of the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ is rather unsatisfying, and a better definition is warranted. The analogue of this desire on the spectral side would be the following:

#### Conjecture 1.3.9.

The graded $\mathbf{Z}[\beta,1/N]$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\QCoh(G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho))$ admits a lift to a $\mathrm{ku}[1/N]$ -linear $\infty$ -category along the degeneration $\mathrm{ku}[1/N]\rightsquigarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[1/N]\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta,1/N]$ .

Note that Conjecture 1.3.9 does not ask for a lift of $G(-2\rho)$ to $\mathrm{ku}$ , or even for a lift of the stack $G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ . A lift as in Conjecture 1.3.9 does exist if we restrict to quasicoherent sheaves over the regular locus $G_{\beta,\mathrm{reg}}(-2\rho)/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ .

Given Theorem 1.3.5, one is naturally led to wonder if there is an analogue of the relative Langlands program, and in particular of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1], in the context of $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic coefficients. We do not have a conjecture as precise as that of loc. cit. in this setting, but we do prove an analogue of Theorem 1.1.10 for some affine homogeneous spherical varieties of rank $1$ with $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic coefficients. For instance, we have the following result describing “ $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic geometrized spherical harmonics” for $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}=\mathrm{SO}_{3}/\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ :

#### Example 1.3.10 (Corollary 4.3.19 and Remark 5.1.19).

There is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\!(t)\!)/\mathbf{G}_{m}(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{V}}}_{\beta}/\mathrm{SL}_{2}(-2\rho)), $$

where ${\check{{V}}}_{\beta}$ is the affine closure of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times^{\mathbf{G}_{a}}(\mathbf{G}_{\beta}\times\mathbf{A}^{1})\subseteq T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}-\{0\})$ , with $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ acting on $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}$ via $b:(x,y)\mapsto(x,y+bx)$ . The scheme ${\check{{V}}}_{\beta}$ can be viewed as a $\beta$ -deformation of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ ; it can be explicitly identified with the open subscheme of $\mathbf{A}^{4}_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}=\mathbf{A}^{4}\times_{\spec\mathbf{Z}}\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ given by the complement of the hypersurface

$$ 1+\beta(cB-aD)=0, $$

where $a$ is in weight $0$ , $c$ is in weight $-2$ , $B$ is in weight $0$ , and $D$ is in weight $-2$ .

The structure that seems to emerge out of these considerations is a $\beta$ -deformation of the notion of a graded Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space, as explained in Section 5; we call this notion a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian space. To define this notion, it is convenient to use the language of shifted symplectic geometry as introduced in [PTVV] (see Recollection 5.1.2 for a brief review).

#### Recollection 1.3.11.

It was shown in [Saf1] that the quotient stack ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/{\check{{G}}}$ admits a $1$ -shifted symplectic structure, and that a graded Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space ${\check{{M}}}$ is equivalent to the data of a Lagrangian morphism ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/{\check{{G}}}$ in the sense of [PTVV]. In particular, the local geometric story of [BZSV] can be restated as the expectation that for certain affine spherical $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ -varieties $G_{\mathbf{C}}/H_{\mathbf{C}}$ , there is a dual Lagrangian morphism to ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/{\check{{G}}}$ such that [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] holds.

#### Observation 1.3.12.

Lagrangian morphisms to $G_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ are by definition $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -varieties. These are roughly graded ${\check{{G}}}$ -varieties ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ with some additional structure and a moment map ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}\to G_{\beta}$ . See Definition 5.1.12. Specializing $\beta=0$ , the aforementioned result from [Saf1] says that $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces specialize to graded Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces. Upon inverting $\beta$ , there is an isomorphism $G_{\beta}[\beta^{-1}]/{\check{{G}}}\cong G/{\check{{G}}}\times_{\spec\mathbf{Z}}\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta^{\pm 1}]$ , and another result from [Saf1] then implies that $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces give rise to quasi-Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces in the sense of [AMM].

#### Remark 1.3.13.

There is some precedence for $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces in the setting of integrable systems. Here are two such manifestations. Just as the phase space of a classical integrable system (such as the Calogero-Moser system and the Toda lattice) forms a Hamiltonian variety, the phase space of a “relativistic” integrable system and its degeneration to a “nonrelativistic” system (such as the Ruijsenaars-Schneider system degenerating into the Calogero-Moser system, and the relativistic Toda lattice degenerating into the classical Toda lattice) naturally forms a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian space. In the case of the relativistic Toda lattice degenerating into the classical Toda lattice, this essentially follows from [BFM] and the calculations of Theorem 3.7.10. We will explain the example of the Ruijsenaars-Schneider system degenerating into the Calogero-Moser system in future work.

Another manifestation of the notion of a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian space is as follows. It is a theorem of [AMM] that in the differential geometric setting, one can identify quasi-Hamiltonian $G$ -spaces with Hamiltonian $LG$ -spaces, where $LG$ is the loop group of the compact Lie group $G$ . Roughly speaking, a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian $G$ -space in the differential geometric setting is a Hamiltonian $L_{\beta}G$ -space equipped with a map to $\mathbf{R}$ , where $L_{\beta}G$ denotes the group over $\mathbf{R}$ whose fiber over $\beta\in\mathbf{R}$ is the group of maps from the circle of radius $|\beta|$ to $G$ . That is, a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian $G$ -space is the data of a Hamiltonian $LG$ -space along with the data of how it limits to a Hamiltonian $G$ -space.

In Proposition 5.1.11, we show that $G_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ admits a $1$ -shifted symplectic structure. Moreover, the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic calculations in the relative rank one cases of types $A_{n}$ , $D_{2}$ , and $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ show that there are equivalences of the form

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)), $$

where ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ is a graded ${\check{{G}}}$ -space over $\spec\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ . The action of $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ , equivalent to $\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho))$ , on the left-hand side of the above equivalence suggests that there is a Lagrangian morphism ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}\to G_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ . One might therefore hope that the local geometric story of [BZSV] admits a $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic analogue.

#### Slogan 1.3.14.

For certain affine spherical $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ -varieties $G_{\mathbf{C}}/H_{\mathbf{C}}$ , there is a dual Lagrangian morphism ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}\to G_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ (that is, a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian space ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ ) such that an analogue of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] holds.

Unfortunately, the structure theory of quasi-Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces does not seem to be as well-developed as that of the theory of Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces, so it is hard at the current moment to make conjectures as precise as those in [BZSV] regarding the nature of these $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -spaces. We do, however, strongly believe that such a theory will play an important role in understanding $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic deformations of the geometric Langlands program.

In any case, we can at least explore consequences of Slogan 1.3.14. For instance, one of the consequences of Slogan 1.3.14 is an analogue of Conjecture 3.5.11, which says that there is an isomorphism ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong T_{H,\beta}/\!\!/W_{H}$ of invariant-theoretic quotients, and that there is a Kostant section $T_{H,\beta}/\!\!/W_{H}\to{\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ . As in the discussion surrounding 1.4 above, equipping ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ with the structure of a $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian ${\check{{G}}}$ -space should furthermore imply that the map

$$ T_{H,\beta}/\!\!/W_{H}\times_{{\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}}T_{H,\beta}/\!\!/W_{H}\to T_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{G_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}}T_{\beta}/\!\!/W $$

is Lagrangian, hence coisotropic (in an appropriate derived sense). Here, we have ignored homological shifts, for simplicity. Under a putative $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic version of the relative derived Satake equivalence, 1.5 identifies with the map

$$ \spec\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H))\to\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G), $$

so one wishes to see that this map is coisotropic. Again, exactly as in the discussion surrounding 1.4, this can be explained using homotopy-theoretic ideas regarding Hochschild (co)homology and ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -centralizers. Namely, at least upon completion, one can show:

#### Proposition (Observation 5.2.11 and Remark 5.2.13).

The natural map

$$ \spf\mathrm{ku}_{H}^{\ast}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}\to\spf\mathrm{ku}_{G}^{\ast}(\Omega G)^{\vee} $$

is coisotropic (in an appropriate derived sense).

As the reader will likely observe (and as mentioned in the beginning of this subsection), the proofs of these statements for $\mathrm{ku}$ ultimately use very little on the specific structure of equivariant connective K-theory, and are almost axiomatic in nature: they only rely on certain basic properties of this equivariant cohomology theory. While proving Theorem 1.1.10 and its $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic variant, we will also describe some calculations of independent interest along the way (such as Remark 4.3.4 and Remark 5.4.4, which identifies the homology of $\Omega^{2}\mathrm{SU}(n)$ , even with $\mathbf{Z}$ -coefficients, with the cohomology of the classifying stack of a shearing of the group scheme of length $n-1$ Witt vectors over $\mathbf{Z}$ ).

### 1.4. Generalized coefficients

One long-term goal, of which this project is a part, is to understand a version of the (relative) geometric Langlands program with coefficients in the sphere spectrum. We do not resolve this problem in this article (far from it!), but instead formulate some very naïve expectations in Section 5.3; I hope that reporting my (meagre) partial progress will motivate further study into this topic.

In order to motivate why this is a natural question, let us begin with some general remarks about the nature of the geometric Satake equivalence. A longstanding expectation has been that Langlands-type equivalences are of a “motivic nature”.

#### Example 1.4.1.

In the arithmetic incarnation of the Langlands program, results of this form are often very deep; for instance, V. Lafforgue has conjectured an independence of $\ell$ result for Langlands parametrization in the case of global function fields (see [Laf, Conjecture 12.12]).

As mentioned earlier in the introduction, it is often simpler to geometrize the archimedean and $p$ -adic settings into the setting of complex curves. In this context, we will treat the word “motivic” as more a “way of life” instead of a precise mathematical word. For instance, the motivic nature of the geometric Langlands equivalence could be interpreted as the expectation that spectral decompositions should exist for sheaves/automorphic forms valued in (modules) over an (essentially) arbitrary base ring.

#### Example 1.4.2.

One reflection of this motivic nature already appears in the geometric Satake equivalence from [MV1], which (re)constructs the Chevalley split form of a reductive group scheme. It is also true of the derived geometric Satake equivalence (see, e.g., [YZ, Zhu1]); namely, Theorem 1.1.7 still holds if the coefficients $\mathbf{C}$ are replaced by some localization $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ of $\mathbf{Z}$ , in which case ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}[2-2\rho]/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]$ is replaced by a lift to $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ .

The field of motivic homotopy theory, as introduced by Morel-Voevodsky in [MV2], suggests that the stable motivic category is a more refined version of (integral) motives (although one which is perhaps less accessible by the general public). Taking this perspective into account suggests that one can generalize the motivic expectation of geometric Langlands equivalences to also include sheaves with coefficients in ring spectra. The discussion of the preceding section (e.g., Theorem 1.3.5) shows that this expectation is not implausible: namely, spectral decompositions do exist, and their nature is modified according to the behaviour of Chern classes for the ring spectrum.

#### Example 1.4.3.

For instance, this relationship to Chern classes is the basic source of the difference between the case of “ordinary” derived geometric Satake (whose spectral side is ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}[2-2\rho]/{\check{{G}}}[-2\rho]$ ) and $\mathrm{KU}$ -theoretic derived geometric Satake (whose spectral side is $G/{\check{{G}}}$ ): indeed, Chern classes in integral cohomology and complex K-theory are very different from each other!1111 11 More precisely, the first Chern class is additive in integral cohomology, but is (essentially) multiplicative in complex K-theory. This distinction manifests itself in many ways in other (related) parts of mathematics; for instance, the Todd class appearing in the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem is just the ratio of the first Chern classes in rational cohomology and K-theory. In the case of elliptic cohomology with associated elliptic curve $E$ (as studied in [Dev2]), the spectral side is in turn replaced by the moduli stack $\mathrm{Bun}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\mathrm{ss},0}(E^{\vee})$ of semistable degree zero ${\check{{G}}}$ -bundles on the dual elliptic curve $E^{\vee}$ . The importance of Chern classes in geometric Langlands is reflected in our setting in Example 1.3.7, as well as in the classical setting of geometric Satake, where the the Chern class of the determinant line bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ for $G$ semisimple can be identified with a regular nilpotent element for the dual Lie algebra ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ (see [Gin2] and Proposition 5.4.1).

Motivated by this discussion, it is natural to wonder:

#### Question 1.4.4.

Is there is an analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in an arbitrary ring spectrum $R$ which admits a theory of Chern classes?

Such ring spectra are called complex-oriented. Associated to any complex-oriented ring spectrum $R$ , one can define a graded ( $1$ -dimensional) formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{R}$ over $\pi_{\ast}(R)$ given by $\spf\pi_{\ast}(R^{hS^{1}})=\spf\pi_{\ast}R^{{\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}_{+}}$ .

#### Observation 1.4.5.

Let $R$ be a complex-oriented ring spectrum. A generalization of the derived geometric Satake equivalence along the lines of Theorem 1.3.5 should involve replacing the $1$ -dimensional group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ by a $1$ -dimensional group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{R}$ which is related to the complex-oriented structure of $R$ . If $T$ is a maximal torus of a reductive algebraic group $G$ , the group scheme $T_{\mathbf{G}}:=\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T),\mathbf{G}_{R})$ would play the role of a Cartan subgroup of a “ $\mathbf{G}_{R}$ -deformation” of the group scheme $G$ .

However, the existence of a theory of Chern classes only grants us access to the formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{R}$ , as opposed to an honest $1$ -dimensional algebraic group. (For instance, in the case of periodic complex K-theory $\mathrm{KU}$ , we have $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{KU}}=\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{m}$ , as opposed to the multiplicative group $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ .) As discussed in [Lur1] (motivated by the Atiyah-Segal completion theorem), the data of a decompletion $\mathbf{G}_{R}$ of $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{R}$ can be viewed as an algebraic incarnation of a genuine $S^{1}$ -equivariant analogue $R_{S^{1}}$ of $R$ . Namely, $\mathbf{G}_{R}$ can be understood as the graded group scheme $\spec\pi_{\ast}^{S^{1}}(R_{S^{1}})$ over $\pi_{\ast}(R)$ underlying $\spec R_{S^{1}}$ . Note that the group structure on $\mathbf{G}_{R}$ comes from the coproduct

$$ R_{S^{1}}\to R_{S^{1}\times S^{1}}\xleftarrow{\sim}R_{S^{1}}\otimes_{R}R_{S^{1}}; $$

in particular, it is important that the assignment $T\mapsto R_{T}$ from tori satisfy the Künneth formula. Therefore, one should require the additional data of a genuine equivariant refinement of $R$ in order to answer Question 1.4.4.

#### Remark 1.4.6.

There is in fact a universal example of a complex-oriented ring spectrum, given by complex cobordism $\mathrm{MU}$ . This is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring whose origin is geometric in nature (via cobordism classes of stably almost-complex manifolds), but nevertheless exerts strong control over the $\infty$ -category of spectra (in a sense described below). In similar fashion, there is a universal ring $L_{\ast}$ carrying a $1$ -dimensional formal group equipped with a coordinate; a theorem of Lazard’s shows that $L_{\ast}$ – called the Lazard ring – is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra on infinitely many generators (which encode the coefficients of the group law in the chosen coordinate). In [Qui], Quillen showed the following profound and deeply influential statement:

#### Theorem (Quillen).

The map $L_{\ast}\to\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU})$ classifying the $1$ -dimensional formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{MU}}$ is an isomorphism. In other words, the universal $1$ -dimensional formal group with a coordinate can be identified with the homotopically-defined formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{MU}}$ .

If $G$ is a compact Lie group, there is also a notion of $G$ -equivariant complex cobordism $\mathrm{MU}_{G}$ , defined using equivariant Thom spaces (and not geometrically via equivariant cobordism, thanks to the failure of equivariant transversality); see [Uri] for a survey. However, setting $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{MU}}=\spec\pi_{\ast}^{S^{1}}(\mathrm{MU}_{S^{1}})$ does not produce a $1$ -dimensional group scheme! The problem is precisely the failure of the Künneth formula for the assignment $T\mapsto\mathrm{MU}_{T}$ . Instead, as explained in [Hau], the appropriate structure encoded by the assignment $T\mapsto\mathrm{MU}_{T}$ is that of a graded group law. This is a functor $\mathbf{G}$ from abelian compact Lie groups to graded commutative rings satisfying a certain condition which forces $\spec\mathbf{G}(S^{1})$ to behave like a $1$ -dimensional group scheme over $\mathbf{G}(\ast)$ — but it is not a group scheme in the usual sense. (See Definition 5.3.3 for further discussion.) In [Hau, Theorem C], Hausmann showed that the assignment $T\mapsto\pi_{\ast}^{T}\mathrm{MU}_{T}$ defines the universal graded group law; this can be regarded as an analogue of Quillen’s theorem about $\mathrm{MU}$ .

A positive answer to Question 1.4.4 in the universal case of $\mathrm{MU}$ would therefore suggest that if ${\check{{G}}}$ is a (split) reductive algebraic group (over $\mathbf{Z}$ , say) with a chosen maximal torus ${\check{{T}}}$ , then every graded group law $\mathbf{G}$ defines a “ $\mathbf{G}$ -analogue” ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{G}}$ of ${\check{{G}}}$ , where the role of the Cartan subgroup is played by ${\check{{T}}}_{\mathbf{G}}:=\spec\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}({\check{{T}}}))$ . Unfortunately, I do not know how to define such a $\mathbf{G}$ -analogue. If $\mathbf{G}$ comes from a $1$ -dimensional algebraic group, Setup 1.3.4 suggests defining ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{G}}:=\Hom(\mathbf{G}^{\vee},{\check{{G}}})$ , where $\mathbf{G}^{\vee}$ is the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}$ (but this definition is also somewhat lacking).1212 12 For instance, it cannot be correct if $\mathbf{G}$ is an elliptic curve, since its Cartier dual is the zero group. However, one could instead define the quotient stack ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{G}}/{\check{{G}}}$ as $\mathrm{Map}(\Hom(\mathbf{G},B\mathbf{G}_{m}),B{\check{{G}}})$ ; this, too, is not quite correct in the case of an elliptic curve, but for more subtle reasons. The definition of a graded group law, however, is so general that it is not clear how to define Cartier duals in this context (or even if it should be possible to do so!). Nevertheless, we propose some expectations in Section 5.3 about a putative derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in $\mathrm{MU}$ , but (as the reader will see) we could not make it very far before getting stuck.

#### Remark 1.4.7.

It is quite easy to give a positive answer to Question 1.4.4 in the case of a torus: namely, for any reasonable definition of $T$ -equivariant sheaves of $\mathrm{MU}$ -modules on (ind-finite) $T$ -spaces such that $\mathrm{Shv}_{T}^{c}(\ast;\mathrm{MU})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T_{\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{MU}}})$ , there will be an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{T\times T}^{c}(\mathcal{L}T;\mathrm{MU})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T_{\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{MU}}}\times B{\check{{T}}}). $$

#### Remark 1.4.8.

The sphere spectrum $S^{0}$ is not complex-oriented, so it might not be clear that there should be an analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in $S^{0}$ . Nevertheless, the sphere spectrum admits a “local” complex-orientation, in the sense that the unit map $S^{0}\to\mathrm{MU}$ behaves as an fpqc cover. More precisely, work of Quillen and Landweber-Novikov suggests that rather than considering $\spec\pi_{\ast}(S^{0})$ , it is more appropriate to consider the stack $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ of $1$ -dimensional formal groups equipped with a square root of the dualizing line bundle; the stacky nature of $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ corresponds to the failure of $S^{0}$ to be complex-oriented. This means that studying the dependence of an analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in $\mathrm{MU}$ on the choice of complex orientation should be the first step in understanding some analogue of the derived geometric Satake equivalence with coefficients in $S^{0}$ .

Most of the aforementioned difficulties come from attempting to view the effect of genuine equivariance on (spectral) algebraic geometry. However, some aspects of Langlands duality do not require working with equivariant cohomology. For instance, recall from [Gin2] (see Proposition 5.4.1) that there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{C})\cong U({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{e})$ of Hopf algebras, with $e$ being the principal nilpotent element corresponding to the Chern class of the determinant line bundle $\Omega G\to{\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}$ . In Section 5.4, we prove an analogue of this isomorphism for the sphere spectrum in the case $G=\mathrm{SU}(n)$ . This calculation is rather simple, and it would be interesting to prove an analogue for arbitrary compact Lie groups.

### 1.5. Notation

In writing this article, I discovered that it is extremely easy to fall into grading hell1313 13 Especially as a graduate student!, and escaping it is a painful task; I hope the following list of conventions is helpful to the reader.

#### Notation 1.5.1.

We will always use homological degrees. For instance, if $X$ is a space, a class $x\in\mathrm{H}^{n}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ in cohomology lives in homological degree $-n$ .

#### Notation 1.5.2.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional affine space over a (possibly graded) commutative ring $R$ , so that $V=\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V^{\ast})$ . We will denote $V(n)$ to denote the affine space $V$ with weight $n$ . Then, we have

$$ V(n)\cong\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V(n)^{\ast})\cong\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V^{\ast}(-n)). $$

We will also write $\mathbf{A}^{n}(i_{1},\cdots,i_{n})$ to denote the product $\prod_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{A}^{1}(i_{j})$ .

#### Notation 1.5.3.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional affine space over a (possibly graded) commutative ring $R$ , so that $V=\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V^{\ast})$ . If $n\in\mathbf{Z}$ , we will write $V[n]$ to denote the derived $R$ -scheme which underlies the graded derived $R$ -scheme $V[n](n)=\spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V(n)^{\ast})$ . Note that by Lemma 2.1.6, this definition may not be well-behaved unless $n$ is even (but this will be the case in all examples of interest). Note that

$$ \mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V(n)^{\ast})=\bigoplus_{j\geq 0}\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}V^{\ast}(-nj)=\bigoplus_{j\geq 0}V^{\ast}(-nj)[-nj], $$

so that $V[n](n)$ is the graded derived $R$ -scheme where the coordinate lives in degree $n$ and weight $n$ . More generally, we will make it a point to distinguish between weights and degrees.

#### Notation 1.5.4.

We will write $\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}$ to denote the divided power hull of $\mathbf{G}_{a}$ at the origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}^{\sharp}$ to denote its completion at the divided power filtration.

#### Warning 1.5.5.

Note that $V[n]$ is generally not equivalent to the derived $R$ -scheme $\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V^{\ast}[-n])$ ! For example, suppose $n=-2$ , and say that $V=\mathbf{A}^{1}_{R}$ itself. Then the ring of functions $\mathcal{O}_{V[-2]}$ is the polynomial algebra $R[x]$ with $|x|=2$ , but $\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(V^{\ast}[-n])=\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(R[2])$ is isomorphic to the sheared divided power algebra $\bigoplus_{j\geq 0}\Gamma^{j}_{R}(R)[2j]$ by décalage. Another isomorphism along similar lines is $\mathbf{G}_{a}[2]\cong B^{2}\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}$ . Of course, if $R$ is a $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebra, the two algebras $\mathcal{O}_{V[-2]}$ and $\Sym^{\ast}_{R}(R[2])$ are isomorphic to each other, but it is often (psychologically) safer to not make this assumption.

#### Notation 1.5.6.

If $A$ is a ring spectrum with even homotopy groups, one obtains a graded affine scheme $\spec\pi_{\ast}A$ . In particular, a class $x\in\pi_{n}A$ defines a map $\spec\pi_{\ast}A\to\mathbf{A}^{1}(-n)$ , i.e., lives in weight $n$ . This is somewhat opposed to standard practice in homotopy theory, where a class in $\pi_{2n}A$ lives in weight $n$ (as opposed to our convention, where it has weight $2n$ ).

On the topic of ring spectra: we will often refer to ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -rings where $1\leq n\leq\infty$ ; the reader uninterested in homotopy-coherent subtleties can mostly treat ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -rings as associative (differential graded) algebras, ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings as commutative (differential graded) algebras, and ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -rings as commutative (differential graded) algebras with a Poisson bracket of degree $n-1$ . These replacements are correct for ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebras, but not so otherwise.

#### Notation 1.5.7.

If $G$ is a topological group and $A$ is a ring spectrum, we will sometimes write $A^{hG}$ to denote the cochains $C^{\ast}(BG;A)$ ; this is the homotopy fixed points of the trivial $G$ -action on $A$ . This should be distinguished from the notation $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;A)$ or $A_{G}$ , which will denote the genuine equivariant version of $G$ -equivariant $A$ -cohomology. It differs from $A^{hG}$ by a completion (namely, $A^{hG}$ is the completion of $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;A)$ at the fiber of the map $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;A)\to A$ ).

#### Notation 1.5.8.

If $X$ is a space and $A$ is a ring spectrum, we will on occasion write $A[X]$ to denote the $A$ -chains on $X$ ; so $A[X]=A\otimes\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}X$ . If $G$ acts on $X$ , the notation $A[X]^{hG}$ will denote the homotopy fixed points of $G$ acting on $A[X]$ , so that $A[X]^{hG}$ can be identified with the Borel-equivariant homology $C_{\ast}(X;A)^{hG}$ . Note, also, that what we call equivariant homology does not seem to be the same thing studied in the equivariant homotopy theory literature. For us, Borel-equivariant (say) homology will mean $C_{\ast}(X;A)^{hG}$ . However, the equivariant homotopy theory literature might use the same term to denote $C_{\ast}(X_{hG};A)$ . This poses no problems in cohomology (where $C^{\ast}(X;A)^{hG}=C^{\ast}(X_{hG};A)$ ), but these notions crucially differ in the case of homology. For instance, if $X=\Omega Y$ with $G$ acting on $Y$ through based maps, the homotopy fixed points $C_{\ast}(X;A)^{hG}$ will admit the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ - $A^{hG}$ -algebra, but $C_{\ast}(X_{hG};A)$ will not have any such multiplicative structure (it will generally be a highly divisible $A^{hG}$ -module).

#### Notation 1.5.9.

If $G$ is a compact Lie group acting on a finite space/CW-complex $X$ , we will write $\mathcal{F}_{G}(X)$ to denote the “ $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -cochains of $X$ ”, i.e., $C^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathrm{ku})$ . Its $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -linear dual will be denoted $\mathcal{F}_{G}(X)^{\vee}$ ; this is the “ $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -chains of $X$ ”, i.e., $C^{G}_{\ast}(X;\mathrm{ku})$ . The reader uninterested in $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic generalizations should simply replace $\mathcal{F}_{G}(X)$ by $C^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ , and $\mathcal{F}_{G}(X)^{\vee}$ by $C^{G}_{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ .

#### Notation 1.5.10.

We will often write $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ to denote a localization of the ring of integers. This will essentially always mean that the prime $2$ has been inverted. In some instances, it will denote the localization $\mathbf{Z}[1/|W|]$ obtained by inverting the order of a Weyl group.

#### Notation 1.5.11.

The symbol $\mathrm{HC}$ will denote Hochschild cohomology, and $\mathrm{HH}$ will denote Hochschild homology.

#### Notation 1.5.12.

We will always write a double-slash to mean GIT quotients, and not stacky quotients (which will be denoted by a single slash). For instance, $\mathfrak{g}(2)/\!\!/G=\spec\Sym(\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}(-2))^{G}$ , while $\mathfrak{g}(2)/G$ is a graded stack over $BG$ .

#### Notation 1.5.13.

If $X$ is a scheme over a base ring (often $\mathbf{C}$ ), we will write $X(\!(t)\!)$ to mean the functor $R\mapsto X(R(\!(t)\!))$ (and similarly for $X[\![t]\!]$ ). The exception to this is that when $X=G/H$ is a homogeneous variety, we will sometimes write $X(\!(t)\!)$ to mean $G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!)$ (and similarly $X[\![t]\!]$ to mean $G[\![t]\!]/H[\![t]\!]$ ); this need not be the same as $(G/H)(\!(t)\!)$ , even if $G/H$ is affine.

#### Notation 1.5.14.

On the “geometric”/topological side, we will often write $G$ to mean a compact Lie group, but also use the same symbol to denote its complexification $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ ; the symbol $\mathfrak{g}$ will denote the Lie algebra of the complexification $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ . Whether $G$ denotes the compact Lie group or its complexification should hopefully be clear from context and not cause confusion. For example, the equivariant cohomology $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;k)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G_{\mathbf{C}}}(\ast;k)$ ; and similarly the based loop space $\Omega G$ is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega G_{\mathbf{C}}$ . Sometimes, we will say that $G$ is a compact Lie group and then write symbols such as $G[\![t]\!]$ or $G(\!(t)\!)$ ; these should be understood to mean $G_{\mathbf{C}}[\![t]\!]$ or $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!)$ , respectively.

## 2. Equivariant connective K-theory

### 2.1. Shearing and the Koszul sign rule

The operation of shearing will play a vital role in many of our constructions below. Outside of a few sources like [Lur2] and [Rak, Proposition 3.3.4], there does not seem to be much literature developing this notion from a homotopy-coherent perspective. Let us recall the shearing functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}:\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ as constructed in [Rak, Proposition 3.3.4] (it is denoted there by ${\mathrm{sh}}$ ). Throughout this section, we will let $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ denote the set of integers viewed as a discrete space.

#### Construction 2.1.1.

Recall from the universal property of Day convolution that a lax ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal functor $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ is the same data as a lax ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal functor $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\times\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}$ . Let $f:\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -composite

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\xrightarrow{{\Omega^{2}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}\to\mathrm{BU})}}\mathrm{BU}\times\mathbf{Z}\xrightarrow{{J}}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp}). $$

This defines a lax ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal functor via the composite

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\times\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}=\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\times\Fun(\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}},\mathrm{Sp})\xrightarrow{{f,\mathrm{ev}}}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})\times\mathrm{Sp}\xrightarrow{{\otimes}}\mathrm{Sp}. $$

It is not difficult to see that the lax ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal functor $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ constructed above is in fact a strictly ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal equivalence. This functor will be denoted by $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}$ , and will be called shearing. Explicitly, it sends $M_{\bullet}\mapsto M_{\bullet}[2\bullet]$ , with $\bullet$ denoting the weight.

#### Remark 2.1.2.

In [DHL+, Proposition 3.10], it is shown that the functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}:\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ is in fact a framed ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal functor. However, it cannot be made into an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -monoidal functor (see [DHL+, Remark 3.11]).

Let $\mathrm{MU}$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring of complex cobordism. A first simple observation is the following (the reader uninterested in this generality can simply replace $\mathrm{MU}$ by $\mathbf{Z}$ in the statement).

#### Lemma 2.1.3.

The shearing functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}:\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ admits a natural symmetric monoidal structure.

#### Proof.

The same argument as in Construction 2.1.1 will show that the shearing functor $\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ is symmetric monoidal, as long as the map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\xrightarrow{{f}}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})\to\Pic(\mathrm{MU})$ admits an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -structure. Let $J:\mathrm{BU}\times\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ denote the $J$ -homomorphism, so that $J$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map. Since $\mathrm{MU}$ is the Thom spectrum of the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -composite $\mathrm{BU}\to\mathrm{BU}\times\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\xrightarrow{{J}}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ , it can be understood as the initial ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $R$ equipped with a nullhomotopy of the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $\mathrm{BU}\xrightarrow{{J}}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})\to\Pic(R)$ . In particular, there is a commutative diagram of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -maps:

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{BU}\times\mathbf{Z}=\Omega^{\infty}\mathrm{ku}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{J} \textstyle{\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\simeq\Omega^{\infty}\tau_{\leq 0}\mathrm{ku}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Pic(\mathrm{MU}),} $$

which proves the desired claim. ∎

#### Remark 2.1.4.

One might wonder whether there is also an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal structure on the functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}:\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ which sends $M_{\bullet}\mapsto M_{\bullet}[\bullet]$ . In fact, one can already ask whether there is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal structure on the functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}:\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ which sends $M_{\bullet}\mapsto M_{\bullet}[\bullet]$ . The essential difficulty is that of the Koszul sign rule. Namely, suppose that there was an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal structure on $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}$ . Applying $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}$ to the graded ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebra $\mathbf{Z}[x]$ with $x$ in degree zero and weight $1$ would produce a graded ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra $\mathbf{Z}[w]$ with $w$ in degree $1$ and weight $1$ . The Koszul sign rule forces $w^{2}=-w^{2}$ , i.e., $2w^{2}=0$ , which is a contradiction. This is one of the basic topological reasons for why we will work with evenly-graded objects throughout this article.

#### Notation 2.1.5.

In the remainder of this article, we will write ${\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}(M_{\bullet})$ to denote the underlying ungraded spectrum of $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}(M_{\bullet})=M_{\bullet}[2\bullet]$ .

Let us note the following related result (which is just a fancy restatement of the Koszul sign rule):

#### Lemma 2.1.6.

There is no ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ sending $1\mapsto\mathbf{Z}[1]$ . However, there is a unique ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ sending $1\mapsto S^{1}$ , and hence the method of Construction 2.1.1 produces an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -monoidal structure on the functor $\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}:\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\to\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let us first show that there is a unique ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ sending $1\mapsto S^{1}$ . This is easy, since $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ is the group completion of the free ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -space $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ on a single class: the choice of $S^{1}\in\pi_{0}\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ defines an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ , which factors through $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ since $\Pic(\mathrm{Sp})$ is group-complete.

To show that there is no ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ sending $1\mapsto\mathbf{Z}[1]$ , let us make the following observation. There is an fiber sequence of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -spaces

$$ \tau_{\geq 1}\Pic(\mathbf{Z})=\mathrm{BGL}_{1}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{R}P^{\infty}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})\to\pi_{0}\Pic(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}, $$

where the final $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ is generated by $S^{1}$ . An ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ would give an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -splitting of this fiber sequence, which we claim is impossible. Indeed, let $\picsp(\mathbf{Z})$ denote the connective spectrum delooping $\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ ; then the above fiber sequence deloops to a cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma\mathfrak{gl}_{1}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{F}_{2}[1]\to\picsp(\mathbf{Z})\to\mathbf{Z}. $$

One can use the $J$ -homomorphism and the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $\mathrm{MSO}\to\mathbf{Z}$ to show that $\picsp(\mathbf{Z})\simeq\tau_{\leq 1}\mathrm{ko}$ . (Applying $\Omega^{\infty}$ , this amounts to the identification $\Pic(\mathbf{Z})\simeq(\mathbf{Z}\times\mathrm{BO})/\mathrm{BSO}$ .) Therefore, the boundary map in 2.2 identifies with the first $k$ -invariant of $\mathrm{ko}$ , which is given by the composite

$$ \mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{F}_{2}\xrightarrow{{\mathrm{Sq}^{2}}}\mathbf{F}_{2}[2]. $$

In particular, 2.2 is not split as a cofiber sequence of spectra (this can be viewed as a manifestation of the Koszul sign rule). However, the above description of the boundary map also lets us show that 2.1 does not split as a fiber sequence of ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -spaces. Namely, if 2.1 did split as a fiber sequence of ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -spaces, then the twice-delooped fiber sequence

$$ K(\mathbf{Z}/2,3)\to B^{2}\Pic(\mathbf{Z})\to B^{2}\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}={\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty} $$

would also admit a splitting. But the boundary map ${\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}\to K(\mathbf{Z}/2,4)$ in this fiber sequence represents the generator of $\mathrm{H}^{4}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};\mathbf{Z}/2)$ , which is certainly nonzero. ∎

#### Remark 2.1.7.

There is no ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ sending $1\mapsto\mathbf{Z}[1]$ , because the fiber sequence $\mathbf{R}P^{\infty}\to\Pic(\mathbf{Z})\to\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ of 2.1 does not even split as a map of ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -spaces. Indeed, the ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -bar construction of the classifying map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to K(\mathbf{Z}/2,2)$ of this fibration is already nontrivial (since it defines the nontrivial generator of $\mathrm{H}^{4}({\mathbf{C}P}^{2};\mathbf{Z}/2)$ ).

#### Remark 2.1.8.

Lest Lemma 2.1.6 seem like a problem specific to $\Pic(\mathbf{Z})$ , we note that the same problem persists for $\Pic(\mathbf{Q})$ (as well as for $\Pic(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ with $p>2$ , but not for $\Pic(\mathbf{F}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}$ ). Indeed, the Postnikov fiber sequence for $\picsp(\mathbf{Q})$ is given by

$$ \Sigma\mathfrak{gl}_{1}(\mathbf{Q})=\mathbf{Q}^{\times}[1]\to\picsp(\mathbf{Q})\to\pi_{0}\picsp(\mathbf{Q})=\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}. $$

Recall that $\mathbf{Q}^{\times}\cong\mathbf{Z}/2\oplus\bigoplus_{\text{primes}}\mathbf{Z}$ . Under this identification, the boundary map $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}\to\mathbf{Q}^{\times}[2]$ composes to give the map

$$ \mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{Z}/2[2]\oplus\bigoplus_{\text{primes}}\mathbf{Z}[2]\xrightarrow{{\mathrm{pr}}}\mathbf{Z}/2[2], $$

which identifies with 2.3. Since this composite is not null as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map upon applying $\Omega^{\infty}$ by the argument of Lemma 2.1.6, the map $\Pic(\mathbf{Q})\to\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{ds}}$ does not admit an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -splitting.

#### Remark 2.1.9.

Consider the fully faithful functor $2:\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ which doubles the weight. Then the composite

$$ \mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\xrightarrow{{2}}\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}}\xrightarrow{{\widetilde{\mathrm{sh}}^{1/2}}}\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{gr}} $$

identifies with the usual shearing functor, and hence admits an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal structure.
