#### Lemma 3.1.16.

Let $\mathcal{F}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ be $\ast$ -even, and suppose that the map $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{F})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})$ is surjective for every $\lambda\in P$ . Then the same is true of $i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}$ for any $\mu\in P$ .

Similarly, let $\mathcal{G}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ be $!$ -even, and suppose that the map $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{G})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{G})$ is injective for every $\lambda\in P$ . Then the same is true of $i_{\mu}^{!}\mathcal{G}$ for any $\mu\in P$ .

#### Proof.

The proof for $\mathcal{G}$ is analogous to the proof for $\mathcal{F}$ , so we will only prove the latter. First, it is clear that $i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}$ is $\ast$ -even for any $\mu\in P$ . To prove the surjectivity claim, it evidently suffices to assume that $X_{\lambda}$ is contained in the support of $i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}$ (otherwise $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})=0$ ). Let $\lambda$ be such that $X_{\lambda}$ is contained in $X_{<\mu}=X_{\leq\mu}-X_{\mu}$ , so that $i_{\mu}:X_{<\mu}\hookrightarrow\supp(\mathcal{F})$ is the inclusion. Then, we have maps

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{F})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{<\mu};i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}). $$

The composite is surjective, and hence the map $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{<\mu};i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})$ is surjective. This gives the desired claim, since $j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}\cong j_{\lambda}^{\ast}i_{\mu}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.1.3.

Let us begin by showing that if $\mathcal{F}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ is even, the map $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{F})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F})$ is surjective for every $\lambda\in P$ ; and that if $\mathcal{G}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ is even, the map $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{G})\to\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{G})$ is injective for every $\lambda\in P$ . The claim for $\mathcal{F}$ follows from the fact that it is even, and hence $!$ -even, and the second exact sequence of Lemma 3.1.11. Similarly, the claim for $\mathcal{G}$ follows from the fact that it is even, and hence $\ast$ -even, and the first exact sequence of Lemma 3.1.11.

Let us now prove Theorem 3.1.3. Assume that $\mathcal{F}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ is even, and that $\mathcal{G}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})$ is even. The preceding paragraph implies that the assumptions of Lemma 3.1.15 are satisfied. We will show by induction that the canonical map $\Ext^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})\to\Hom^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathbf{Q})}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{F}),\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{G}))$ is an isomorphism. Let $\lambda\in P$ be such that $X_{\lambda}$ is open in the union of the supports of $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ . There is a map of sequences

$$ \textstyle{\Ext^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X_{<\lambda};\mathbf{Q})}(i_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F},i_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{F})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\alpha} \textstyle{\Hom^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{<\lambda};\mathbf{Q})}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{<\lambda};i_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{F}),\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{<\lambda};i_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{G})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Ext^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathbf{Q})}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\beta} \textstyle{\Hom^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathbf{Q})}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{F}),\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;\mathcal{G}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Ext^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})}(j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{F},j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{G})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\gamma} \textstyle{\Hom^{\bullet}_{\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})}(\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X;j_{\lambda,!}j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{F}),\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{G})).} $$

By Lemma 3.1.10, the left vertical composite is a short exact sequence. By Lemma 3.1.15, the right vertical composite is left exact (i.e., the first map is injective, and it is exact in the middle). By Lemma 3.1.16 and the inductive hypothesis, the map denoted $\alpha$ is a graded isomorphism. The map $\gamma$ is also a graded isomorphism: indeed, since $\mathcal{F}$ is $!$ -even, $j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{F}$ is a direct sum of constant sheaves (in even degrees); similarly, since $\mathcal{G}$ is $\ast$ -even, $j_{\lambda}^{\ast}\mathcal{G}$ is also a direct sum of constant sheaves (in even degrees). In particular, $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};j_{\lambda}^{!}\mathcal{F})$ is a projective $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(X_{\lambda};\mathbf{Q})$ -module, so Lemma 3.1.12(a) implies that the map denoted $\gamma$ is also a graded isomorphism. This implies that the map denoted $\beta$ is also a graded isomorphism, as desired. ∎

### 3.2. Review of derived geometric Satake

Using the results of the preceding section, we will now review an argument for the derived geometric Satake equivalence of [BF1], because it will serve as a model for the arguments appearing later in this article. We will use this as an opportunity to review some facts from geometric representation theory, and to point out some simplifications coming from homotopy theory (see Remark 3.2.23).

#### Setup 3.2.1.

Fix a connected semisimple compact Lie group $G$ throughout this section, and let $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ denote the associated complex algebraic group over $\mathbf{C}$ (so that $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ is a connected semisimple group). Let ${\check{{G}}}$ denote the Chevalley form over $\mathbf{Z}$ of the split semisimple algebraic group (over $\mathbf{Z}$ ) whose root datum is Langlands dual to that of $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ . We will simply write ${\check{{G}}}$ to denote the base-change of ${\check{{G}}}$ to $\mathbf{Q}$ ; the base over which ${\check{{G}}}$ is defined will be clear from context.

Later in this section, we will also fix a Borel subgroup ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ , and write ${\check{{N}}}$ to denote its unipotent radical. Let $\Phi$ denote the set of roots of ${\check{{G}}}$ (i.e., coroots of $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ ), and $\Lambda$ will denote the character lattice of ${\check{{G}}}$ (i.e., cocharacter lattice of $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ ). The choice of ${\check{{B}}}$ defines a subset $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots, and $\Delta\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ will denote a base of simple roots. Let $\Lambda^{+}$ denote the subset of dominant weights of ${\check{{G}}}$ , so that $\Lambda^{+}$ is in (order-preserving) bijection with the set of orbits of the $G$ -action on $\Omega G$ by [Zhu2, Theorem 1.6.1 and Equation 2.1.1]. We will add checks above each of these symbols to denote coroots, positive coroots, and simple coroots, respectively.

#### Definition 3.2.2.

Let $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ denote the $\infty$ -category of $G$ -equivariant sheaves of $\mathbf{Q}$ -modules on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}(\mathbf{C})$ which are constructible for the orbit stratification. More precisely, if we write $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}(\mathbf{C})$ as the direct limit $\colim_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}}\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\leq\lambda}(\mathbf{C})$ of the finite-dimensional $G$ -equivariant Schubert strata $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\leq\lambda}(\mathbf{C})$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}$ , the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ is defined to be the inverse limit $\lim_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}}\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G}^{\leq\lambda}(\mathbf{C});\mathbf{Q})$ along $!$ -pullbacks.

In addition to Theorem 3.1.3, there are two key results needed to prove the derived Satake theorem. The first of these is the following.

#### Theorem 3.2.3 (Abelian geometric Satake, [MV1]).

Let $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G(\mathcal{O})}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ denote the abelian $1$ -category of $G(\mathcal{O})$ -equivariant perverse sheaves on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , so that $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G(\mathcal{O})}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ admits a symmetric monoidal structure arising from convolution on the affine Grassmannian. Then there is a symmetric monoidal equivalence $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G(\mathcal{O})}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ .

#### Remark 3.2.4.

We will not need to spell out the definition of $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G(\mathcal{O})}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ in the remainder of this article; in fact, all that we will need is the consequence that there is a fully faithful functor $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ .

#### Definition 3.2.5.

The action of $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G(\mathcal{O})}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ on $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ via convolution defines, via Theorem 3.2.3, an action of $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ on $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ . Let $\mathrm{IC}_{0}\in\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ denote the pushforward $i_{!}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}$ of the constant sheaf along the inclusion $i:\{\ast\}\hookrightarrow\Omega G$ of the basepoint. Let $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})$ generated by $\mathrm{IC}_{0}$ under the action of $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}})$ .

#### Notation 3.2.6.

Let $2\rho=\sum_{{\check{{\alpha}}}\in{\check{{\Phi}}}^{+}}{\check{{\alpha}}}$ denote the sum of the positive coroots, so that it defines a homomorphism $2\rho:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to{\check{{T}}}$ . The adjoint action defines an action of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ on ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ via $(2-2\rho)$ , which fixes the element $e$ . The adjoint action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ refines to a graded action if ${\check{{G}}}$ is equipped with the grading coming from $2\rho$ . We will only view ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ (resp. ${\check{{G}}}$ ) as a graded scheme via the $(2-2\rho)$ -action (resp. $-2\rho$ -action). To emphasize this, we will denote these graded schemes as ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)$ and ${\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ .

For instance, if ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , the grading equips the entries of an element $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&-a\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ with the gradings where $a$ lives in weight $-2$ , $b$ lives in weight $0$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-4$ ; similarly, the entries an element $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ have the gradings here $a$ and $d$ live in weight $0$ , $b$ lives in weight $2$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-2$ .

We then have (see [BF1]):

#### Theorem 3.2.7 (Derived geometric Satake).

There is a monoidal equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)) $$

of $\mathbf{Q}$ -linear $\infty$ -categories.

#### Remark 3.2.8.

Let us make two comments regarding Theorem 3.2.7.

- (a) The shifts appearing in Theorem 3.2.7 are different than those which appear in [BF1]; this is because Theorem 3.2.7 is stated using the arithmetic shearing of [BZSV, Section 6.7].

- (b) One can wonder about an analogue of Theorem 3.2.7 for sheaves with coefficients in other commutative rings. The discussion in [CR] suggests that there should be an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathbf{Z})\simeq\mathrm{Coh}((\{1\}\times_{{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\{1\})/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}), $$

with ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ being the Chevalley split form of the Langlands dual. Presumably this can be proved using the ideas of [CR]. The $\infty$ -category on the right-hand side of this equivalence is generally not equivalent to $\mathrm{Coh}((\{0\}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\{0\})/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{\ast}[2]/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}})$ ; but such an equivalence will exist after inverting some integer $n$ . 1515 15 Indeed, there is an isomorphism $\{1\}\times_{{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\{1\}\cong\{1\}\times_{\widehat{{\check{{G}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}}\{1\}$ , where $\widehat{{\check{{G}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ denotes the completion of ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ at $1\in{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}}$ . It therefore suffices to show that there is an isomorphism $\widehat{{\check{{G}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}\cong\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ after inverting some integer $n$ , where $\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ denotes the completion of ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ at the origin. For this, it suffices that ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ admit the datum of an ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ -equivariant splitting of the map $\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^{2}={\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}^{\ast}$ , where $\mathcal{I}$ is the ideal sheaf cutting out $\{1\}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ . (Since ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ is smooth, this is exactly the datum of a quasi-logarithm ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[1/n]}$ in the sense of [KV, Section 1.8].) However, such a splitting exists over $\mathbf{Q}$ since $\mathrm{Rep}({\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Q}})$ is semisimple, and hence is defined over $\mathbf{Z}[1/n]$ for some $n\gg 0$ , as desired. Sometimes such a splitting exists without inverting any primes: for example, such a quasi-logarithm exists over $\mathbf{Z}$ for ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ (see [FN, Proposition 6.3]).

To prove Theorem 3.2.7, we need a few ingredients. First, we need to explain the theory of the Kostant slice.

#### Recollection 3.2.9.

Since ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ is semisimple, the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ from the Killing form is a ${\check{{G}}}$ -equivariant isomorphism. This implies that ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ , and the Chevalley restriction theorem gives an isomorphism ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ . In particular, there is an isomorphism $\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ . There is also an ungraded isomorphism $\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ .

This can be upgraded to a graded isomorphism as follows. Let ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)=\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{\mathbf{Q}}({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}(-2))$ denote the $\mathbf{Q}$ -vector space where the coordinate has weight $-2$ . Similarly, let $\mathfrak{t}(2)$ denote $\spec\Sym^{\ast}_{\mathbf{Q}}(\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}(-2))$ denote the $\mathbf{Q}$ -vector space where the coordinate has weight $-2$ . Then, there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathfrak{t}(2)/\!\!/W\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}. $$

#### Definition 3.2.10.

Fix a Borel subgroup ${\check{{B}}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ , and let ${\check{{N}}}$ denote its unipotent radical. Let $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ be a principal nilpotent element, i.e., an element $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}$ such that for each simple root $\alpha\in\Delta$ , the image of $e$ under the following composite is nonzero:

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}\twoheadrightarrow{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}/[{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}},{\check{{\mathfrak{n}}}}]\cong\prod_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathbf{G}_{a}\xrightarrow{{\mathrm{pr}_{\alpha}}}\mathbf{G}_{a}. $$

Let $i:\mathfrak{sl}_{2}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ denote the Lie algebra homomorphism arising from the Jacobson-Morozov theorem, so that $i$ sends $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ to $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ . Let $h\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ denote the image of $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ , and let $f\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ denote the image of $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ , so that $f\in\mathfrak{b}^{-}$ . The adjoint action of $h$ equips $e$ with weight $2$ and $f$ with weight $-2$ . In fact, the adjoint action of $h$ on ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ equips it with a grading where all the weights are even integers.

Let ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}$ denote the centralizer of $f$ in ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ . The Kostant slice is defined to be the affine subspace $\kappa:e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\hookrightarrow{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , so that $\kappa$ is a closed immersion. The grading on ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ via $(2-2\rho)$ restricts to a grading on $e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ .

#### Theorem 3.2.11 (Kostant, [Kos2, Theorem 1.2]).

Fix notation as in Definition 3.2.10, and equip $e+{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{-}$ with the grading coming from the adjoint action of $2-2\rho$ . Then the adjoint action of ${\check{{N}}}^{-}$ on $e+{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{-}$ is one of graded schemes. The natural maps

$$ e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\to(e+{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{-})/{\check{{N}}}^{-}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\leftarrow\mathfrak{t}(2)/\!\!/W $$

are isomorphisms of graded schemes. Moreover, the closed subscheme $e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)$ meets every regular orbit exactly once, and transversally so.

#### Remark 3.2.12.

Thanks to Theorem 3.2.11, we will often abusively view the Kostant slice as a graded map $\kappa:\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W\cong e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , which provides a section to the quotient map ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathfrak{t}/\!\!/W$ .

Motivated by Theorem 3.2.11, we are led to the following definition.

#### Definition 3.2.13.

Let ${\check{{C}}}$ denote the (graded) subgroup scheme of ${\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)$ consisting of those pairs $(g,x)$ such that $x$ is regular and $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)=x$ . Write ${\check{{J}}}$ to denote the fiber product ${\check{{C}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}}(e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f})$ . The projection ${\check{{J}}}\to(e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f})$ equips ${\check{{J}}}$ with the structure of a graded group scheme over $(e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ ; we will call ${\check{{J}}}$ the group scheme of regular centralizers. The fibers of the map ${\check{{J}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ are commutative group schemes, so ${\check{{J}}}$ is a commutative group scheme over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Example 3.2.14.

In classical cases, the group scheme of regular centralizers can be described very explicitly. (The descriptions below are closely related to well-known descriptions of spectral curves in the Hitchin fibration for classical groups.)

- • When ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ , we may identify ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}$ with coordinates $c_{1},\cdots,c_{n}$ . Since a matrix commutes with a regular matrix $x\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ if and only if it can be expressed as a polynomial in $x$ , the Cayley-Hamilton theorem implies that ${\check{{J}}}$ is the group scheme whose fiber over $(c_{1},\cdots,c_{n})$ is given by the group of units in $k[t]/(t^{n}+c_{1}t^{n-1}+\cdots+c_{n})$ . Specifically, any such unit $f(t)$ defines an element of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ by evaluation on $\kappa(c_{1},\cdots,c_{n})$ . Note that the fiber of ${\check{{J}}}$ over $(c_{1},\cdots,c_{n})=(0,\cdots,0)$ is the group of units in $k[t]/t^{n}$ ; this is isomorphic to $\mathbf{G}_{m}\times\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ , where $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ is the (integral) Witt vectors of length $n-1$ . The case of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ leads to explicit descriptions of ${\check{{J}}}$ for other classical groups.

- • If ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ , we may identify ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}$ with coordinates $p_{1},\cdots,p_{n}$ . Observe that $k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n})$ admits the structure of a symplectic vector space: the symplectic pairing sends

$$ (f,g)\mapsto\text{coefficient of }t^{2n-1}\text{ in }f(t)g(-t). $$

Using this, one can view ${\check{{J}}}$ as the group scheme whose fiber over $(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n})$ is the subgroup of those units $f(t)$ in $k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n})$ such that $f(t)^{-1}=f(-t)$ . Note that multiplication by $f(t)$ leaves the above symplectic pairing invariant.

- • If ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ , we may identify ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}$ with coordinates $p_{1},\cdots,p_{n}$ . Observe that $k[t]/(t^{2n+1}+p_{1}t^{2n-1}+\cdots+p_{n}t)$ admits the structure of a quadratic vector space: the associated symmetric bilinear form pairing sends

$$ (f,g)\mapsto\text{coefficient of }t^{2n}\text{ in }f(t)g(-t). $$

Just as above, one can describe ${\check{{J}}}$ as the group scheme whose fiber over $(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n})$ is the subgroup of those units $f(t)$ in $k[t]/(t^{2n+1}+p_{1}t^{2n-1}+\cdots+p_{n}t)$ such that $f(t)^{-1}=f(-t)$ .

- • If ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ , we may identify ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}$ with coordinates $p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n}$ . Observe that $k[t,v]/(tv-c_{n},t^{2n-2}+p_{1}t^{2n-4}+\cdots+p_{n-1}+v^{2})$ admits the structure of a quadratic vector space: the associated symmetric bilinear form sends

$$ (f,g)\mapsto\text{coefficient of }t^{2n-2}\text{ in }f(t,v)g(-t,-v). $$

Using this, one can view ${\check{{J}}}$ as the group scheme whose fiber over $(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n})$ is the subgroup of those units $f(t,v)$ in $k[t,v]/(tv-c_{n},t^{2n-2}+p_{1}t^{2n-4}+\cdots+p_{n-1}+v^{2})$ such that $f(t,v)^{-1}=f(-t,-v)$ .

It is also possible to use the description of the regular centralizer group scheme for $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ to get at ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}$ for exceptional ${\check{{G}}}$ . Here is a fun example:

- • Suppose ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{G}_{2}$ , so that it is the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_{7}$ stabilizing a certain $3$ -form $\phi$ on $\mathbf{A}^{7}$ (this $3$ -form was discovered by Engel and Reichel). If an element of $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}$ , we will set $\lambda_{3}=-(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})$ ; the corresponding matrix in $\mathrm{GL}_{7}$ has eigenvalues $0,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},-\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3}$ . Moreover, the scheme $\mathfrak{g}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{G}_{2}$ can be described as $\spec k[c_{2},c_{6}]$ , where $\displaystyle c_{2}$ $\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2},$ $\displaystyle c_{6}$ $\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}^{2}\lambda_{2}^{2}(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})^{2}.$ If $e_{j}$ denotes the $j$ th elementary symmetric polynomial in the variables $0,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},-\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3}$ , then one directly calculates that

$$ e_{j}=\begin{cases}1&j=0,\\ -2c_{2}&j=2,\\ c_{2}^{2}&j=4,\\ -c_{6}&j=6,\\ 0&j\text{ odd, or }j\geq 8.\end{cases} $$

Therefore, the characteristic polynomial of an element of $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}$ is given by

$$ \chi(t)=t^{7}-2c_{2}t^{5}+c_{2}^{2}t^{3}-c_{6}t. $$

The ring $k[c_{2},c_{6},t]/\chi(t)$ is a free $k[c_{2},c_{6}]$ -module of rank $7$ , and the Engel-Reichel $3$ -form $\phi$ defines a $k[c_{2},c_{6}]$ -linear $3$ -form on $k[c_{2},c_{6},t]/\chi(t)$ . This $3$ -form can be described explicitly, but its description is not very enlightening (at least, to me). One can describe ${\check{{J}}}_{\mathrm{G}_{2}}$ as the group scheme over $\mathfrak{g}_{2}^{\ast}/\!\!/\mathrm{G}_{2}$ whose fiber over $(c_{2},c_{6})$ is given by a certain subgroup of those units $f(t)\in(k[t]/\chi(t))^{\times}\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{7}$ such that the automorphism of $k[t]/\chi(t)$ given by multiplication by $f(t)$ stabilizes the aforementioned $3$ -form.

#### Theorem 3.2.15 ([BFM, YZ]).

There is an isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Q})\cong{\check{{J}}} $$

of commutative graded group schemes over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ .

#### Remark 3.2.16.

Suppose $G$ is simply-connected. The Borel-completion of $\mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Q})$ is simply $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Q}[\Omega G]^{hG}$ , which is Koszul dual to $\mathbf{Q}[G]$ acting on $\mathbf{Q}[\Omega G]$ . According to rational homotopy theory, this can in turn be viewed as a deformation of $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Q}[\Omega G]$ along $\{0\}\hookrightarrow\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Q}^{hG}\cong\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}(2)}/\!\!/W$ . But $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Q}[\Omega G]$ can be identified with the universal enveloping algebra $U(\pi_{\ast}(\Omega G)_{\mathbf{Q}})$ , which is isomorphic to the dual Lie algebra $({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{e})^{\ast}$ by Theorem 3.2.15 (or Proposition 5.4.1). Theorem 3.2.15 implies that the relevant deformation of $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Q}[\Omega G]$ along $\{0\}\hookrightarrow\widehat{{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}(2)}/\!\!/W$ is precisely the relative enveloping algebra of Lie algebra of (the completion of) ${\check{{J}}}$ .

#### Corollary 3.2.17 ([Ngo]).

The classifying stack $B_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{J}}}$ is isomorphic to the stacky quotient ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ . In particular, there is a graded isomorphism

$$ ({\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho))/{\check{{J}}}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2-2\rho)^{\mathrm{reg}}. $$

#### Proof.

For notational simplicity, let us drop the gradings. By definition of ${\check{{J}}}$ , the classifying stack $B_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{J}}}$ is a $1$ -stack whose objects given by the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of the Kostant slice $e+{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{f}\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , and such that an isomorphism $x\xrightarrow{{\sim}}y$ is given by an element $g\in{\check{{G}}}$ such that $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)=y$ . By Theorem 3.2.11, the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of the Kostant slice is precisely ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ , so we obtain the desired result. ∎

### 3.3. Spherical varieties

In this section, we will review some of the theory of spherical varieties. Since the examples we will study in this article are rather simple (from the perspective of representation theory), we do not, strictly speaking, need the general theory. However, the recollections of this section will nevertheless be useful in placing basic phenomena that we will observe later into a broader context (see Section 3.4).

We will not give any proofs in this section, but instead refer to [BLV, LV, Tim, BZSV] for details; in particular, this section is not intended to be an introduction to the theory of spherical varieties or to the theory of their Hamiltonian duals. (Instead, the reader should see [Per] for a very readable introduction to spherical varieties.) The base field in this section will always be the complex numbers, $G$ will always be a connected reductive algebraic group over $\mathbf{C}$ , $B\subseteq G$ will denote a chosen Borel subgroup, and $N$ will be its unipotent radical.

#### Definition 3.3.1.

A subgroup $H\subseteq G$ is called spherical if any of the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

- (a) For any $G$ -variety $X$ and any $H$ -fixed point $x\in X$ , the closure $\overline{G\cdot x}$ contains finitely many $G$ -orbits.

- (b) There are finitely many $H$ -orbits in the flag variety $G/B$ of $G$ .

- (c) There is an open $H$ -orbit in $G/B$ .

- (d) The action of $B$ on $G/H$ has an open dense orbit.

An irreducible $G$ -variety $X$ is called spherical if it is normal and admits a dense open $B$ -orbit ${X}^{\circ}\subseteq X$ . In this case, $X$ also contains an open $G$ -orbit given by $G\cdot{X}^{\circ}$ . If $x\in{X}^{\circ}$ and $H$ is its stabilizer, there is an isomorphism ${X}^{\circ}=G/H$ , and $H$ is a spherical subgroup of $G$ .

Before delving into examples, let us mention that the condition of being a spherical $G$ -variety is relevant for our purposes because of the following result:

#### Theorem 3.3.2 ([GN1, Theorem 3.2.1]).

Let $H\subseteq G$ be a subgroup. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

- (a) $G/H$ is a spherical $G$ -variety.

- (b) The group $H(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ acts on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}(\mathbf{C})=G(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))/G(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ with countably many orbits.

- (c) The group $G(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ acts on $(G/H)(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ with countably many orbits.

#### Remark 3.3.3.

We refer the reader to [GN1] for a proof of Theorem 3.3.2, but since the argument is so short, let us recall why (b) implies (a). Suppose $\lambda:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to G$ is a subgroup, so that we obtain a point $x_{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Gr}_{G}(\mathbf{C})$ . Then the $G$ -orbit $X_{\lambda}=G\cdot x_{\lambda}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ is a flag variety of $G$ , and by (b), the number of $H(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ -orbits intersecting $X_{\lambda}$ is countable. This implies that there is an $H(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ -orbit which intersects $X_{\lambda}$ in an open set. If we choose a point $y\in X_{\lambda}$ in this open set, this implies that there is a surjection $\mathfrak{h}\twoheadrightarrow T_{y}X_{\lambda}$ . If $\mathfrak{p}_{y}$ is the Lie algebra of the parabolic subgroup of $G$ stabilizing $y$ , the tangent space $T_{y}X_{\lambda}$ can be identified with $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{p}_{y}$ . In particular, if we choose $\lambda$ to be regular, $\mathfrak{p}_{y}$ is isomorphic to a Borel subalgebra $\mathfrak{b}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}$ , and hence there is a surjection $\mathfrak{h}\twoheadrightarrow\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{b}$ . But this implies that $H$ has an open orbit in $G/B$ , so $H$ is spherical.

There are a lot of examples of spherical varieties: it includes the class of flag varieties, symmetric spaces (essentially by the Iwasawa decomposition), and toric varieties.

#### Example 3.3.4.

The quotient $\mathrm{GL}_{n}/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ is an affine spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ -variety; it is isomorphic to the variety $\{(x,V)\in\mathbf{C}^{n+1}\times\mathrm{Gr}_{n}(\mathbf{C}^{n+1})|x\not\in V\}$ . The fact that the $\mathbf{C}$ -points of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ is homotopy equivalent to $S^{2n-1}$ motivates the terminology “spherical”.

#### Example 3.3.5.

As mentioned above, any symmetric space is a spherical variety. In particular, since $G$ is the fixed points of the involution on $G\times G$ which swaps the two factors, we see that $G\cong(G\times G)/G^{\Delta}$ is a spherical $G\times G$ -variety. This will often be called the group case.

#### Example 3.3.6.

Suppose $G=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . Since the flag variety of $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ , a subgroup $H\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is spherical if and only if it has an open orbit in $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ . This is equivalent to saying that it is a subgroup of positive dimension. It is not difficult to see that all positive-dimensional subgroups of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ can be conjugated either to $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ itself, the diagonal torus $\mathbf{G}_{m}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , its normalizer $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(\mathbf{G}_{m})\cong\mathrm{PO}_{2}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , or $S\cdot N\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , where $N$ is the strictly upper-triangular matrices and $S\subseteq\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . In general, a spherical subgroup $H\subseteq G$ is called horospherical if $H$ contains the unipotent radical of the Borel $B\subseteq G$ ; the motivation for this term being, of course, that horocycles in $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbf{R})/\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ are orbits of the subgroup of strictly upper-triangular matrices in $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ . These kinds of spherical varieties are not considered in the present article.

#### Warning 3.3.7.

If $G$ is a semisimple algebraic group and $T\subseteq G$ is a maximal torus, the quotient $G/T$ is generally not a spherical $G$ -variety. Indeed, there generally will not be an open dense $T$ -orbit in $G/B$ , since $|\Phi^{-}|$ is often larger than $\mathrm{rank}(T)$ , where $\Phi^{-}$ is the set of negative roots of $G$ . For instance, although the quotient $\mathrm{SL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ is a spherical $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -variety, the quotient $\mathrm{SL}_{3}/T$ is not a spherical $\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ -variety.

#### Remark 3.3.8.

There is a finite list of closed connected spherical subgroups of simple algebraic groups: see [KR, Kra].

#### Example 3.3.9.

Let $G$ be a torus $T$ . Then a $T$ -variety $X$ is spherical if it is normal and contains a dense orbit, and hence is precisely an affine toric variety. Let $\Lambda$ denote the monoid of weights of $T$ . Note that $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ is a $T$ -submodule of $\mathcal{O}_{T}$ , and so $\mathcal{O}_{X}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in S_{X}}\mathbf{C}_{\lambda}$ for some subset $S_{X}\subseteq\Lambda$ . A standard fact from the theory of affine toric varieties is that a subset $S_{X}\subseteq\Lambda$ arises from an affine toric variety if and only if $S_{X}=C\cap\Lambda$ for some convex cone $C\subseteq\Lambda_{\mathbf{R}}$ generated by finitely many elements of $\Lambda$ which span $\Lambda_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Equivalently, if ${\check{{C}}}\subseteq{\check{{\Lambda}}}$ denotes the dual cone, one observes that $C$ spans $\Lambda_{\mathbf{R}}$ if and only if ${\check{{C}}}$ is strictly convex (i.e., contains no line). Therefore, affine toric varieties are classified by strictly convex rational polyhedral cones of ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{\mathbf{R}}$ .

Example 3.3.9 is the first indication that certain spherical varieties admit interesting combinatorial data. In particular, this combinatorial data will be useful in defining the Langlands dual group to a spherical variety. We will recall some generalities on defining this dual group below, and then explain its manifestation in examples.

To define this dual group following [SV], let us now suppose that $X$ is a homogeneous quasi-affine spherical $G$ -variety. In this case, if ${X}^{\circ}\subseteq X$ is the open $B$ -orbit, we will write $H$ to be the stabilizer of a point ${X}^{\circ}(\mathbf{C})$ , so that $X=G/H$ and $B\cdot H\subseteq G$ is open.

#### Construction 3.3.10.

Let $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})$ denote the fraction field of $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ , and let $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{(B)}$ denote the subset of $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})-\{0\}$ consisting of the nonzero rational $B$ -eigenfunctions. Then the lattice $\mathcal{X}_{X}$ is simply the group of $B$ -eigencharacters, and there is an exact sequence

$$ 1\to\mathbf{C}^{\times}\to\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{(B)}\to\mathcal{X}_{X}\to 1; $$

in other words, for a fixed $\lambda\in\mathcal{X}_{X}$ , the functions $f\in\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{(B)}$ which are $\chi$ -eigenvectors are all proportional by a scalar in $\mathbf{C}^{\times}$ (this follows from $X$ being spherical). Let $\Lambda_{X}$ denote the dual lattice to $\mathcal{X}_{X}$ . Then $\Lambda_{X}$ defines a torus $T_{X}$ , and we will write $\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ to denote $\Lambda_{X}\otimes\mathbf{Q}$ . The rank of the lattice $\Lambda_{X}$ (which is also the rank of $\mathcal{X}_{X}$ ) is called the rank of $X$ .

#### Remark 3.3.11.

Suppose $X=G/H$ is a homogeneous quasi-affine $G$ -variety, and let $\mathcal{X}_{X}=\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{(B)}/\mathbf{C}^{\times}$ as above. It is not difficult to see that $X$ is spherical if and only if $\mathcal{X}_{X}$ is a lattice of finite rank. If $K$ is a maximal compact subgroup of $G(\mathbf{C})$ , [Akh2] shows that

$$ \mathrm{rank}(X)=\dim(K\backslash X(\mathbf{C})). $$

This is a purely topological description of the rank of $X$ .

#### Construction 3.3.12.

The stabilizer of the open $B$ -orbit ${X}^{\circ}\subseteq X$ is a parabolic subgroup $P(X)$ . We will write $L(X)$ to denote the Levi quotient of $P(X)$ ; it will often be viewed as a subgroup of $P(X)$ when convenient. Let $T$ be a maximal torus of $B\cap L(X)$ ; then the torus $T_{X}$ from above can be identified with $T/(T\cap B)$ . The $T_{X}$ -orbit of a point in the open $B$ -orbit ${X}^{\circ}(\mathbf{C})$ defines an embedding $T_{X}\hookrightarrow{X}^{\circ}(\mathbf{C})$ . In other words, the $B$ -action on ${X}^{\circ}$ defines a $T$ -action on ${X}^{\circ}/\!\!/N=\spec\mathcal{O}_{X}^{N}$ , and this $T$ -action factors through the quotient $T\twoheadrightarrow T_{X}$ .

#### Remark 3.3.13.

In [Kno1, Lemma 3.1], Knop showed that if $X$ is quasi-affine, the set of coroots in the span of $\Delta_{L(X)}$ in $\Lambda$ is precisely the set of coroots ${\check{{\alpha}}}\in\Lambda$ which are perpendicular to $\Lambda_{X}$ .

#### Construction 3.3.14.

Suppose $v:\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{\times}\to\mathbf{Q}$ is a discrete valuation which is trivial on $\mathbf{C}^{\times}$ . Then the restriction of $v$ to $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_{X})^{(B)}$ defines a homomorphism $\Lambda_{X}\to\mathbf{Q}$ , i.e., a point of $\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ . It is known that the map from $G$ -invariant valuations to $\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ is an injection, and so we will write $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ to denote the subspace of $G$ -invariant valuations. Let ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}^{+}$ denote the intersection $\Lambda_{X}\cap\mathcal{V}$ of $G$ -invariant $\mathbf{Z}$ -valued valuations.

It turns out that the subset $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ is a fundamental domain for the Weyl group $W_{X}$ of a root system in $\Lambda$ (where the weight lattice is $\Lambda_{X}$ ). In other words, the reflections over faces of $\mathcal{V}$ of codimension $1$ generate a finite reflection subgroup $W_{X}\subseteq\mathrm{GL}(\mathfrak{t}_{X})$ , and this Weyl group $W_{X}$ is called the little Weyl group of $X$ . One can canonically identify $W_{X}$ with a subgroup of $W$ which normalizes the Weyl group $W_{L(X)}$ of $L(X)$ (with respect to the chosen torus $T$ ).

#### Remark 3.3.15.

The definition of the little Weyl group given above does not immediately relate to the microlocal nature of $X$ . In [Kno1, Kno2], Knop gave an alternative construction of $W_{X}$ using the Hamiltonian $G$ -action on $T^{\ast}X$ . Very briefly, let us review this construction. The quotient map $\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h}$ defines an inclusion $(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h})^{\ast}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}$ , and we will denote this by $\mathfrak{h}^{\perp}$ (it can be viewed as a subspace of $\mathfrak{g}$ via the isomorphism $\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{g}$ given by the Killing form). Consider the moment map $\mu:T^{\ast}X\cong(G\times\mathfrak{h}^{\perp})/H\to\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}$ of the Hamiltonian $G$ -action on $T^{\ast}X$ . Composing with the characteristic polynomial map $\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}\to\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}/\!\!/G\cong\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}/\!\!/W$ defines a map $T^{\ast}X\to\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}/\!\!/W$ . Observe also that the quotient map $T\twoheadrightarrow T_{X}$ induces an inclusion $\mathfrak{t}_{X}^{\ast}\hookrightarrow\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}$ .

Fix a character $\chi:T_{X}\to\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . Then, there is a $(P(X),\chi)$ -eigenfunction $f_{\chi}\in\mathcal{O}_{{X}^{\circ}}$ (unique up to scalar multiplication) defines a section $d\mathrm{log}(f_{\chi}):{X}^{\circ}\to T^{\ast}{X}^{\circ}$ . This section is independent of the choice of $f_{\chi}$ , since $f_{\chi}$ is unique up to scalar multiplication. Ranging over all characters $\chi$ , one obtains a map $\mathfrak{t}_{X}^{\ast}\times{X}^{\circ}\to T^{\ast}{X}^{\circ}$ . If $\mathcal{P}$ denotes the set of conjugates of the parabolic subgroup $P(X)$ , we further obtain a map $\mathfrak{t}_{X}^{\ast}\times(\mathcal{P}\times{X}^{\circ})\to T^{\ast}X$ . Knop showed that the image of this map is dense, and that there is an isomorphism $(T^{\ast}X)/\!\!/G\cong\mathfrak{t}_{X}^{\ast}/\!\!/W_{X}$ . Said slightly differently, the fiber product $T^{\ast}X\times_{\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}/\!\!/W}\mathfrak{t}^{\ast}$ generally has multiple irreducible components. If $C$ is an irreducible component which dominates $T^{\ast}X$ , we obtain a covering $C\to T^{\ast}X$ , and $W_{X}$ is the Galois group of this covering. In particular, note that this construction describes $W_{X}$ as a subquotient of $W$ . (However, there is in fact a canonical embedding $W_{X}\hookrightarrow W$ .)

In [Kno2], Knop reinterpreted the above construction as follows: if $\mathcal{O}_{B}(X)$ is the set of $B$ -orbits in $X$ , Knop constructed an action of $W$ on $\mathcal{O}_{B}(X)$ . There is a canonical bijection between $\mathcal{O}_{B}(X)$ and the set of irreducible components of $T^{\ast}X\times_{\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}$ (given by taking the conormal bundle), where $\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}$ is the Grothendieck-Springer resolution. The action of $W$ on $\mathcal{O}_{B}(X)$ can be understood as arising from the action of the Steinberg scheme $\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}\times_{\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}$ by convolution and the isomorphism of [CG, Theorem 3.4.1]. In any case, the stabilizer of the open $B$ -orbit is isomorphic to $W_{X}\ltimes W_{L(X)}$ . A related result was proved in [Res]: namely, if $H\subseteq G$ is a reductive spherical subgroup and $X=G/H$ , the Weyl group of $H$ can be recovered as the stabilizer inside $W$ of a(ny) minimal rank $B$ -orbit on $X$ viewed as an element of $\mathcal{O}_{B}(X)$ .

#### Remark 3.3.16.

Continuing Theorem 3.3.2, one can show (see [LV, Proposition 4.10] or [GN1, Theorem 3.2.1]) that the $G(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbits on $(G/H)(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ are in bijection with $H(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ -orbits on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}(\mathbf{C})$ , which in turn are in bijection with ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}/W_{X}\cong{\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}^{+}$ . This generalizes the Cartan decomposition, in the sense that when applied to the group case of Example 3.3.5, it recovers the standard parametrization of the $G(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbits on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . The bijection between $G(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbits on $(G/H)(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ and ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}^{+}$ sends a map $\lambda:\mathcal{O}_{G/H}\to\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!)$ to the valuation given by the composite

$$ \mathcal{O}_{G/H}\to\mathcal{O}_{G/H}\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}\mathcal{O}_{G}\xrightarrow{{\lambda}}\mathcal{O}_{G}(\!(t)\!)\xrightarrow{{v_{t}}}\mathbf{Z}. $$

This is a $G$ -invariant discrete valuation of $\mathcal{O}_{G/H}$ ,

#### Construction 3.3.17.

Let $\mathcal{V}^{\perp}$ denote the cone $\{\chi\in\mathfrak{t}_{X}^{\ast}|\langle{\chi,v}\rangle\leq 0\text{ for each }v\in\mathcal{V}\}$ . Let $\Sigma_{X}$ denote the set of generators of intersections of extremal rays of $\mathcal{V}^{\perp}$ with $\Lambda_{X}$ . It turns out that the elements of $\Sigma_{X}$ are linearly independent; they are known as the spherical roots of $X$ . In fact, they form the set of simple roots of the based root system mentioned in Construction 3.3.14.

#### Remark 3.3.18.

It turns out that for each spherical root $\gamma\in\Sigma_{X}$ , there is some element $n\in\{\tfrac{1}{2},1,2\}$ such that $\gamma^{\prime}=n\gamma$ is either a positive root of $G$ , or is the sum $\alpha+\beta$ of two positive roots which are orthogonal to each other and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are elements of some system of simple roots. These simple roots need not correspond to the choice of $B$ ! Let $\Delta_{X}$ denote the set $\{\gamma^{\prime}|\gamma\in\Sigma_{X}\}$ ; then $\Delta_{X}$ is called the set of normalized spherical roots. Moreover, if $\Phi_{X}$ denotes the set of $W_{X}$ -translates of $\Delta_{X}$ , it is shown in [SV, Proposition 2.2.1] that the pair $(\Phi_{X},W_{X})$ defines a root system (called the normalized spherical root system of $X$ ) where $\Delta_{X}$ forms a set of simple roots. Let $({\check{{\Phi}}}_{X},W_{X})$ denote the dual root system, and ${\check{{\Delta}}}_{X}$ the set of simple coroots.

#### Theorem 3.3.19 ([SV, Proposition 2.2.2], [KS]).

Suppose that $\Sigma_{X}$ does not contain any elements of the form $2\alpha$ for $\alpha$ being a root of $G$ . Then, $(\Lambda_{X},\Phi_{X},{\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X},{\check{{\Phi}}}_{X})$ forms a root datum, with associated split complex reductive group $G_{X}$ .

#### Definition 3.3.20.

Let ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ denote the complex reductive group with maximal torus ${\check{{T}}}_{X}$ with root datum given by the dual of that of Theorem 3.3.19. We will refer to ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ as the (Langlands) dual group of $X$ . It admits a morphism to ${\check{{G}}}$ . Also see [GN1, KS].

#### Example 3.3.21.

As in Example 3.3.5, if $X=G$ is viewed as a spherical $G\times G$ -variety, the group ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ is simply the Langlands dual ${\check{{G}}}$ of $G$ itself.

#### Example 3.3.22 (Spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ -varieties).

Recall the classification of spherical subgroups $H\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ from Example 3.3.6. Let us describe the root datum of $X=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/H$ from Theorem 3.3.19 in each case.

- (a) If $H=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , the quotient $X$ is a point, and everything is trivial.

- (b) If $H=\mathbf{G}_{m}$ , the orbits of $B$ on $X$ are the same as orbits of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ on $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ . There are therefore three orbits, given by $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (the open orbit) and the points $0$ and $\infty$ . To describe the spherical roots, let us instead consider $\mathrm{SL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{1})-\mathbf{P}^{1}_{\mathrm{diag}}$ . Note that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\cong\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}V_{n\alpha}$ , where $\alpha$ is the positive root of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $V_{n\alpha}$ is the representation with highest weight $n$ . It follows that $\Lambda_{X}\cong\mathbf{Z}$ , generated by $\alpha$ . A little calculation implies that $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathfrak{t}_{X}$ identifies with $\{v\in\mathfrak{t}_{X}|\langle{v,\alpha}\rangle\leq 0\}$ . This implies that $\Sigma_{X}=\Delta_{X}=\{\alpha\}$ , and so ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . If we worked with $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ instead, we would find that ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

- (c) If $H=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(\mathbf{G}_{m})$ , the sublattice $\Lambda_{X}\subseteq\Lambda_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ has index two. In particular, by (b) above, we see that $\Lambda_{X}=\mathbf{Z}\cdot 2\alpha$ , and $\Sigma_{X}=\{2\alpha\}$ . In particular, Theorem 3.3.19 does not apply to this particular case.

- (d) If $H=S\cdot N\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , the orbits of $B$ on $X$ are the same as orbits of $H$ on $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ . There are therefore two orbits, given by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (the open orbit) and the point $\infty$ . Let us assume for simplicity that $S=\{1\}$ . Again, $\Lambda_{X}\cong\mathbf{Z}$ , and one now calculates that $\Sigma_{X}$ is empty. One therefore finds that ${\check{{G}}}_{X}={\check{{T}}}$ . In general, the dual group of horospherical varieties is the Cartan subgroup.

The cases (b), (c), and (d) above are known as types $T$ , $N$ , and $U$ . The spherical $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\times\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ (i.e., the group case of Example 3.3.5) is known as type $G$ .

#### Remark 3.3.23.

If $\alpha$ is a simple root of $G$ (or $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are two orthogonal simple roots of $G$ ) and $P_{\alpha}$ (or $P_{\alpha\beta}$ ) is the associated parabolic subgroup, then the spherical variety ${X}^{\circ}P_{\alpha}/U_{P_{\alpha}}$ is isomorphic to one of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/T$ for $T$ being a torus, $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(T)$ , or $(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\times\mathrm{PGL}_{2})/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}$ . Correspondingly, the unique element of $\Sigma_{X}$ is a normalized spherical root, and its type is as defined in Example 3.3.22. In particular, the condition of Theorem 3.3.19 asks that $X$ have no normalized spherical root of type $N$ .

#### Remark 3.3.24.

Assume from now on that $X$ does not have any spherical roots of type $N$ . As in [SV, Section 3.6], the embedding ${\check{{G}}}_{X}\hookrightarrow{\check{{G}}}$ commutes with the image of a principal $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to{\check{{L}}}(X)$ . In particular, there is a map $\iota:{\check{{G}}}_{X}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to{\check{{G}}}$ such that upon restriction to the diagonal torus $\mathbf{G}_{m}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , the map $\mathbf{G}_{m}\to{\check{{L}}}(X)$ is given by $2\rho_{L(X)}=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}_{L(X)}}\alpha$ (regarded as a coweight of ${\check{{G}}}$ ). Since we will mainly deal with spherical varieties of rank $1$ below, where ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ itself will sometimes be $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , we will distinguish the $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ above with a superscript: namely, we will write it as $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ .

### 3.4. Whittaker induction and [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]

In this section, we will review the notion of Whittaker induction (following [BZSV, Section 3.4]), and the statement of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]. This construction takes as input a map $H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ and produces a functor from Hamiltonian $H$ -spaces to Hamiltonian $G$ -spaces. We warn the reader that our notation will differ slightly from that of [BZSV, Section 3.4].

#### Recollection 3.4.1.

A Hamiltonian $G$ -space is a smooth symplectic variety $M$ (with symplectic form $\omega$ ) equipped with a Hamiltonian $G$ -action (i.e., the map $i:\mathfrak{g}\to T_{M}$ given by the derivative of the $G$ -action lands in the subspace of Hamiltonian vector fields on $M$ ). The moment map $\mu:M\to\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}$ is characterized by the property that for each $x\in\mathfrak{g}$ , we have $d\langle{\mu,x}\rangle=\langle{i(x),\omega}\rangle$ . We will often simply specify a Hamiltonian $G$ -space as the pair $(M,\omega)$ along with its moment map. There will frequently be a grading present, which we encode by an action of $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{rot}}$ on $M$ , $G$ , and $\omega$ . We will say that $(M,\omega,\mu:M\to\mathfrak{g}^{\ast})$ is a graded Hamiltonian $G$ -space (for a given $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action on $G$ ) if $M$ has a $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action which acts on $\omega$ with weight $2$ , and the moment map $\mu$ is $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -equivariant.

Let us review the basic example of Whittaker induction.

#### Example 3.4.2.

Let $G$ be a connected reductive group (over $\mathbf{C}$ ), and let $e\in\mathfrak{g}$ be a principal nilpotent element, so that the Jacobson-Morozov theorem produces a map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ . Let $H$ be the trivial group, and let $M$ denote the trivial Hamiltonian $H$ -space. Then the Whittaker induction of $M$ along the map $\iota:\{1\}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ is given by $\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)=(e+\mathfrak{b}^{-})\times^{N^{-}}G$ , where $N^{-}$ is the unipotent radical of the opposite Borel subgroup $B^{-}$ corresponding to $e$ , and $\mathfrak{b}^{-}$ is the Lie algebra of $B^{-}$ . Note that Theorem 3.2.11 gives isomorphisms

$$ \mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)/G\cong(e+\mathfrak{b}^{-})/N^{-}\cong\mathfrak{g}/\!\!/G. $$

Let us now describe the construction in general.

#### Construction 3.4.3.

Suppose we are given a map $H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ of reductive algebraic groups over $\mathbf{C}$ such that $H$ centralizes the map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ . Let $f\in\mathfrak{g}$ be the image of $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ inside $\mathfrak{g}$ . The action of $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ defines a decomposition

$$ \mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{z}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\oplus\overline{\mathfrak{n}}\oplus\mathfrak{n}_{0}\oplus\mathfrak{n}, $$

where $\mathfrak{z}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ is the centralizer of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to\mathfrak{g}$ , and $\overline{\mathfrak{n}}$ , $\mathfrak{n}_{0}$ , and $\mathfrak{n}$ are the negative, zero, and positive weight spaces. Let $N$ denote the associated unipotent subgroup of $G$ . Note that all the weights of the $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ -action on $\mathfrak{g}$ are integers, and that $e\in\mathfrak{n}$ . Note that the orthogonal complement to $\mathfrak{z}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}$ is a Levi subalgebra $\mathfrak{l}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}$ . Let $L\subseteq G$ denote the associated subgroup.

Let $\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ denote the subspace of ${\mathfrak{n}}$ of elements with weight $\geq 2$ , and let $N_{+}$ denote the associated unipotent subgroup. One can then equip ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ with the structure of a Hamiltonian $H{N}$ -space. There is an $H$ -invariant symplectic form $\omega$ on ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ , given by $\omega(x,y)=\langle{f,[x,y]}\rangle$ .1919 19 Note that this symbol is well-defined: if $x\in\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ , then $[x,y]$ lives in weight $\geq 3$ , so $\langle{f,[x,y]}\rangle=0$ since $f$ has weight $-2$ . Moreover, this form is indeed nondegenerate: if $x\in{\mathfrak{n}}$ is nonzero of weight $1$ , then $[f,x]$ is a nonzero element of weight $-1$ . This implies that there is some $y\in{\mathfrak{n}}$ of weight $1$ such that $\langle{[f,x],y}\rangle=\langle{f,[x,y]}\rangle$ is nonzero, as desired. Since $H$ preserves $\omega$ , we obtain a homomorphism $H\to\mathrm{Sp}({\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+})$ , and hence a map $\mathfrak{h}\to\mathfrak{sp}_{{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}}$ . The group $H$ acts on ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ by the adjoint action. Moreover, the group ${N}$ acts on ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\cong{N}/N_{+}$ via translation. The moment map $\mu:{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\to\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}\oplus{\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}$ is defined as follows:

- • The map ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\to\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}$ is adjoint to the map

$$ {\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\oplus\mathfrak{h}\to{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\oplus\mathfrak{sp}_{{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}}\xrightarrow{{(x,g)\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\omega(gx,x)}}\mathfrak{g}_{a}. $$

- • The map ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\to\mathfrak{n}^{\ast}$ is given by the composite

$$ {\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}\xrightarrow{{\omega}}({\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+})^{\ast}\xrightarrow{{x\mapsto f+x}}{\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}. $$

Here, $f$ is viewed as an element of ${\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}$ via the identification ${\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{n}$ . Under this isomorphism, the image of ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ inside $\mathfrak{n}$ is simply $f+\mathfrak{n}_{1}$ , where $\mathfrak{n}_{1}$ is the weight $1$ eigenspace.

#### Remark 3.4.4.

There is a natural grading defined on ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ , as well as a natural $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action on ${N}$ via the conjugation action of $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ . If $H$ is equipped with the trivial $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action, the Hamiltonian $H{N}$ -space ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ from Construction 3.4.3 can be viewed as a graded Hamiltonian $H{N}$ -space.

#### Definition 3.4.5.

Fix a map $\iota:H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ of reductive algebraic groups over $\mathbf{C}$ such that $H$ centralizes the map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ . The conjugation action of $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{Arth}}$ on $G$ composed with the square character equips $G$ with a grading (which we will think of as a $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action). Let $M$ be a graded Hamiltonian $H$ -space. Then the Whittaker induction $\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)$ is defined as

$$ \mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)=(M\times{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+})\times^{H{N}}_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}\oplus{\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}}(T^{\ast}G), $$

where $T^{\ast}G$ is regarded as a Hamiltonian $H{N}$ -space via restriction along $H{N}\subseteq G$ . There is a natural grading on $\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)$ , coming from the grading on $M$ , the grading on ${\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+}$ from Remark 3.4.4, and the grading on $T^{\ast}G$ coming from the $\mathbf{G}_{m,\mathrm{gr}}$ -action on $G$ . In particular, note that there is an isomorphism of stacks

$$ \mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)/G\cong((M\times{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+})\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}\oplus{\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}}\mathfrak{g}^{\ast})/H{N}. $$

The simplest way to understand Whittaker induction in the case when $M$ is a symplectic $H$ -representation is as follows.

#### Lemma 3.4.6 ([BZSV, Section 3.4.8]).

Suppose $M$ is a symplectic $H$ -representation, and fix an isomorphism $\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{g}$ . Then there is an isomorphism of stacks

$$ \mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)/G\cong(M\oplus(\mathfrak{h}^{\perp}\cap\mathfrak{g}^{e}))/H $$

over $BG$ .

#### Proof.

Using [GG1, Lemma 2.1], one obtains an inclusion $f+\mathfrak{g}^{e}\subseteq f+\mathfrak{n}_{+}^{\perp}$ which is a slice of the $N$ -action on $f+\mathfrak{n}_{+}^{\perp}$ . Therefore, there is an isomorphism

$$ \displaystyle N\times(M\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}}\mathfrak{g}^{e}) \displaystyle\to(M\times{\mathfrak{n}}/\mathfrak{n}_{+})\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}\oplus{\mathfrak{n}}^{\ast}}\mathfrak{g}^{\ast} \displaystyle\cong\{(v,x)\in M\times(f+\mathfrak{n}_{+}^{\perp})\text{ such that }\mu(v)=x|_{\mathfrak{h}}\}, $$

sending $(n,v,y)\mapsto(v,n\cdot(f+y))$ . This isomorphism is $H$ -equivariant, so it follows that $\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{G}(M)/G$ is isomorphic to $(M\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}}\mathfrak{g}^{e})/H$ as stacks over $BG$ . This implies the desired claim, since $M\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}}\mathfrak{g}^{e}\cong M\oplus(\mathfrak{h}^{\perp}\cap\mathfrak{g}^{e})$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.4.7.

An alternative way to describe Whittaker induction using the language of shifted symplectic geometry (reviewed briefly in Section 5.1) is as follows. Recall (see [Saf1]) that a Lagrangian morphism $L\to\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}/H$ is equivalent to the data of a Hamiltonian $H$ -space $M$ ; the correspondence sets $L=M/H$ . Moreover, intersecting Lagrangian correspondences produces another Lagrangian correspondence (see Recollection 5.1.2). From this perspective, one can describe Whittaker induction as follows. Let $\iota:H\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ be a map of reductive algebraic groups over $\mathbf{C}$ such that $H$ centralizes the map $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to G$ . Let $f+\mathfrak{g}^{e}$ denote the Slodowy slice of the $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple; then, there is a Lagrangian correspondence

$$ \textstyle{(f+\mathfrak{g}^{e})/H\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}/H} \textstyle{\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}/G,} $$

and Whittaker induction amounts to intersecting the above Lagrangian correspondence with the Lagrangian $M/H\to\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}/H$ . (This will produce a Lagrangian morphism $(M\times_{\mathfrak{h}^{\ast}}(f+\mathfrak{g}^{e})/H\to\mathfrak{g}^{\ast}/G$ , which is identified with the Hamiltonian $G$ -variety of Definition 3.4.5.)

Let us now recall a statement of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1]; our presentation will follow [BZSV, Section 4.3]. Assume for now that $X$ is an affine spherical $G$ -variety over $\mathbf{C}$ which is the affine closure of its open $G$ -orbit (for instance, this holds if $X$ is affine and homogeneous).

#### Definition 3.4.8.

A color of $X$ is an irreducible $B$ -stable divisor which is not $G$ -stable (if $X$ is homogeneous, this is simply an irreducible $B$ -stable divisor). Following [BZSV, Definition 4.3.4], a standard parabolic $P\subseteq G$ is said to be of even spherical type if the spherical $P/U_{P}$ -variety $X^{\circ}P/U_{P}$ is isomorphic to either the spherical $\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ -variety $\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ or the spherical $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{G}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ . (Note that there are diffeomorphisms $\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\cong S^{2n}$ and $\mathrm{G}_{2}/\mathrm{SL}_{3}\cong S^{6}$ .) A color $D$ is said to be of even spherical type if it meets $X^{\circ}P$ for a standard parabolic $P$ of even spherical type. Let $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ denote the set of colors of $X$ of even spherical type.

Suppose that the elements of $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ freely generate a direct summand of ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}$ . Let $\mathcal{D}_{X}$ denote the set of dominant $W_{X}$ -translates of $\mathcal{C}_{X}\subseteq{\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}$ , and let $\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\max}$ denote the subset of maximal elements of $\mathcal{D}_{X}$ (with respect to the ordering via coroots of ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ ). Let $S_{X}$ denote the ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ -representation with highest weights $\mathcal{D}_{X}^{\max}$ . It is expected (see [BZSV, Conjecture 4.3.16]) that $S_{X}$ admits an ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ -invariant symplectic form.

#### Example 3.4.9 ([BZSV, Example 4.3.9]).

Consider the example of the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ -variety $X=\mathrm{GL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (in which case ${\check{{G}}}_{X}={\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ ). Then $U\backslash X^{\circ}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2}$ via the map $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\mapsto(b,d^{-1}\mathrm{det})$ . The colors of $X$ are given by the vanishing loci of $b$ and $d$ , and are both of even spherical type. As explained in [BZSV, Example 4.3.9], this implies that $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ is the subset $\{{\check{{\alpha}}}_{1},-{\check{{\alpha}}}_{2}\}$ of ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}={\check{{\Lambda}}}$ , which in turn implies that $S_{X}=\mathbf{A}^{2}\oplus(\mathbf{A}^{2})^{\ast}\cong T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ as an ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ -representation. However, as remarked in [BZSV], the condition that the elements of $\mathcal{C}_{X}$ freely generate a direct summand of ${\check{{\Lambda}}}_{X}$ is not true in the example of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (whose dual group is ${\check{{G}}}_{X}={\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ). Nevertheless, the variant of Definition 3.4.8 discussed in [BZSV, Section 4.4] shows that $S_{X}$ is the ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ -representation $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ .

#### Example 3.4.10.

For $n>2$ , the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ -variety $X=\mathrm{GL}_{n}/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ still has ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , but the representation $S_{X}$ is zero. (I am very grateful to Justin Hilburn and Yiannis Sakellaridis for this point.) For instance, when $n=3$ , the Whittaker induction $\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{\mathrm{GL}_{3}}S_{X}$ along the map $\iota:\mathrm{GL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\mathrm{Arth}}\to\mathrm{GL}_{3}$ of Remark 3.3.24 can be identified with $T^{\ast}(\mathrm{GL}_{3}/\mathrm{GL}_{2})$ using Lemma 3.4.6.

#### Example 3.4.11.

Consider the example of the spherical $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\cdot\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ (in which case ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ). Since $\mathrm{Spin}_{4}\cong\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ , under which the embedding of $\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ into $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}$ is given by the diagonal. Therefore, there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{3}\cong\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ , and this spherical $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}$ -variety can be understood as the group case for $\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ . Using this, one can show that ${\check{{G}}}\backslash\mathrm{WhitInd}_{\iota}^{{\check{{G}}}}S_{X}\cong\mathfrak{sl}_{2}/{\check{{G}}}_{X}$ .

### 3.5. The $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -(co)homology of $\mathcal{L}(G/H)$

Fix a compact Lie group $G$ , and let $H\subseteq G$ be a closed subgroup. Throughout this section, we will always assume that $H$ and $G$ are connected, and also (for simplicity) that $G/H$ has finite fundamental group (so that $\Omega(G/H)$ has finitely many connected components). Recall Notation 1.5.14: we will write $G(\!(t)\!)$ or $G[\![t]\!]$ below to mean $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\!(t)\!)$ or $G_{\mathbf{C}}[\![t]\!]$ , respectively.

Before proceeding to the proof of Theorem 3.4.16, we need some general statements about the $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -(co)homology of the free loop space $\mathcal{L}(G/H)=\mathrm{Map}(S^{1},G/H)$ . Let us remind the reader uninterested in $\mathrm{ku}$ , but interested in $\mathbf{Z}$ , that one should feel free to replace $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ everywhere below by the equivariant cochains $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z})$ (and similarly for other symbols involving $\mathrm{ku}$ ); and moreover, any instance of the symbol $\beta$ can be set to zero to obtain a corresponding statement over $\mathbf{Z}$ .

The following basic result is an analogue of the algebro-geometric fact that $G\backslash T^{\ast}(G/H)\cong H\backslash(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h})^{\ast}$ , or its homotopic analogue that $(G/H)_{+}^{hG}\simeq(S^{\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{h}})^{hH}$ .

#### Proposition 3.5.1.

Let $H$ act on $G/H$ , and hence on $\Omega(G/H)$ , by conjugation (equivalently, left-translation). Then the $G$ -space $\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ is $G$ -equivariantly homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{Ind}_{H}^{G}\Omega(G/H)$ . In particular, there is an equivalence of orbispaces

$$ G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/H)\simeq H\backslash\Omega(G/H). $$

#### Proof.

It is a classical fact that the map $m:G\times\Omega G\to\mathcal{L}G$ sending $(g,\gamma)$ to the loop $\gamma_{g}:t\mapsto g\gamma(t)$ is a homotopy equivalence. The left action of $G$ on $\mathcal{L}G$ is simply given by

$$ G\ni g^{\prime}:\gamma_{g}(t)\mapsto\gamma_{g^{\prime}g}(t), $$

which allows us to identify $\mathcal{L}G\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_{\{1\}}^{G}\Omega G$ . Recall that there is a principal fibration

$$ H\to G\to G/H, $$

which gives equivalences $\Omega(G/H)\simeq\Omega G/\Omega H$ and $\mathcal{L}(G/H)\simeq\mathcal{L}G/\mathcal{L}H$ . Since and the diagram

$$ \textstyle{H\times\Omega H\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{m} \textstyle{G\times\Omega G\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{m} \textstyle{\mathcal{L}H\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathcal{L}G} $$

commutes, we find that there is an equivalence of $G$ -spaces

$$ \mathcal{L}G/\mathcal{L}H\simeq(\mathrm{Ind}_{\{1\}}^{G}\Omega G)/(\mathrm{Ind}_{\{1\}}^{H}\Omega H)\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_{H}^{G}\Omega(G/H), $$

as desired. Alternatively, this also follows from 3.6 using that $\ast\times_{\ast\times_{\ast/G}\ast/H}\ast\simeq\Omega(G/H)$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.5.4.

There is a multiplicative presentation of $\Omega(G/H)$ as $\colim X_{\lambda}$ via finite $H$ -spaces $X_{\lambda}$ , and the induced $G$ -spaces $\mathrm{Ind}_{H}^{G}X_{\lambda}$ defines a presentation of $\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ by finite $G$ -spaces. It follows that there is an equivalence $\mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))\cong\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -algebras, where the right-hand side is viewed as an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -algebra via its natural $\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ -algebra structure and the canonical map $\mathrm{ku}_{G}\to\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ .

#### Warning 3.5.5.

Although there is an equivalence $\mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))\cong\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -algebras, there is not an equivalence $\mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))^{\vee}\cong\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}$ of $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -modules. Indeed, $\mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))^{\vee}$ denotes the $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -linear dual of $\mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))$ , while $\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}$ denotes the $\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ -linear dual of $\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))$ . (To clarify, this dual is not taken in the naive sense: rather, if $\Omega(G/H)=\colim X_{\lambda}$ as in Remark 3.5.4, $\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}$ means $\colim_{\lambda}\mathcal{F}_{H}(X_{\lambda})^{\vee}$ .)

#### Remark 3.5.6.

Proposition 3.5.1 breaks the natural symmetry on $G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ . Namely, since the action of $G$ on $\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ is defined via the $G$ -action on $G/H$ , the orbispace $G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ has an action of the circle $S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ given by rotating loops. However, this structure is not naturally visible on the orbispace $\Omega(G/H)/H$ . Indeed, the proof of Proposition 3.5.1 used the splitting $G\times\Omega G\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathcal{L}G$ ; but this splitting is not $S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ -equivariant.

A slight variant of Proposition 3.5.1 lets us describe the $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -cohomology of $\mathcal{L}(G/H)$ . The following result is proved nonequivariantly in [Dev2, Remark A.6].

#### Proposition 3.5.7.

There is an $S^{1}_{\mathrm{rot}}$ -equivariant equivalence of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -algebras

$$ \mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))\simeq\mathrm{HH}(\mathrm{ku}_{H}/\mathrm{ku}_{G}), $$

where the right-hand side denotes the relative Hochschild homology of the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $\mathrm{ku}_{H}\to\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ (equipped with its natural $S^{1}$ -action).

#### Proof.

Since $G/H$ is itself the fiber product $\ast\times_{\ast/G}\ast/H$ in orbispaces, there is an equivalence

$$ G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/H)\simeq G\backslash(\ast\times_{\mathcal{L}(\ast/G)}\mathcal{L}(\ast/H))\simeq\ast/G\times_{\mathcal{L}(\ast/G)}\mathcal{L}(\ast/H). $$

But $\mathcal{L}(\ast/G)\simeq\ast/G\times_{\ast/G\times\ast/G}\ast/G$ , where the two maps $\ast/G\to\ast/G\times\ast/G$ are both given by the diagonal. Therefore, we can identify

$$ \displaystyle G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/H) \displaystyle\simeq\ast/G\times_{\ast/G\times_{\ast/G\times\ast/G}\ast/G}(\ast/H\times_{\ast/H\times\ast/H}\ast/H) \displaystyle\simeq\ast/H\times_{\ast/H\times_{\ast/G}\ast/H}\ast/H. $$

By construction of equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ , it follows that there is an equivalence of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -algebras

$$ \mathcal{F}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!))\simeq\mathrm{ku}_{H}\otimes_{\mathrm{ku}_{H}\otimes_{\mathrm{ku}_{G}}\mathrm{ku}_{H}}\mathrm{ku}_{H}=\mathrm{HH}(\mathrm{ku}_{H}/\mathrm{ku}_{G}). $$

Moreover, the equivalence of 3.6 is manifestly $S^{1}$ -equivariant, so we obtain the desired claim. ∎

Base-changing Proposition 3.5.7 along the map $\mathrm{ku}\to\mathbf{Q}$ and using the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem (in the form proved in [Rak, MRT]), one finds:

#### Corollary 3.5.8.

Let $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}=\spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{H}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ and $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}=\spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})$ are (the shearings of) the Chevalley bases for ${\check{{H}}}$ and ${\check{{G}}}$ , respectively, so that $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ (and similarly for $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}$ ). There is an equivalence

$$ C^{\ast}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq L\Omega^{\ast}_{\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}}, $$

where the right-hand side is derived Hodge cohomology. In other words, there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec C^{\ast}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\cong T[-1](\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}). $$

This equivalence identifies the loop rotation action of $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}$ on the left-hand side with the de Rham differential on the right-hand side; this implies that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec C^{\ast}_{G[\![t]\!]\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathrm{Def}_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}), $$

where the right-hand side denotes the deformation to the normal cone of the morphism $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}\to\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{G}}}}^{\ast}$ in the sense of [GR1, Section 9.2], living over the base $\spec C^{\ast}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\hbar}[2]$ .

#### Example 3.5.9.

For instance, in the group case (so $G=H\times H$ with $H$ embedded diagonally), the first isomorphism of Corollary 3.5.8 says that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec C^{\ast}_{H[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{Gr}_{H};\mathbf{Q})\cong T[-1](\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}\times{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast})\cong T[-2](\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\spec(\mathbf{Q})). $$

Similarly, there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec C^{\ast}_{H[\![t]\!]\rtimes\mathbf{G}_{m}^{\mathrm{rot}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{H};\mathbf{Q})\cong\mathrm{Def}_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}/\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}\times{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}); $$

since $\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}\times{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}\cong\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}\times_{\spec(\mathbf{Q})}\mathfrak{c}_{{\check{{H}}}}^{\ast}$ , this recovers the isomorphism of [BF1, Theorem 1]. We have already discussed this perspective before in [Dev2, Example A.8].

Let us note that away from characteristic zero, or especially well-behaved cases like the map $\mathrm{GL}_{n}\to\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}$ , one needs to be very careful in modeling the map $C^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;R)\to C^{\ast}_{H}(\ast;R)$ via shearing. See Remark 2.1.12 for an example of the sort of subtlety that can arise.

Suppose $G/H$ is an affine spherical $G$ -variety, and assume that 3.5 of Remark 3.4.13 holds for $G/H$ (which would follows from Conjecture 3.4.12). Then Corollary 3.5.8 implies that if $\mu:{\check{{M}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}$ denotes the moment map, there is an isomorphism (ignoring gradings for simplicity)

When $G=H\times H$ , so that ${\check{{M}}}=T^{\ast}{\check{{H}}}$ , this is precisely the Kostant functor of [BF1, Section 2.6]. This functor is compatible with the commutative diagram 3.7, in that the following diagram is its analogue on the spectral side:

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\kappa_{{\check{{M}}}}} \textstyle{\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}T[-1]({\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}/{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\text{zero section}^{\ast}} \textstyle{\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{restriction}} \textstyle{\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}),} $$

For instance, when $G=H\times H$ , so that ${\check{{M}}}=T^{\ast}{\check{{H}}}$ , the map $\kappa$ is simply the Kostant slice for ${\check{{H}}}$ .
