#### Example 3.6.24 (Gan-Gross-Prasad).

For instance, suppose $H\subseteq G$ is the inclusion $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ , so that ${\check{{H}}}=\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ and ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ . In this case, one can show that

$$ {\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}\cong\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n}) $$

as a $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\times\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ -variety (this is the Gan-Gross-Prasad period), so that Theorem 3.6.4 implies that if Hypothesis 3.5.2 is true in this example, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times H)[\![t]\!]}((G\times H)(\!(t)\!)/H^{\mathrm{diag}}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n})/(\mathrm{SO}_{2n}\times\mathrm{Sp}_{2n})(-2\rho))$ for a certain grading on $\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n})$ . When $n=1$ , this gives an alternative perspective on Corollary 4.3.19 in the special case $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}=\mathrm{SO}_{3}/\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ .

To prove 3.21, one must describe a morphism

$$ ({\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})/({\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}})\hookrightarrow\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n}). $$

We will construct this morphism below; the key step is to define a Kostant slice

$$ \kappa:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n}) $$

as in Conjecture 3.5.11. With a bit more work, one can check that it is an open immersion with complement of codimension $2$ , from which 3.21 follows.

Let us now describe the Kostant slice $\kappa$ . Recall from Example 3.2.14 that:

- • We may identify

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong\spec k[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n}]\cong\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}}(\ast;k), $$

and ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}$ is the group scheme whose fiber over $\vec{p}:=(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n})$ is the subgroup of those units $f(t)\in k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n})$ such that $f(t)^{-1}=f(-t)$ . Recall that $k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n})$ admits the structure of a symplectic vector space.

- • We may identify

$$ {\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\cong\spec k[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n}]\cong\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{SO}_{2n}}(\ast;k), $$

and ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{H}}}}$ is the group scheme whose fiber over $(\vec{p},c_{n}):=(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n})$ is the subgroup of those units $f(t,v)\in k[t,v]/(tv-c_{n},t^{2n-2}+p_{1}t^{2n-4}+\cdots+p_{n-1}+v^{2})$ such that $f(t,v)^{-1}=f(-t,-v)$ . Recall that $k[t,v]/(tv-c_{n},t^{2n-2}+p_{1}t^{2n-4}+\cdots+p_{n-1}+v^{2})$ admits the structure of a quadratic vector space.

The map $\pi:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}$ is induced by the inclusion

$$ \pi:k[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n}]\hookrightarrow k[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n}],\ p_{n}\mapsto c_{n}^{2}. $$

The map $\pi$ induces a map of $2n$ -dimensional $k$ -vector spaces

$$ \varphi_{\vec{p},c_{n}}:k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n-1}t^{2}+c_{n}^{2})\\
\cong k[t]/(t^{2n}+p_{1}t^{2n-2}+\cdots+p_{n})\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}}\\
\to k[t,v]/(tv-c_{n},t^{2n-2}+p_{1}t^{2n-4}+\cdots+p_{n-1}+v^{2}); $$

in other words, this is a linear map $\varphi_{\vec{p},c_{n}}:\mathrm{std}_{2n}\to\mathrm{std}_{2n}$ . That is, $\pi$ induces a map

$$ \kappa:{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\cong\spec k[p_{1},\cdots,p_{n-1},c_{n}]\to\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n}),\ (\vec{p},c_{n})\mapsto\varphi_{\vec{p},c_{n}}. $$

This is the relevant Kostant slice, and so we obtain a map

$$ {\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}\times{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}\to\Hom(\mathrm{std}_{2n},\mathrm{std}_{2n}) $$

by taking the ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}$ -orbit of $\kappa$ . This map factors through the quotient by ${\check{{J}}}_{{\check{{G}}}}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ , and therefore produces the desired map 3.22.

#### Remark 3.6.25.

One rather curious phenomenon which can be observed empirically, but we do not have a general explanation for, is a relationship between ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ and closures of minimal nilpotent orbits. Namely, suppose $H\subseteq G$ is a closed subgroup (not necessarily spherical), so that $H^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq G\times H$ ; this need not be spherical even if $H\subseteq G$ is spherical. Assume that there is a reductive group scheme ${\check{{K}}}$ equipped with an embedding ${\check{{G}}}\times{\check{{H}}}\subseteq{\check{{K}}}$ of group schemes such that ${\check{{G}}}$ is the centralizer of ${\check{{H}}}$ , and conversely ${\check{{H}}}$ is the centralizer of ${\check{{G}}}$ . In other words, $({\check{{G}}},{\check{{H}}})$ form a (reductive) dual pair in ${\check{{K}}}$ . It turns out that ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ , as defined in Construction 3.6.19, can sometimes be identified with the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of ${\check{{K}}}$ .

Let us give three examples to illustrate this; a general explanation of this observation would be very interesting!

- • Let $\mathrm{SL}_{3}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{8}={\check{{K}}}$ via the adjoint action of $\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ on $\mathfrak{sl}_{3}$ equipped with its Killing form. From [DG1, Table 1], one finds that the centralizer of $\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ is $\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ , and $(\mathrm{SL}_{3},\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2})$ forms a dual pair in $\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ . (It corresponds to the inclusion $H=\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2}/\mu_{3}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{3}=G$ of the maximal torus; note that this is not a spherical subgroup!) Then ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ can be identified with $\overline{T^{\ast}(\mathrm{SL}_{3}/{\check{{N}}})}$ , and this is isomorphic to the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit in $\mathfrak{so}_{8}$ . This was explicitly studied in [Jia, Kaz, LS].

- • Let $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{3}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}_{8}={\check{{K}}}$ . Again from [DG1, Table 1], one finds that the centralizer of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ is $\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3}$ , and $(\mathrm{SL}_{2},\mathrm{SL}_{2}^{\times 3})$ forms a dual pair in $\mathrm{SO}_{8}$ . (It corresponds to $H=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}=G$ .) Interpreting [MT, Equation 4.1] correctly, one is led to the prediction that ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ can again be identified with the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit in $\mathfrak{so}_{8}$ . See [Dev4, Remark 3.10].

- • Let $\mathrm{SL}_{3}\subseteq\mathrm{E}_{6}={\check{{K}}}$ as in [DG1, Equation 1]. Again from [DG1, Table 1], one finds that the centralizer of $\mathrm{SL}_{3}$ is $\mathrm{SL}_{3}^{\times 2}$ , and $(\mathrm{SL}_{3},\mathrm{SL}_{3}^{\times 2})$ forms a dual pair in $\mathrm{E}_{6}$ . (It corresponds to $H=\mathrm{PGL}_{3}^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{3}^{\times 2}=G$ .) Using [MT, Section 4.2], proved mathematically in [BFN, Section 5(iv)], one finds that ${\check{{\mathcal{M}}}}^{\ddagger}$ can be identified with the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit in $\mathrm{E}_{6}$ .

The preceding Example 3.6.24 also fits into this paradigm, up to some “metaplectic” correction. Namely, $(\mathrm{SO}_{2n},\mathrm{Sp}_{2n})$ forms a dual pair in $\mathrm{Sp}_{4n^{2}}$ , and the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of $\mathrm{Sp}_{4n^{2}}$ can be identified with $\mathbf{A}^{4n^{2}}/\!\!/\{\pm 1\}$ (i.e., the image of the moment map $\mathbf{A}^{4n^{2}}\to\mathfrak{sp}_{4n^{2}}$ ). Up to this order two quotient, one can therefore identify the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of $\mathrm{Sp}_{4n^{2}}$ with the tensor product of the standard representations of $\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ and $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ , which is what appeared in Example 3.6.24.

To generalize the discussion of this section to $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic coefficients, we need some preliminary results.

### 3.7. $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic derived geometric Satake

Recall from the proof of Theorem 3.2.7 that the key step in the argument, once given Theorem 3.2.3, is Theorem 3.2.15. Our goal in this section is to prove a $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic analogue of Theorem 3.2.15 in the case when $G$ is assumed to be simply-laced and connected. Throughout, $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ will denote the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ .

#### Definition 3.7.1.

Let $X$ be a (possibly graded) scheme over a commutative ring $R$ . The $\mathrm{ku}$ -loop space $\mathcal{L}_{\beta}X$ of $X$ is defined to be the graded $R[\beta]$ -scheme $\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee},X_{R[\beta]})$ .

The following is a slight variant of the main result of [MRT] (see also [Mou2, Corollary 6.1]).

#### Lemma 3.7.2.

Let $X$ be a derived scheme over a commutative ring $R$ . Then the pushforward of the structure sheaf along the canonical map $\mathcal{L}_{\beta}(X)/\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\spec(R[\beta])/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ corresponds (under the equivalence between quasicoherent sheaves on $\spec(R[\beta])/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ and filtered $R$ -modules) to the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg filtration on the Hochschild homology $\mathrm{HH}(X/R)$ .

#### Proof.

In [MRT], it is shown that if $R$ is a $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ -algebra, $W$ is the ring scheme of $p$ -typical Witt vectors, and $F$ is its Frobenius, the pushforward of the structure sheaf along the canonical map $\mathrm{Map}(W[F=\beta^{p-1}],X)/\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\spec(R[\beta])/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ corresponds to the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg filtration on $\mathrm{HH}(X/R)$ . It therefore suffices to identify $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ with a completion of $W[F=\beta^{p-1}]$ . As shown in [Dev3, Proposition C.6], there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}\cong\spf\mathbf{Z}_{p}\left[\beta,\tfrac{y(y-\beta)\cdots(y-(n-1)\beta)}{n!}\right]^{\wedge} $$

where the element $y$ is primitive (i.e., the coproduct sends $y\mapsto y\otimes 1+1\otimes y$ ) and lives in weight $2$ . Here, the completion is taken with respect to the $\beta$ -deformed divided power filtration (i.e., with respect to $\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(y-j\beta)$ for $n\geq 1$ ). The desired identification with the completion of $W[F=\beta^{p-1}]$ is now given by [Dev3, Remark C.7]. Using the arithmetic fracture square, it only remains to prove the lemma when $R$ is a $\mathbf{Q}$ -algebra. In this case, $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ is isomorphic to $\spf\mathbf{Q}[\beta][\![y]\!]\cong\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}$ , from which the desired result follows since the the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg filtration on $\mathrm{HH}(X/R)$ splits, and the Hodge complex of $X$ over $R$ can be identified with the global sections of the mapping stack $\mathrm{Map}(B\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{a},X)$ . ∎

#### Definition 3.7.3.

Let $H$ be a graded algebraic group over a commutative ring $R$ . Let $H_{\beta}$ denote the graded group scheme over $R[\beta]$ given by $\Hom(\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee},H_{R[\beta]})$ . Note that there is a canonical action of $H_{R[\beta]}$ on $H_{\beta}$ by conjugation, and the quotient stack $H_{\beta}/H_{R[\beta]}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{L}_{\beta}(BH)=\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee},BH_{R[\beta]})$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.4.

If $H$ is a graded algebraic group, there is an isomorphism $H_{\beta}[\beta^{-1}]/\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong H$ , and a graded isomorphism $H_{\beta}/\beta\cong\mathfrak{h}(2)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\mathrm{Map}(B\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}(-2)},BH)\cong\mathfrak{h}(2)/H$ by Example 5.1.6, and $\mathrm{Map}(B\mathbf{Z},BH)\cong H/H$ , it suffices to show that $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}[\beta^{-1}]/\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\mathbf{Z}$ , while $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}/\beta$ is isomorphic to the completion $\widehat{\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}(-2)}$ of the PD-hull of the origin in $\mathbf{G}_{a}(-2)$ at the divided power filtration. This in turn follows from the fact that $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}[\beta^{-1}]/\mathbf{G}_{m}\cong\mathbf{G}_{m}$ and $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}/\beta\cong\mathbf{G}_{a}(2)$ , and that $\mathbf{Z}$ (resp. $\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}(-2)$ ) is the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ (resp. $\mathbf{G}_{a}(2)$ ). ∎

#### Remark 3.7.5.

In Definition 3.7.1, there was no reason to restrict to considering maps out of $B\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ : we could have considered any $1$ -dimensional group scheme over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ in place of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ . (This sort of philosophy fits very naturally into Section 5.4, which more generally suggests that it should be very interesting to study the universal case, where $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ is replaced with the Lazard ring carrying the universal formal group law itself.) We can even input $1$ -dimensional formal group schemes into the above cosntruction. For instance, a particularly important example which arises naturally in chromatic homotopy theory is the following. Fix a prime $p$ , and consider the formal group over $\mathbf{Q}[\beta]$ whose logarithm is given by the invertible “ $p$ -typical polylogarithmic” power series

$$ \ell_{F}(x)=\sum_{j\geq 0}\beta^{p^{nj}-1}\tfrac{x^{p^{nj}}}{p^{j}}. $$

Here, the class $x$ lives in weight $-2$ . That the power series $F(x,y)=\ell_{F}^{-1}(\ell_{F}(x)+\ell_{F}(y))$ has coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}_{(p)}[\beta]$ is a consequence of Hazewinkel’s functional equation lemma [Haz, Section I.2]; write $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)}$ to denote the associated formal group law over $\mathbf{Z}_{(p)}[\beta]$ . When base-changed to $\mathbf{F}_{p}[\beta]$ , we will denote it by $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k(n)}$ . The Cartier dual of $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k(n)}$ was computed in [DM2, Example 4.5.14], where it was shown that

$$ \widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k(n)}^{\vee}\cong\spec\mathbf{F}_{p}[\beta][y_{0},y_{1},\cdots]/(y_{n+j-1}^{p}-\beta^{p^{j}(p^{n}-1)}y_{j}). $$

Here, the classes $y_{j}$ live in weight $2p^{j}$ . Observe that for $\beta=0$ , one recovers the Cartier dual $\mathbf{G}_{a}^{\sharp}$ of $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{a}$ . For $n=1$ , the formal group $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k(1)}$ is isomorphic to the $p$ -typification of $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{\beta}$ .

To connect this to chromatic homotopy theory, note that $\ell_{F}(x)$ only depends on $\beta$ through $\beta^{p^{n}-1}$ ; so $\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k_{\mathbf{Z}}(n)}$ is in fact defined over $\mathbf{Z}_{(p)}[\beta^{p^{n}-1}]$ . The class $\beta^{p^{n}-1}$ is often denoted $v_{n}$ , and the resulting formal group law over $\mathbf{Z}_{(p)}[v_{n}]$ is the one associated to the complex orientation of (a form of) integral Morava K-theory of height $n$ . When $H$ is a group scheme over $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ , the group scheme $\Hom(\widehat{\mathbf{G}}_{k(n)}^{\vee},H)$ is closely related to the combinatorial constructions of [DM2], and we expect it to capture a lot of interesting aspects of the modular representation theory of $H$ . For instance, when $n=1$ , it essentially reduces to the group scheme $H_{\beta}$ studied in the present section (the only difference is the completion of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ ). In general, it is an interesting deformation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}(2)$ to $\mathbf{F}_{p}[\beta]$ . We will not discuss this generalization of $H_{\beta}$ further here, but plan to in [Dev5].

#### Lemma 3.7.6.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $K$ be a commutative group scheme over $R$ with Cartier dual $K^{\vee}$ . Then there is an isomorphism $\Hom(K^{\vee},\mathbf{G}_{a})\cong\mathrm{Lie}(K)$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.7.

Let $B\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ denote the Borel subgroup of upper-triangular matrices, graded by the action of $2n\rho:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ . If $R_{\ast}$ is a graded $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -algebra, the group scheme $B_{\beta}(R_{\ast})$ is isomorphic to the subgroup of $B(R_{\ast})$ consisting of matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}1+\beta x&\beta y\\ 0&1+\beta w\end{pmatrix}$ , where $x,w\in\mathbf{G}_{\beta}(R)\subseteq R_{-2}$ and $y\in R_{2n-2}$ .

#### Proof.

There is a graded extension

$$ \mathbf{G}_{a}(-2n)\to B\to\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2}, $$

which implies that there is a graded extension

$$ \mathbf{G}_{a}(-2n)_{\beta}\to B_{\beta}\to(\mathbf{G}_{m}^{2})_{\beta}. $$

By construction, $\mathbf{G}_{m,\beta}$ is the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{\vee}$ , i.e., $\mathbf{G}_{m,\beta}\cong\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ . Moreover, Lemma 3.7.6 gives an isomorphism $\mathbf{G}_{a}(-2n)_{\beta}\cong\mathrm{Lie}(\mathbf{G}_{\beta})(-2n)\cong\mathbf{G}_{a}(2-2n)$ . It follows that there is an extension

$$ \mathbf{G}_{a}(2-2n)\to B_{\beta}\to\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{2}. $$

This extension precisely classifies matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}1+\beta x&\beta y\\ 0&1+\beta w\end{pmatrix}$ with $x,w\in\mathbf{G}_{\beta}(R)\subseteq R_{-2}$ and $y\in R_{2n-2}$ . ∎

In the remainder of this section, we will always invert the order $N=|W|$ of the Weyl group $W$ , and write $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[1/N]$ ; in particular, $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.8.

Let ${\check{{G}}}$ be a reductive group over a commutative ring $R$ . Let ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote the open subscheme consisting of those elements $x\in{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ such that the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{G}}}}(x)\subseteq{\check{{G}}}$ has minimal dimension (i.e., the rank of ${\check{{G}}}$ ). Similarly, let ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ denote ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}\cap{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ . Then the morphism ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{B}}}\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}/{\check{{G}}}$ is a ramified $W$ -Galois cover.

#### Definition 3.7.9.

Let $e\in{\check{{G}}}$ be a principal unipotent element, so that $e$ defines a homomorphism $\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to{\check{{G}}}$ by the Jacobson-Morozov theorem. This homomorphism is $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -equivariant if ${\check{{G}}}$ (resp. $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ) is graded by $2\rho:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to{\check{{G}}}$ (resp. the restriction of the $2\rho$ -grading on ${\check{{G}}}$ to $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ). There is an induced homomorphism $B_{\mathrm{SL}_{2},\beta}\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ , where $B_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ is the Borel subgroup of upper-triangular matrices. Let $\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\in B_{\mathrm{SL}_{2},\beta}$ denote the element defined by Lemma 3.7.7; the image of this element in ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ will be denoted by $e_{\beta}$ .

Let $\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}$ denote the map sending $x\mapsto e_{\beta}x$ , so that $\widetilde{\kappa}$ induces a map ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}$ (which will also be denoted by $\widetilde{\kappa}$ ). We will refer to this as the $\beta$ -deformed Kostant slice. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}$ is $W$ -equivariant, so Lemma 3.7.8 implies that the composite

$$ {\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\xrightarrow{{\widetilde{\kappa}}}{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}} $$

descends to a morphism ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ , which we will denote by $\kappa$ . The map $\kappa:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ will also be called the $\beta$ -deformed Kostant slice. It defines a graded map ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\to{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ . (See [BFM, Section 2.1] for a related construction. Note that if ${\check{{G}}}$ is simply-connected, [Ste] gives an identification ${\check{{G}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\cong{\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W$ , as well as the construction of a slice ${\check{{T}}}/\!\!/W\to{\check{{G}}}$ . The above construction is weaker than this, in the sense that the slice lands in the quotient stack ${\check{{G}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ , and not ${\check{{G}}}$ itself.)

Recall that if $G$ is simply-laced and connected, its Langlands dual group ${\check{{G}}}$ is isogenous to $G$ itself. In particular, the action of $G$ on itself by conjugation induces an action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $G$ . For instance, if $G$ is simply-connected, ${\check{{G}}}$ is the quotient of (the Chevalley split form of) $G$ by its center; and the action of $G$ on itself by conjugation descends to an action of ${\check{{G}}}=G/Z(G)$ . Similarly, if $G$ is adjoint, ${\check{{G}}}$ is a $\pi_{1}(G)_{\mathrm{tors}}$ -cover of $G$ , and so the action of $G$ on itself by conjugation restricts to an action of ${\check{{G}}}$ on $G$ .

#### Theorem 3.7.10.

Let $G$ be a simply-laced and connected compact Lie group with associated reductive group $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ over $\mathbf{C}$ , so that $(G\times G)/Z(G)^{\mathrm{diag}}$ acts on $\mathcal{L}G$ by left and right translation. Then there is a graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{ku}^{G/Z(G)}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong{\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)}{\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W $$

of group schemes over ${\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W=\spec\mathrm{ku}_{G/Z(G)}^{\ast}(\ast)$ .

#### Corollary 3.7.11.

In the setup of Theorem 3.7.10, there is a graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear isomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong T_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)}T_{\beta}/\!\!/W $$

of group schemes over $T_{\beta}/\!\!/W=\spec\mathrm{ku}_{G}^{\ast}(\ast)$ , where $G$ on the right-hand side denotes the split form of the compact Lie group over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ , and ${\check{{G}}}$ (which is a central quotient of $G$ ) acts on $G$ by conjugation.

#### Remark 3.7.12.

Corollary 3.7.11 is a simultaneous generalization of [Dev2, Proposition 4.1.5 and Theorem 4.2.5] (which is in turn related to [BFM, Theorem 2.12 and Theorem 2.15]).

The following result is essentially [YZ, Step II of Theorem 6.1].

#### Lemma 3.7.13.

The scheme ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ is flat over ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ after inverting $|W|$ .

#### Proof.

There is a closed immersion

$$ {\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\subseteq{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times{\check{{B}}}, $$

which exhibits the left-hand side as the subgroup of those $(x,g)$ such that $g$ stabilizes $\kappa(x)$ ; in particular, it is cut out by $\dim{\check{{N}}}$ equations, so that the fibers of the projection ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ are at most $\dim{\check{{B}}}-\dim{\check{{N}}}=\dim{\check{{T}}}$ -dimensional. To prove that ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ is flat over ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ , it suffices to show that all the fibers of the projection

$$ {\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{T}}}_{\beta} $$

are $\dim{\check{{T}}}$ -dimensional.

Let $g\in{\check{{B}}}$ and $x\in{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ . Since $\kappa(x)=e_{\beta}x$ , we have $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}\kappa(x)=\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(e_{\beta})\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)\in{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}\subseteq{\check{{B}}}_{\mathbf{Z}[\beta]}$ . Since $x$ is semisimple, the same is true of $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(x)$ . It therefore suffices to show that the subgroup $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(e_{\beta})=\{g\in{\check{{B}}}|\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(e_{\beta})=e_{\beta}\}\subseteq{\check{{B}}}$ is $\dim{\check{{T}}}$ -dimensional. If $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(e_{\beta})=e_{\beta}$ , then $\mathrm{Ad}_{g}(e)=e$ , where $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ is the associated nilpotent element; this implies that $\dim Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(e_{\beta})\leq\dim Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(e)$ . Therefore, it suffices to show that the centralizer $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(e)$ is $\dim{\check{{T}}}$ -dimensional, which is even true with a smaller set of primes inverted (see [Ken]). ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.7.10.

It suffices to show that there is a graded isomorphism

$$ T_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)}T_{\beta}/\!\!/W\cong\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G). $$

By Proposition 2.3.15, $\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega G)^{W}$ , and so by definition of $\kappa$ , it suffices to show that there is a $W$ -equivariant graded isomorphism

$$ {T}_{\beta}\times_{B_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{T}_{\beta}\cong\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega G), $$

for which it in turn suffices to show that there is a $W$ -equivariant graded isomorphism

$$ {\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}\cong\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T/Z(G)}_{\ast}(\Omega G) $$

over ${\check{{T}}}^{\mathrm{ad}}_{\beta}$ .

For simplicity, we will ignore gradings in the following discussion. By equivariant formality for $\Omega G$ , the scheme $\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T/Z(G)}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ is flat over $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T/Z(G)}\cong{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ . The scheme ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ is also flat over ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ by Lemma 3.7.13. Therefore, the argument of [BFM, Section 4.3] reduces us to checking the isomorphism 3.24 in the case when $G$ (equivalently ${\check{{G}}}$ ) has semisimple rank $1$ (this, as usual, is through a Hartogs/codimension $2$ argument). For this, it in turn suffices to prove 3.24 when ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . (Below, we will calculate both sides of 3.24 as schemes over ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ . But checking that the isomorphism 3.24 is one of group schemes is not difficult: using flatness over ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ , one observes that the coproduct/group structure is determined by the coproduct/group structure over the complement ${{\check{{T}}}}^{\circ}_{\beta}$ of all root hypersurfaces. But then this reduces to the case when $G$ is a torus itself, where the isomorphism is evidently one of group schemes.)

Let ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , so $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ , and $Z(G)$ is trivial. Recall that there is a closed immersion

$$ {\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\subseteq{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times{\check{{B}}}, $$

which exhibits the left-hand side as the subgroup of those $(x,g)$ such that $g$ stabilizes $\kappa(x)$ . Since $\kappa(x)\in{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}$ is the matrix

$$ \kappa(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&1+\beta x\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta(1+\beta x)\\
0&1+\beta x\end{pmatrix}, $$

it follows that that if $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\in{\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{Ad}_{g}\kappa(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\beta(1+\beta{x})-b\beta x\\
0&1+\beta x\end{pmatrix}. $$

It follows that $g$ fixes $\kappa(x)$ if and only if

$$ a\beta(1+\beta{x})-b\beta x=\beta(1+\beta x), $$

i.e., if and only if

$$ b=\tfrac{a-1}{x}(1+\beta x). $$

It follows that there is an isomorphism

$$ {\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x}]. $$

Now using [Dev2, Theorem 3.2.12]2424 24 Note that [Dev2, Theorem 3.2.12] asks that $\mathbf{G}$ be an oriented group scheme over $A$ , but this is in fact not necessary: it suffices that $\mathbf{G}$ be preoriented, so that Proposition 2.4.10 continues to hold. In this case, the desired preorientation of $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{ku},\beta}$ is given by Proposition 2.3.11. or Theorem 4.2.13 with $V$ being the weight $2$ representation of $S^{1}$ , one sees that

$$ \mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{[2](x)}], $$

which implies that

$$ \mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}/(\mathbf{Z}/2)}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,[2](x),\tfrac{1}{1+\beta[2](x)},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{[2](x)}]. $$

Therefore, $\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T/Z(G)}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ is isomorphic to ${\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\times_{{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ , as desired. A similar calculation proves 3.24 when ${G}=\mathrm{GL}_{2},\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ (note that in this case $\pi_{1}(G)\cong\mathbf{Z}/2$ is not zero; but the result is still true by direct calculation). ∎

#### Example 3.7.14.

It is important that the order of $W$ is inverted. For instance, Theorem 3.7.10 implies that $\spec\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ is a subgroup of ${\check{{G}}}$ , given by the centralizer of $e_{\beta}\in{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ . Rationally (in fact, after inverting $|W|$ ), this is isomorphic to the centralizer of $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , which identifies with $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Q})[\beta]$ by Theorem 3.2.15. Note, however, that $\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ is (unsurprisingly) not isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Z})[\beta]$ , even as algebras. For instance, let $G=\mathrm{G}_{2}$ . Then [Bot] shows that

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{G}_{2};\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathbf{Z}[a,b,c]/(a^{2}-2b), $$

where $a$ is in weight $2$ , $b$ is in weight $4$ , and $c$ is in weight $10$ . On the other hand, a slight refinement of [Cla, Proposition 7.1] shows that

$$ \mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{G}_{2})\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta,a,b,c]/(a^{2}-2b-\beta a). $$

Of course, when $2$ is inverted, we may express $b=\tfrac{a^{2}-\beta a}{2}$ , and $\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{G}_{2})[1/2]\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{G}_{2};\mathbf{Z}[1/2])[\beta]$ .

We now make the following rather contrived definition.

#### Construction 3.7.15.

Let $G$ be a simply-laced connected compact Lie group, so that Theorem 3.7.10 gives a homomorphism

$$ \spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\hookrightarrow{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times T_{\beta}/\!\!/W $$

of group schemes over $T_{\beta}/\!\!/W$ . Let $H_{\mathbf{C}}\subseteq G_{\mathbf{C}}$ be a connected reductive subgroup, and let $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ be the graded $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -scheme defined in Notation 2.3.14. Then there is a homomorphism (in fact, closed imersion) of graded group schemes

$$ \spec\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H))\to{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times\mathcal{M}_{H} $$

over $\mathcal{M}_{H}\cong\spec\mathrm{ku}^{\ast}_{H}(\ast)$ constructed as the following composite:

$$ \displaystyle\spec\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H)) \displaystyle\to\spec\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\cong\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\times_{\spec\mathrm{ku}_{G}^{\ast}(\ast)}\spec\mathrm{ku}_{H}^{\ast}(\ast) \displaystyle\hookrightarrow({\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times T_{\beta}/\!\!/W)\times_{T_{\beta}/\!\!/W}\mathcal{M}_{H}\cong{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times\mathcal{M}_{H}. $$

Let $A_{\beta}$ denote the $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{H}}$ -algebra of regular functions on the quotient $({\check{{G}}}\times\mathcal{M}_{H})/\spec\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H))$ over $\mathcal{M}_{H}$ , so that $A_{\beta}$ admits a canonical grading, as well as a canonical action of ${\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)$ . Define $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ to be the $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\spec A_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho))$ .

The reason that $H_{\mathbf{C}}$ is assumed to be reductive is precisely thanks to the proof of Theorem 3.6.4, which implies Proposition 3.7.16 below; this result ensures consistency in notation (and showing that Theorem 3.7.18 implies Theorem 3.2.7 at least in the simply-laced and connected case):

#### Proposition 3.7.16.

Let $G$ be a simply-laced and connected compact Lie group, let $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ be the associated algebraic group over $\mathbf{C}$ , and let $H_{\mathbf{C}}\subseteq G_{\mathbf{C}}$ be a connected reductive subgroup which is optimal in the sense of Hypothesis 3.5.2. Let $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]\to\mathbf{Q}$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map given by rationalization and sending $\beta\mapsto 0$ . Then there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\otimes_{\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]}\mathbf{Q}\simeq\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q}). $$

#### Remark 3.7.17.

Construction 3.7.15 is not a good definition (hence the “faux”). For instance, it is not defined intrinsically to the $G$ -action on $G/H$ , and instead uses the algebra of functions on ${{\check{{G}}}}$ ; in other words, as we said in the introduction, it is defined by “playing games” with the subcategory of locally constant sheaves. Its only saving grace is Proposition 3.7.16.

Instead, Construction 3.7.15 is intended to be a replacement of Definition 3.6.1 in the case where one does not have an analogue of Theorem 3.2.3. It might be the case that there is a well-behaved $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\widetilde{\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ of constructible sheaves of $G[\![t]\!]$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -modules defined on ind-finite $G[\![t]\!]$ -spaces such as $G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!)$ . In the nonequivariant case, there is a well-behaved notion of constructible sheaves of $\mathrm{ku}$ -modules defined using exit path categories à la [Lur3, Appendix A]. Roughly, then, $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ would be an “associated graded for the Postnikov filtration” on $\widetilde{\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ .

Namely, suppose that there was a $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -linear $\infty$ -category ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ , and an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -coalgebra $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathcal{R}}}}}$ in $\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}({\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G};\mathrm{ku}))$ which lifted the regular sheaf (corresponding to $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}}\in\mathcal{P}\mathrm{erv}_{G[\![t]\!]\times G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Z})$ ). Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}$ denote the de-equivariantization of ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ with respect to this ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -Hopf algebra, and let $\mathrm{IC}_{0}\in{\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ denote the $!$ -pushforward of the constant sheaf in ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G[\![t]\!]/H[\![t]\!];\mathrm{ku})\simeq{\mathrm{Shv}}^{c}_{H[\![t]\!]}(\ast;\mathrm{ku})$ . Then the full subcategory $\mathcal{C}$ of $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}$ generated by $\mathrm{IC}_{0}\star\widetilde{{\check{{\mathcal{R}}}}}$ can be identified with left modules over the $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra $\widetilde{A}:=\End_{\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathrm{IC}_{0}\star\widetilde{{\check{{\mathcal{R}}}}})$ . Finally, let ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ denote the equivariantization of $\mathcal{C}$ with respect to the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -Hopf algebra $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathcal{R}}}}}$ . If the assumptions of Theorem 3.1.3 applied (see also Remark 3.1.5), we could identify $\pi_{\ast}\widetilde{A}=A_{\beta}$ , and the coaction of $\widetilde{{\check{{\mathcal{R}}}}}$ on $\widetilde{A}$ induces the $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}}$ -coaction on $A_{\beta}$ from Construction 3.7.15. In particular, $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ is an “associated graded” of ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ .

Of course, it would be ideal to work with ${\mathrm{Shv}}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})$ itself instead of the ad hoc $\infty$ -category of Construction 3.7.15. However, carrying out the above program has proven to be very challenging (for both technical and conceptually interesting reasons), and Construction 3.7.15 is an attempt to salvage the situation somewhat.

Corollary 3.7.11 implies the following generalization of Theorem 3.2.7:

#### Theorem 3.7.18.

Let $G$ be a simply-laced and connected compact Lie group. There is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal equivalence of $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear $\infty$ -categories

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(G\times G)[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)), $$

where again the symbol $G$ on the right-hand side denotes the split form of the compact Lie group over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

By Construction 3.7.15, we need to check that there is a graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{O}_{{G}(-2\rho)_{\beta}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{({\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times{T}_{\beta}/\!\!/W)/({T}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{G(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)}T_{\beta}/\!\!/W)}, $$

for which it in turn suffices to check that there is a graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -linear isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{({\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)\times{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W)/({\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\times_{{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)}{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W)}. $$

For simplicity, let us momentarily ignore gradings. We claim that the ${\check{{G}}}$ -orbit of the image of $\kappa:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}/\!\!/W\to{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ is isomorphic to ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ , so that the right-hand side above is $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}}$ . For this, it suffices to show that the ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit of the image of $\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}$ is isomorphic to ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ where $\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}\to{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{B}}}$ is as in Definition 3.7.9. First, we claim that ${\check{{B}}}\cdot\im(\widetilde{\kappa})\subseteq{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ . Indeed, if $x\in{\check{{T}}}_{\beta}$ , then for a fixed $b\in{\check{{B}}}$ , there is an isomorphism $Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(b\cdot\widetilde{\kappa}(x))\to Z_{{\check{{B}}}}(\widetilde{\kappa}(x))$ sending $g\mapsto bgb^{-1}$ . It is not difficult to show that both ${\check{{B}}}\cdot\im(\widetilde{\kappa})$ and ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ are flat over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ (the latter because it is an open subscheme of ${\check{{B}}}_{\beta}$ , which is smooth over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ ), so it suffices to show that the inclusion ${\check{{B}}}\cdot\im(\widetilde{\kappa})\subseteq{\check{{B}}}_{\beta}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is an isomorphism after inverting $\beta$ and setting $\beta=0$ . By Lemma 3.7.4, this is equivalent to the following pair of well-known facts: the inclusions ${\check{{B}}}\cdot\im(\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{T}}}\to{\check{{B}}})\subseteq{\check{{B}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ and ${\check{{B}}}\cdot\im(\widetilde{\kappa}:{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}})\subseteq{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ are isomorphisms. (This reduces to the Jordan decomposition and the fact that $e_{\beta=1}$ and $e_{\beta=0}$ are representatives for the open ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbits in the ${\check{{N}}}$ and $\mathfrak{n}$ , respectively.)

Since ${\check{{G}}}_{\beta}$ is normal and irreducible, the desired isomorphism $\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\beta}}\cong\mathcal{O}_{{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}}$ is therefore a consequence of the following claim (and the algebraic Hartogs lemma): the complement of ${\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\beta}\subseteq{\check{{G}}}(-2\rho)_{\beta}$ is of codimension $\geq 2$ . This complement is flat over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ , and so it suffices to check the claim after inverting $\beta$ and setting $\beta=0$ . Again, this reduces to the well-known facts (see e.g., [Hum, Theorem 4.13] for the group case) that the closed subschemes in ${\check{{G}}}$ and ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ of irregular elements has complement of codimension $\geq 2$ . ∎

## 4. Case-by-case analysis

### 4.1. Summary

The main results of this section can be summarized below in Table 3, refining Table 1. This table should be read as follows: there is an equivalence of $\mathbf{Q}$ -linear $\infty$ -categories

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}({\check{{Y}}}/{\check{{G}}}_{X})\times\text{``Normalization''}), $$

where ${\check{{Y}}}$ is a ${\check{{G}}}_{X}$ -space, and the normalization term can be identified with $\mathfrak{l}_{X}^{\wedge}/\!\!/L^{\wedge}_{X}$ , where $L^{\wedge}_{X}$ is the subgroup of ${\check{{G}}}$ from [KS]. This is not the Lie algebra of the dual Levi ${\check{{L}}}(X)$ . Here, ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ for each of the varieties in Table 3.

#### Warning 4.1.1.

Throughout this section, we will assume Hypothesis 3.5.2 holds for these spherical varieties. As mentioned in Remark 3.6.3, it is possible that this hypothesis simply fails; so it should perhaps be stated at the outset that our actual goal in this section is to explicitly verify the conditions of Theorem 3.6.4, and that Hypothesis 3.5.2 only comes in when using Theorem 3.6.4 to prove an equivalence of $\infty$ -categories.

#### Remark 4.1.2.

Below, we will only prove the bare equivalence 4.1. We have not proved compatibility with the equivalence of Theorem 3.2.7, but we expect it to be possible using the second part of Theorem 3.6.4. One can check the desired compatibility in type $A_{n}$ . In fact, Conjecture 3.6.15 (essentially) implies Corollary 4.3.19.

During the course of proving the equivalence 4.1 in types $A_{n}$ , $D_{2}$ , and $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ , we will in fact prove an analogue of the above equivalence for $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathrm{ku})^{\mathrm{faux}}$ ; the conceptual intepretation of the results thus obtained will be discussed in a later section. The reader only interested in Theorem 3.4.16 should simply set $\beta=0$ everywhere.

#### Remark 4.1.3.

Whenever we work with integral (i.e., non-rational) coefficients, we will always invert the order of the Weyl group of $G$ .

The proof of the equivalence 4.1 for the spherical varieties of Table 3 relies on the criterion of Theorem 3.6.4 (or, in the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic case, Proposition 3.7.20). Namely, in each case, we will:

- • compute the $H$ -equivariant homology $\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Q})$ of $\Omega(G/H)$ ; and

- • show that $\spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Q})$ can be identified with the group scheme ${\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}$ from Theorem 3.6.4(a).

The key input into the first part is the calculation of the $H$ -equivariant homology of the based loop space $\Omega S^{V}$ of the representation spheres (i.e., one-point compactifications) of (unitary) $H$ -representations $V$ . This is accomplished in Corollary 4.2.17. The underlying analytic spaces of each of the rank one spherical varieties in Table 3 are either representation spheres themselves, or can be built as a quotient of a representation sphere, so Corollary 4.2.17 lets us describe the $H$ -equivariant ( $\mathrm{ku}$ -)homology of $\Omega(G/H)$ . Once $\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Q})$ has been computed, the second part is rather straightforward. Indeed, the group scheme ${\check{{J}}}_{X}=\spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Q})$ is quite simple in each example, and the main difficulty in checking Theorem 3.6.4(a) is in bookkeeping weights.

#### Remark 4.1.4.

In applying Theorem 3.6.4, we will see that the only piece of $\spec\mathrm{H}_{H}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}_{H}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/W_{H}\cong{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ which “interacts” with ${\check{{Y}}}/{\check{{G}}}_{X}$ via the Kostant section of Theorem 3.6.4 is the coordinate corresponding to the highest degree fundamental invariant of $W_{H}$ acting on ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}_{H}^{\ast}(2)$ . The remainder of ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}_{H}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/W_{H}$ makes up the normalization term $\mathfrak{l}_{X}^{\wedge}/\!\!/L^{\wedge}_{X}$ .

Since this section is somewhat technical, let us make an observation about the main qualitative difference between root types T and G which appears in the course of the proof. Let us focus on the prototypical cases of types $A_{1}$ (which is of root type T) and $D_{2}$ (which is of root type G). In these cases, there is no normalization term; in general, this normalization term comes from cohomology classes in $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(BG;\mathbf{Q})$ which do not “interact” with $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Q})$ .

- (a) In type $A_{1}$ , there are isomorphisms of derived $\mathbf{Q}$ -schemes

$$ \spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathrm{H}^{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}_{\ast}(\Omega(\mathrm{SO}_{3}/\mathrm{SO}_{2});\mathbf{Q})\cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[b,x]/bx\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]\times_{T^{\ast}[2]\mathbf{A}^{2}[2,0]/\mathrm{SL}_{2}[-2\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}]}\mathbf{A}^{1}[2], $$

where $b$ lives in degree $2$ , and $x$ lives in degree $-2$ . Let ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ denote the above group scheme. Then ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ is not flat over $\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]=\spec\mathbf{Q}[x]$ . The nonflatness of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ over ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ is characteristic of the case of roots of type T. Topologically, this corresponds to the observation that the $H$ -invariant subspace $(G/H)^{H}$ is just $S^{0}$ . (In general, one can use Atiyah-Bott localization and Theorem 3.6.4 to see that the phenomenon of $\Omega(G/H)^{H}$ being rationally contractible is Langlands dual to the triviality of the stabilizer in ${\check{{G}}}$ of a generic point in ${\check{{M}}}$ .)

- (b) In type $D_{2}$ , there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\cong\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ , so that $\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{3}\simeq\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ . Then, there are isomorphisms of derived $\mathbf{Q}$ -schemes

$$ \spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathrm{H}^{\mathrm{SO}_{3}}_{\ast}(\Omega(\mathrm{SO}_{4}/\mu_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{3});\mathbf{Q})\cong\spec\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathrm{H}^{\mathrm{SO}_{3}}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SO}_{3};\mathbf{Q})\\ \cong\spec\mathbf{Q}[x,a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-a^{-1}}{2x}]^{\mathbf{Z}/2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)\times_{\mathfrak{sl}_{2}[2-2\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}]/\mathrm{SL}_{2}[-2\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}]}\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2), $$

where the map $\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)\to\mathfrak{sl}_{2}[2-2\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}]/\mathrm{SL}_{2}[-2\rho_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}]$ is the Kostant slice sending $x^{2}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ x^{2}&0\end{pmatrix}$ . Let ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ denote the above group scheme. Then ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ is flat over $\mathbf{A}^{1}[2]/\!\!/(\mathbf{Z}/2)=\spec\mathbf{Q}[x^{2}]$ , and can be identified with the group scheme of regular centralizers of ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ . The identification of ${\check{{J}}}_{X}$ over ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}^{\ast}[2]/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}$ with (the product of the normalization factor with) the group scheme of regular centralizers of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ is characteristic of the case of roots of type G. Topologically, this corresponds to the observation that the $T$ -invariant subspace $(G/H)^{T}$ is just $S^{1}$ (where $T$ is a maximal torus of $H$ ).

#### Remark 4.1.5.

As the reader will see, the calculations of this section are quite repetitive; it is possible to handle all the type T and type G cases simultaneously, but at the risk of confusing oneself with various gradings (in other words, the repetitive nature of this section is mostly for my purposes, and one can conglomerate these calculations into a more uniform argument if desired). However, the similarity between the examples in Table 3 seems to be related to much deeper phenomena in relative Langlands duality; we hope to explore this in future work. Let us briefly mention the sort of phenomena we hope to explain.

If $X$ is an affine (spherical) $G$ -variety, it is often the case that there is some subgroup ${G}^{\prime}\subseteq{G}$ and a $G^{\prime}$ -variety $X^{\prime}$ such that up to grading, the dual stack ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ associated to the $G$ -variety $X$ via Conjecture 3.4.12 can be identified with the dual stack ${\check{{M}}}^{\prime}/\hat{G}^{\prime}$ associated to $X^{\prime}$ . In particular, the dual groups of $X$ and $X^{\prime}$ are isomorphic.

For instance, suppose $X=\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ . By Theorem 3.4.16, the underlying ungraded dual stack associated to the $\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ -variety $X$ is ${\check{{M}}}/\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}\cong T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})/\mathrm{SL}_{2}\times\mathbf{A}^{n-1}$ . Let $G^{\prime}=\mathrm{SO}_{3}\times\mathrm{SO}_{2n-2}\subseteq{G}=\mathrm{SO}_{2n+1}$ . However, by Theorem 3.4.16, this is also the underlying ungraded dual stack associated to the ${G}^{\prime}$ -variety ${G}^{\prime}/(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{2n-2})$ . The underlying homotopy type of $X$ is the sphere $S^{2n}$ , and the underlying homotopy type of ${G}^{\prime}/(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\times\mathrm{SO}_{2n-2})$ is $S^{2}$ ; there is no direct relation between these homotopy types, but nevertheless, the dual stacks are isomorphic up to grading. (In this sense, the grading plays an absolutely vital role, and getting it right is one of the reasons for the repetitive/tedious nature of this section.) Spencer Leslie has told us that he is working on describing the relationship between such ${G}^{\prime}$ and the “endoscopy of $X$ ”; see [Les].

### 4.2. Homology of loops on a sphere

The proof of Theorem 3.4.16 rests on a key topological calculation, namely that of the equivariant homology $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ for $S^{V}$ being the one-point compactification of a (unitary) representation $V$ of a (compact) torus $T$ . To illustrate this calculation, let us begin with two simple (but exemplifying) examples.

#### Notation 4.2.1.

Recall the group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ from Construction 2.3.6, i.e., the graded group scheme over $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ given by $\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}]$ where $\beta$ lives in weight $2$ , and with coproduct determined by the formula $t\mapsto t\otimes t$ . The invertible class $t$ defines a homomorphism $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}\to(\mathbf{G}_{m})_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]}$ which exhibits $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ as an affine blowup of $(\mathbf{G}_{m})_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]}$ at the identity of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ . The kernel of this map is given by a group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}^{0}$ , whose underlying graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -scheme is isomorphic to $\mathbf{A}^{1}(-2)=\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}]$ , and whose group structure is given by

$$ \tfrac{t-1}{\beta}\mapsto\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}\otimes 1+1\otimes\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}+\beta\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}\otimes\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}. $$

A compact torus $T$ defines a group scheme $T_{\beta}$ given by $\Hom(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T),\mathbf{G}_{\beta})$ , and hence a subgroup scheme $T_{\beta}^{0}=\ker(T_{\beta}\to T)$ . Let $\lambda:T\to S^{1}$ be a character, let $T_{\lambda}$ denote its kernel, and let $n\geq 0$ . Define $T_{\lambda,\beta}^{[n]}$ to be the closed subscheme of $T_{\beta}$ given by the $n$ th infinitesimal neighborhood of $T_{\lambda,\beta}$ ; similarly for $T_{\lambda,\beta}^{0,[n]}$ . Let $x_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{O}_{T_{\beta}}$ denote the function which cuts out $T_{\lambda,\beta}$ .

Since $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}=\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}]$ , if we call $x=\tfrac{t-1}{\beta}$ (so that $x$ lives in weight $-2$ ), this ring can be identified with $\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x}]$ . It will often be more convenient to consider this presentation of $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ . For $n\in\mathbf{Z}$ , we will write $[n](x)$ to denote the $n$ -fold sum of $x$ in the group structure on $\mathbf{G}_{\beta}$ , so that $[n](x)=\frac{(1+\beta x)^{n}-1}{\beta}$ .

#### Example 4.2.2.

Let $\mathrm{std}$ denote the standard $1$ -dimensional complex representation of $S^{1}$ , and consider the one-point compactification $S^{\mathrm{std}}$ (so that its underlying nonequivariant space is $S^{2}$ ). We will be interested in computing the (for the moment) Borel-equivariant homology $\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}};\mathbf{Z})=\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}$ . There is a homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}};\mathbf{Z})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};\mathbf{Z})\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}. $$

The $E_{2}$ -page can be computed easily to be

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathbf{Z}[a,b][\![x]\!]/a^{2}, $$

where $x\in\mathrm{H}^{2}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};\mathbf{Z})$ is the first Chern class, $a\in\mathrm{H}_{1}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}};\mathbf{Z})$ coming from the inclusion $S^{1}\subseteq\Omega S^{2}$ , and $b\in\mathrm{H}_{2}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}};\mathbf{Z})$ coming from the map $S^{2}\to\Omega S^{2}$ adjoint to the Hopf fibration $S^{3}\to S^{2}$ . There is a single differential $d_{2}(a)=bx$ (if $\mathrm{std}$ is replaced by $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}$ for some $n\geq 1$ , this differential is simply replaced by $nbx$ ). After running this differential, the spectral sequence is concentrated in even degrees, and we find that

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[b][\![x]\!]/bx. $$

Compare to Example 3.5.16(b) with $n=1$ . Exactly the same calculation holds with $\mathbf{Z}$ replaced by $\mathrm{ku}$ :

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}}]^{hS^{1}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[\beta,b][\![x]\!]/b[n](x). $$

#### Remark 4.2.3.

Note that the quotient $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}/x$ is precisely the nonequivariant homology $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}};\mathbf{Z})$ . Indeed, Example 4.2.2 says that the class $b$ is $x$ -torsion in $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}$ ; therefore, if we kill $x$ , the class $bx$ in degree zero bumps up to a class $\sigma(bx)$ in degree $1$ .

One interesting observation is that the homotopy quotient $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]_{hS^{1}}$ (which would compute what is traditionally called equivariant homology) is not concentrated in even degrees: namely, the fact that $b$ is $x$ -torsion implies that the $\mathbf{Z}[\![x]\!]$ -linear dual of $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}$ will have odd homotopy groups.

Let us mention that the fact that $\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}}]^{hS^{1}}$ is concentrated in even degrees is an absolutely crucial fact (related to the subtleties of Lemma 2.1.6), which has important implications in the Langlands duality of Theorem 3.4.16, and emphasizes the role of equivariance in our discussion.

#### Example 4.2.4.

Again, let $\mathrm{std}$ denote the standard $1$ -dimensional complex representation of $S^{1}$ , and consider the one-point compactification $S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ (so that its underlying nonequivariant space is $S^{3}$ ). We will be interested in computing the (for the moment) Borel-equivariant homology $\mathrm{H}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}};\mathbf{Z})=\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hS^{1}}$ . There is a homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}};\mathbf{Z})\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathrm{H}^{\ast}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};\mathbf{Z})\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hS^{1}}. $$

Now, the $E_{2}$ -page is simply $\mathbf{Z}[b][\![x]\!]$ , where again $x\in\mathrm{H}^{2}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};\mathbf{Z})$ is the first Chern class, and $b\in\mathrm{H}_{2}(\Omega S^{3};\mathbf{Z})$ is the generator. The entire spectral sequence is concentrated in even degrees, so there can be no differentials, and the spectral sequence degenerates. This implies that

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hS^{1}}\cong\mathbf{Z}[b][\![x]\!]. $$

Compare to Example 3.5.16(a) with $n=1$ .

#### Remark 4.2.5.

Note that in Example 4.2.4, the class $bx$ is topologically nilpotent, so that $1+bx$ is invertible. The inclusion $S^{\mathbf{R}}\subseteq S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ induces a map $\mathbf{Z}\cong\Omega S^{\mathbf{R}}\to\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ ; this map is in fact just the inclusion of the $S^{1}$ -fixed points of $\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ . Therefore, there is a map $\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathbf{R}}]\cong\mathbf{Z}[a^{\pm 1}]\to\mathbf{Z}[\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hS^{1}}$ , and it is not difficult to check that this map sends $a\mapsto 1+bx$ .

In order to describe the main calculation, we need to introduce some notation.

#### Setup 4.2.6.

Let $T$ be a compact torus, and let $V$ be a (unitary) representation of $T$ with no nonzero fixed vectors. Let $\Lambda(V)$ denote the set of weights of $V$ , and let $\chi_{V}:T\to S^{1}$ to denote the character of $V$ . Moreover, if $\lambda:T\to S^{1}$ is a character, we will write $T_{\lambda}$ to denote the kernel of $\lambda$ . Note that $\langle{\chi_{V},\lambda}\rangle$ is the dimension of the $\lambda$ -weight space of $V$ (as a complex vector space).

#### Setup 4.2.7.

Throughout, when we talk about coefficients in a homology theory, we will invert the prime $2$ . This will be implicit in the notation, and we will write $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ to denote $\mathbf{Z}[1/2]$ .

#### Definition 4.2.8.

In Setup 4.2.6, fix an integer $j\in\mathbf{Z}$ , and define $\mathcal{C}_{V}$ to be the graded $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -scheme given by the union

$$ \mathcal{C}_{V}(-j)=(T_{\beta}^{0}\times\{0\})\cup\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda(V)}(T_{\lambda,\beta}^{0,[\langle{\chi_{V},\lambda}\rangle]}\times\mathbf{A}^{1}(-j)). $$

We will call $\mathcal{C}_{V}(-j)$ the $V$ -coordinate axes with weight $j$ .

#### Definition 4.2.9.

In Setup 4.2.6, consider the blowup

$$ X:=\mathrm{Bl}\left(\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda(V)}(T_{\lambda,\beta}^{[\langle{\chi_{V},\lambda}\rangle]}\times\{1\})\subseteq T_{\beta}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}\right). $$

Let $\mathcal{B}_{V}$ denote the complement of the proper preimage of $\{0_{T_{\beta}}\}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}$ from $X$ , so that $\mathcal{B}_{V}$ is an affine blowup of $T_{\beta}\times\mathbf{G}_{m}$ .

#### Example 4.2.10.

Suppose $T=S^{1}$ , and let $V$ denote the weight $n$ representation of $T$ . Then there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{C}_{V}(-j)\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,b]/bx, $$

where $x$ lives in weight $-2$ and $b$ lives in weight $j$ . This is the reason for the terminology of Definition 4.2.8: we are more concerned with the weight of the function $b$ on $\mathcal{C}_{V}(-j)$ . Similarly, there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{B}_{V}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,t^{\pm 1},\tfrac{t-1}{\beta},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{(a-1)\beta}{t-1}]\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x}], $$

where $t$ lives in weight $0$ (so $\frac{t-1}{\beta}$ lives in weight $2$ ), and $a$ lives in weight $0$ (so $\tfrac{(a-1)\beta}{t-1}$ lives in weight $2$ ).

#### Example 4.2.11.

More generally, let $T=(S^{1})^{m}$ , and let $V$ denote the representation $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}d_{i}\mathrm{std}_{i}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n_{i}}$ . Then

$$ \mathcal{C}_{V}(-j)\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x_{1},\cdots,x_{m},\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x_{i}},b]/b\prod_{i=1}^{m}[n_{i}](x_{i})^{d_{i}}, $$

with each $x_{i}$ in weight $-1$ and $b$ in weight $j$ . Similarly, we have

$$ \mathcal{B}_{V}\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x_{1},\cdots,x_{m},\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x_{i}},a^{\pm 1},\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tfrac{a-1}{[n_{j}](x_{j})^{d_{j}}}], $$

where each $x_{i}$ lives in weight $-1$ , and $a$ lives in weight $0$ (so $\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tfrac{a-1}{[n_{j}](x_{j})^{d_{j}}}$ lives in weight $2\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{j}=\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V)$ ). This immediately implies:

#### Lemma 4.2.12.

In Setup 4.2.6, the fiber of the projection map $\mathcal{B}_{V}\to\mathbf{G}_{m}$ over $\{1\}\in\mathbf{G}_{m}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{C}_{V}(-\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))$ .

#### Theorem 4.2.13.

In Setup 4.2.6, let $S^{V}$ denote the one-point compactification of $V$ . Then there are graded isomorphisms of $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}$ -algebras

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V}) \displaystyle\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}_{V}(2-2\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))}, \displaystyle\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}) \displaystyle\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{B}_{V}}. $$

In particular, both $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ and $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}})$ are concentrated in even weights, and are graded commutative $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}$ -algebras.

#### Remark 4.2.14.

If $T$ acts on a pointed space $X$ (and we are given some multiplicative presentation of $\Omega X$ as a $T$ -space), the equivariant homology $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega X)$ need not be a commutative $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -algebra in general: a priori, it is only an associative $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -algebra, since $\Omega X$ generally only admits the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -space. Although $\Omega S^{V}$ is still generally only an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -space (unless $V$ is isomorphic to $\emptyset$ , $\mathbf{R}$ , or $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ ), Theorem 4.2.13 implies that $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ and $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}})$ are in fact concentrated in even weights, and generated (as a $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}$ -algebra) by a single class. In particular, it is necessarily a commutative $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -algebra2525 25 This is a manifestation of the fact that in classical algebra, an associative algebra being commutative is a property, whereas in homotopy theory, it is more structure.. We will implicitly use this observation throughout this article, by rewriting Theorem 4.2.13 as a pair of graded isomorphisms of $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]$ -schemes

$$ \displaystyle\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V}) \displaystyle\cong{\mathcal{C}_{V}(2-2\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))}, \displaystyle\spec\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}) \displaystyle\cong{\mathcal{B}_{V}}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 4.2.13.

Let us first compute the Borel $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -homology of $\Omega S^{V}$ . Write $V=\mathbf{C}^{n}$ ; then there is a homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}^{hT}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]}\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathbf{C}^{n}})\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V}]^{hT}. $$

The EHP sequence for $\Omega S^{V}$ is the fibration given by

$$ S^{2n-1}\to\Omega S^{2n}\to\Omega S^{4n-1}. $$

Note that the map $S^{2n-1}\to\Omega S^{2n}\simeq\Omega\Sigma S^{2n-1}$ is not defined equivariantly: the unit sphere $S(V)$ does not have $T$ -fixed points (by assumption on $V$ ), so there is no $T$ -equivariant basepoint of $S(V)$ with respect to which the reduced suspension can be constructed. In any case, the EHP sequence splits after inverting the prime $2$ (this is the reason for Setup 4.2.7), which implies that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{2n})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,a,b]/a^{2}, $$

where $|a|=2n-1$ and $|b|=4n-2$ . (See, e.g., Example 3.5.16 for a massively overblown derivation of this isomorphism.)

#### Remark 4.2.15.

That the EHP sequence splits after inverting the prime $2$ goes all the way back to Serre: on [Ser, p. 281], he showed that there is a equivalence

$$ \mathrm{can}\times\Omega[\iota_{2n},\iota_{2n}]:S^{2n-1}\times\Omega S^{4n-1}\to\Omega S^{2n} $$

after inverting $2$ . Here, $[\iota_{2n},\iota_{2n}]\in\pi_{4n-1}(S^{2n})$ denotes the Whitehead product of $\iota_{2n}\in\pi_{2n}(S^{2n})$ with itself.

It follows that the $E_{2}$ -page can be identified with

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\mathcal{O}_{T_{\beta}}^{\wedge}[a,b]/a^{2}. $$

Each weight $\lambda\in\Lambda(V)$ defines a function $x_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{O}_{T_{\beta}}$ , and there is a single differential in this spectral sequence, given by

$$ d_{\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V)}(a)=b\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda(V)}x_{\lambda}. $$

One can see this by reducing to the case when $V$ is one-dimensional, in which case 4.2 follows from Example 4.2.2. The $E_{\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V)+1}$ -page of the spectral sequence is then concentrated entirely in even degrees, and therefore degenerates. This implies that

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V}]^{hT}\cong\mathcal{O}_{T_{\beta}}^{\wedge}[b]/b\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda(V)}x_{\lambda}. $$

Note that this is nearly $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}_{V}(2-2\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))}$ , except for the completion.

The above calculation of $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V}]^{hT}$ is enough to imply the desired calculation of $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ . Indeed, let $e_{j}$ be a given basis vector of $\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)$ , let $T_{j}$ denote the kernel of $e_{j}:T\to S^{1}$ , and let $V_{j}$ denote the fixed locus $V^{T_{j}}$ . Let $\mathcal{U}_{j}$ denote the complement of the union of the closed subschemes $T^{\prime}_{\beta}$ ranging over all closed subgroups $T^{\prime}\subseteq T$ which do not contain $T_{j}$ . Then Lemma 2.4.6 gives an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})|_{\mathcal{U}_{j}}\simeq\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V_{j}})|_{\mathcal{U}_{j}}. $$

Indeed, since $(\Omega S^{V})^{T_{j}}\simeq\Omega(S^{V})^{T_{j}}$ , it suffices to note that $(S^{V})^{T_{j}}\simeq S^{V_{j}}$ . Using the fracture square and induction on the dimension of $V$ , one finds that there is a Cartesian square

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V}]^{hT}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}|_{T_{\beta}-\bigcup_{1\leq j\leq m}T_{j,\beta}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}^{tT}.} $$

This precisely has the effect of correcting the completion in 4.3, which recovers $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}_{V}(2-2\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))}$ .

Turning to $\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ , let us first compute the Borel $T$ -equivariant $\mathrm{ku}$ -homology of $\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}$ . Write $V=\mathbf{C}^{n}$ ; then there is a homotopy fixed points spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}\cong\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}^{hT}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta]}\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathbf{C}^{n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hT}. $$

There is an isomorphism $\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathbf{C}^{n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})\cong\mathrm{ku}_{\ast}[b]$ , where $|b|=2n$ . This implies that the entire spectral sequence is concentrated in even degrees, so there are no differentials, and we find that

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}[\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}]^{hT}\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,b][\![x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}]\!]. $$

To compute $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}})$ , we will again use the fracture square. Again, it is not difficult to reduce to the case when $T=S^{1}$ and $V={\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}}$ . Then there is a Cartesian square

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})^{\wedge}_{x}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})[x^{-1}]\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})^{\wedge}_{x}[x^{-1}].} $$

Note that the $S^{1}$ -fixed point set $(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})^{S^{1}}$ is simply $\Omega S^{1}\cong\mathbf{Z}$ , so that Lemma 2.4.6 lets us identify the bottom-left corner with $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{T}[a^{\pm 1}]$ . By 4.5, we can identify the above Cartesian square with

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,b][\![x]\!]\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,a^{\pm 1},x^{\pm 1},\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x}]\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,b](\!(x)\!),} $$

where the bottom map sends $a\mapsto 1+bx$ . It follows that

$$ \mathrm{ku}^{S^{1}}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{\mathrm{std}^{\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}n}\oplus\mathbf{R}})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[\beta,x,\tfrac{1}{1+\beta x},a^{\pm 1},\tfrac{a-1}{x}]\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{B}_{V}}, $$

where $\tfrac{a-1}{x}\mapsto b$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.2.16.

The evenness of Theorem 4.2.13 is always true for $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}})$ (in fact, more generally for $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}^{2n+1}})$ for any $n\geq 0$ ), but it is not true for $\mathrm{ku}^{T}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}^{2n}})$ if $n>0$ .

The following result is an immediate consequence of Theorem 4.2.13 and Proposition 2.3.15.

#### Corollary 4.2.17.

Let $G$ be a connected compact Lie group whose $\pi_{1}$ is torsion-free, and let $T\subseteq G$ be a maximal torus with associated Weyl group $W$ . If $V$ is a (unitary) $G$ -representation with no nonzero $T$ -fixed vectors, there are graded isomorphisms of $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -schemes

$$ \displaystyle\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V}) \displaystyle\cong\mathcal{C}_{V}(2-2\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(V))/\!\!/W, \displaystyle\spec\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V\oplus\mathbf{R}}) \displaystyle\cong\mathcal{B}_{V}/\!\!/W. $$

#### Remark 4.2.18.

If $H$ is a compact Lie group with maximal torus $T$ and $V$ is a (unitary) $H$ -representation with no nonzero $T$ -fixed vectors, then we implicitly view $\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ as a commutative algebra over $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ as in Remark 4.2.14. In the case-by-case analysis below, this is in fact not as abusive as it might seem: namely, if $G$ is a compact Lie group and $H\subseteq G$ is a closed inclusion of subgroups such that $S^{V}\cong G/H$ as $H$ -equivariant spaces, the natural ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -algebra structure on the $\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ -linear dual of $\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega S^{V})$ in fact upgrades to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra structure via Corollary 3.5.12. In particular, the commutative ring structure on the completion of $\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega S^{V})$ does indeed have a homotopical origin.

### 4.3. Type $A_{n}$ : $\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}/\mathrm{GL}_{n}$

Our goal in this section is to prove Theorem 3.4.16 in type $A_{n}$ , i.e., for the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}$ -variety $\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}/\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ . We will write $G=\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}$ and $H=\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ , so ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{GL}_{n+1}$ . Recall from Table 3 that ${\check{{G}}}_{X}=\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ . Equip $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ with the grading where the entries of a matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ have the following weights: $a$ and $d$ live in weight zero, $b$ lives in weight $2n$ , and $c$ lives in weight $-2n$ ; we will write $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(-2n\rho_{{\check{{G}}}_{X}})$ to denote this graded group.

#### Theorem 4.3.1 (Theorem 3.4.16 in type $A_{n}$ ).

There is an equivalence of $\mathbf{Q}$ -linear $\infty$ -categories

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{G[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(G(\!(t)\!)/H(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T^{\ast}[2n](\mathbf{A}^{2}[2n,0])/\mathrm{GL}_{2}[-2n\rho_{{\check{{G}}}_{X}}]\times\mathfrak{gl}_{n-1}[2]/\!\!/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}). $$

#### Example 4.3.2.

For instance, if $n=1$ , we have ${\check{{G}}}_{X}={\check{{G}}}$ , and so Theorem 4.3.1 states that there is an equivalence of $\mathbf{Q}$ -linear $\infty$ -categories

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\!(t)\!)/\mathbf{G}_{m}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T^{\ast}[2](\mathbf{A}^{2}[2,0])/\mathrm{GL}_{2}[-2\rho_{{\check{{G}}}_{X}}]). $$

The Koszul dual of this statement is also proved as [BF2, Theorem 1.8(2)]. A variant of this equivalence is a special case of Corollary 4.3.19:

$$ \mathrm{Shv}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}[\![t]\!]}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\!(t)\!)/\mathbf{G}_{m}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}(T^{\ast}[2](\mathbf{A}^{2}[2,0])/\mathrm{SL}_{2}[-2\rho_{{\check{{G}}}_{X}}]). $$

In other words, the Hamiltonian $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -variety dual to $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ is $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})$ . Let us quickly check part of Conjecture 3.5.11 in this case. The poset of $B$ -orbit closures in $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ is the same as the poset of $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -orbit closures in $\mathbf{P}^{1}\cong\mathrm{PGL}_{2}/B$ ; this is simply

$$ \{0\}\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{1}\supseteq\{\infty\}. $$

Similarly, the poset of ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit closures in $\mathbf{A}^{2}$ is given by

$$ \{(0,0)\}\subseteq\{y=0\}\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{2}, $$

which is indeed in bijection with the above set. (One can also see this poset of ${\check{{B}}}$ -orbit closures by computing the set of irreducible components of $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\ast}}\{0\}$ . This is cut out inside $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})\cong\mathbf{A}^{4}$ by the ideal $(v_{1}w_{1}-v_{2}w_{2},v_{2}w_{1})$ , whose primary decomposition is

$$ (v_{1}w_{1}-v_{2}w_{2},v_{2}w_{1})=(v_{1}v_{2})\cap(w_{1},w_{2})\cap(w_{1}^{2},v_{2}w_{1},v_{1}w_{1}-v_{2}w_{2},v_{2}^{2}); $$

so the fiber product $T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\ast}}\{0\}$ has three irreducible components.)

#### Remark 4.3.3.

There is a relationship between Theorem 4.3.1 and the mirabolic Satake equivalence of [BFGT], which studies the spectral decomposition of the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ -variety $(\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1})/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ . In our language, their main result states that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1})[\![t]\!]}((\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1})(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\\
\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathrm{GL}_{n}\backslash T^{\ast}(\Hom(\mathbf{A}^{n},\mathbf{A}^{n-1}))/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}), $$

where $\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}$ denotes the $\infty$ -category of perfect complexes on a shearing. (We have omitted the precise gradings for brevity.) If $n=2$ , the above equivalence specializes to

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{(\mathrm{GL}_{2}\times\mathrm{GL}_{1})[\![t]\!]}((\mathrm{GL}_{2}\times\mathrm{GL}_{1})/\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\!(t)\!));\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathrm{GL}_{2}\backslash T^{\ast}\mathbf{A}^{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}), $$

and forgetting the $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -quotient on the coherent side is equivalent to extending $\mathrm{GL}_{2}[\![t]\!]\times\mathrm{GL}_{1}[\![t]\!]$ -equivariance to $\mathrm{GL}_{2}[\![t]\!]\times\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\!(t)\!)$ -equivariance on the left-hand side; this in turn recovers Theorem 4.3.1 for the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ -variety $\mathrm{GL}_{2}/\mathbf{G}_{m}$ .

If $n>2$ , then using the equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}[\![t]\!]}(\ast;\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n-1}^{\ast}/_{\psi}N_{n-1}) $$

with $N_{n-1}$ being the unipotent radical of a Borel subgroup of $\mathfrak{gl}_{n-1}$ and $\psi$ being a nondegenerate character on its Lie algebra, the mirabolic Satake equivalence implies that

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{\mathrm{GL}_{n}[\![t]\!]}(\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\!(t)\!)/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}(\!(t)\!);\mathbf{Q})\simeq\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathrm{GL}_{n}\backslash T^{\ast}(\Hom(\mathbf{A}^{n},\mathbf{A}^{n-1}))/_{\psi}N_{n-1}). $$

Justin Hilburn informed me that using the results of [NT], one obtains an isomorphism of stacks

$$ \mathrm{GL}_{n}\backslash T^{\ast}(\Hom(\mathbf{A}^{n},\mathbf{A}^{n-1}))/_{\psi}N_{n-1}\cong T^{\ast}(\mathbf{A}^{2})/\mathrm{GL}_{2}\times\mathfrak{gl}_{n-2}/\!\!/\mathrm{GL}_{n-2}, $$

which shows that Theorem 4.3.1 (up to the question of matching up gradings) is in fact a consequence of the mirabolic Satake equivalence of [BFGT]. This also follows from the Cartesian square 3.19 applied to the example of $H^{\mathrm{diag}}=\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}^{\mathrm{diag}}\subseteq G\times H=\mathrm{GL}_{n}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ (see Remark 3.6.22).

#### Remark 4.3.4.

One can use the analogue of Theorem 4.3.1 for sheaves with coefficients in $\mathbf{Z}$ to show that there is an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Loc}(\Omega(\mathrm{U}(n+1)/\mathrm{U}(n));\mathbf{Z})\simeq\\
