$$ \mu_{g}:\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(g)\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(g). $$

It is not difficult to see that this map is compatible with composition in $g$ , in the sense that if $g^{\prime}:B^{\prime}\to B^{\prime\prime}$ is another morphism and $c:\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(g)\otimes_{A}\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(g^{\prime})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(g^{\prime}\circ g)$ is the composition coming from functoriality of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ -centers, there is a commutative digram of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $A$ -algebras

Since $A$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(\mathrm{LMod}_{A}(\mathcal{C}))$ admits an ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -monoidal structure. Taking $g=g^{\prime}=\mathrm{id}_{B}$ , we find that the map $\widetilde{\mu}:=\mu_{\mathrm{id}_{B}}$ can be upgraded to a map $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}$ -algebras in ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $A$ -algebras, i.e., of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $A$ -algebras. In particular, this equips $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})$ -algebra.

The factorization through the centralizer $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(f)$ is a consequence of the construction of $\widetilde{\mu}$ . Namely, the unit map $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)$ can be regarded as giving a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{id}_{B}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes A)\otimes_{A}B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B} $$

of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $A$ -algebra maps, which is in turn obtained via a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{f} \textstyle{\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{id}_{B}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes A)\otimes_{A}B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B,} $$

where the square is given by the tensor product in $\mathcal{C}$ . The universal property of the centralizer $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(f)$ implies that there is a factorization

$$ \textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{id}_{B}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes A)\otimes_{A}B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mathrm{id}_{B}} \textstyle{(\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(f)\otimes A)\otimes_{A}B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B,} $$

which in turn gives the desired $A$ -linear map $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(f)\otimes A\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)$ factoring the unit $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(A/\mathcal{C})\otimes\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(B/A)$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.2.8.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a presentably symmetric monoidal stable $\infty$ -category, let $A\in\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}(\mathcal{C})$ , and let $B\in\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(\mathrm{Mod}_{A}(\mathcal{C}))$ with unit map $f:A\to B$ . Then the fiber $\fib(f)$ admits the structure of a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ .

#### Proof.

The map $f$ factors as a composite

$$ A\xrightarrow{{g}}\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(B/\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{{h}}B, $$

where $g$ is a map of ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebras in $\mathcal{C}$ , and the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -map $h:\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(B/\mathcal{C})\to B$ is the unit. Let $T_{B/\mathcal{C}}^{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ denote the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -cotangent complex of $B$ (viewed as an object of $\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(\mathcal{C})$ ), so that $T_{B/\mathcal{C}}^{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}[-n]$ admits the structure of a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ , and there is a map $T_{B/\mathcal{C}}^{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}[-n]\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(B/\mathcal{C})$ of nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebras. We claim that there is a Cartesian square

$$ \textstyle{\fib(f)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{T_{B/\mathcal{C}}^{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}[-n]\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{g} \textstyle{\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}(B/\mathcal{C}),} $$

so that $\fib(f)$ is canonically equipped with the structure of a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ . To see this, note that the factorization of $f$ as $h\circ g$ implies a fiber sequence

$$ \fib(g)\to\fib(f)\to\fib(h). $$

It therefore remains to identify $\fib(h)$ with $T_{B/\mathcal{C}}^{\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}[-n]$ ; but this follows from [Fra, Theorem 1.1] (or equivalently [Lur3, Theorem 7.3.5.1]). ∎

#### Remark 5.2.9.

Proposition 5.2.8 immediately implies [HL, Corollary 8.8], which states that if $A$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebra in $\mathrm{Sp}$ , $B$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $B$ -algebra, and $\alpha\in\pi_{\ast}(A)$ maps to zero in $\pi_{\ast}(B)$ , then all the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra Dyer-Lashof operations on $\alpha$ also map to zero in $B$ . Indeed, if $f:A\to B$ is the unit map, $\alpha$ lifts to $\pi_{\ast}\fib(f)$ by assumption; but $\fib(f)$ is a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra by Proposition 5.2.8, so all ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -power operations on $\alpha$ must also map to zero in $\pi_{\ast}(B)$ , as desired.

We are now in a position to explain the “coisotropic” property of the map 5.2 (or more generally of 5.3). To motivate the use of this term, let us make the following observation.

#### Observation 5.2.10.

Let $P_{\ast}$ be a graded adic algebra with Poisson bracket of weight $n$ , and let $Q_{\ast}$ be a graded commutative adic $P_{\ast}$ -algebra. The map $\spf Q_{\ast}\to\spf P_{\ast}$ is coisotropic if the unit map $P_{\ast}\to Q_{\ast}$ is surjective, and its kernel is closed under the Poisson bracket. Suppose that the Poisson structure on $P_{\ast}$ arises from an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -ring $P$ with $\pi_{\ast}P\cong P_{\ast}$ , and $Q_{\ast}$ arises as the homotopy groups of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $P$ -algebra $Q$ with unit map $f:P\to Q$ . Then, Proposition 5.2.8 implies that $\fib(f)$ admits a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{n+1}}}$ -algebra structure. We therefore find that the map $\spf Q_{\ast}\to\spf P_{\ast}$ is the inclusion of a coisotropic subvariety precisely when the map $\pi_{\ast}P\to\pi_{\ast}Q$ is surjective (since its kernel is then $\pi_{\ast}\fib(f)\subseteq\pi_{\ast}P$ , which is closed under the Poisson bracket).

Using Observation 5.2.10 with $n=2$ , one can show that the map of 5.2 is very nearly coisotropic: the only obstructions are given by a completion issue, and that the map 5.2 need not be a closed immersion (i.e., the unit map is $\mathrm{ku}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G)\to\mathrm{ku}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H))$ need not be surjective). Keeping these in mind, we are led to the following.

#### Observation 5.2.11.

Let $H\subseteq G$ be a closed subgroup of a compact Lie group such that the $\mathrm{ku}_{G}$ -linear dual $\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\Omega G)^{\vee}}$ of $\mathcal{F}_{G}(\Omega G)$ and the $\mathrm{ku}_{H}$ -linear dual $\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}}$ of $\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))$ are concentrated in even degrees2828 28 This is a very mild condition, which can be checked to hold in all examples in this article. However, it is somewhat subtle, in the sense that working equivariantly is crucial. See, e.g., Example 4.2.2.. Remark 5.2.6 and Lemma 5.2.7 together imply that the unit map $\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\Omega G)^{\vee}}\to\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}}$ exhibits $\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}}$ as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\Omega G)^{\vee}}$ -algebra, and so Proposition 5.2.8 implies that the fiber of the unit map admits a nonunital ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -algebra structure. For instance, this means that if the unit map induces a surjection on homotopy (which is not common!), the map $\spf\pi_{\ast}\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{H}(\Omega(G/H))^{\vee}}\to\spf\pi_{\ast}\widehat{\mathcal{F}_{G}(\Omega G)^{\vee}}$ will be the inclusion of a coisotropic subvariety.

#### Remark 5.2.12.

Applying Lemma 5.2.7 to Proposition 5.2.8 is of course quite “lossy”, in the sense that the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -algebra structure from Lemma 5.2.7 is of a very specific kind. The setup of Lemma 5.2.7 hopefully exhibits further special features which allows us to understand Expectation 5.2.1 further.

#### Remark 5.2.15.

The coisotropicity of Observation 5.2.11 can be understood from the perspective of boundary theories for topological quantum field theories (TQFTs for short). Namely, consider an $n$ -dimensional TQFT $Z:\mathrm{Bord}_{n}\to\mathrm{Cat}_{(\infty,n-1)}$ (valued in, e.g., some $(\infty,n)$ -category of “presentable” $\mathbf{C}$ -linear $(\infty,n-1)$ -categories). Then $Z(S^{j})$ is naturally with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{j+1}}}$ -algebra object in the $(\infty,n-j)$ -category of $\mathbf{C}$ -linear $(\infty,n-j-1)$ -categories, since $S^{j}$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{j+1}}}$ -algebra in $\mathrm{Bord}_{n}$ . Indeed, if $I$ is a set of $n$ points on $\mathbf{R}^{j+1}$ , the manifold $S^{j+1}-I$ can be viewed as a cobordism $\amalg_{i=0}^{n}S^{j}\rightsquigarrow S^{j}$ .

A boundary theory $\mathcal{B}$ for $Z$ is a natural transformation from the trivial $n$ -dimensional TQFT (i.e., whose value on a point is the unit object) to $Z$ , so that $\mathcal{B}$ is an $(n-1)$ -dimensional TQFT. In particular, $\mathcal{B}(S^{n-2})$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ -algebra object of the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ -monoidal $\infty$ -category $Z(S^{n-2})$ . The cell decomposition $S^{n-1}\cong D^{n-1}\amalg_{S^{n-2}}D^{n-1}$ implies that $Z(S^{n-1})$ is the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -algebra (in $\mathbf{C}$ -modules) given by the ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ -center of $Z(S^{n-2})$ . This implies that $\mathcal{B}(S^{n-2})$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $Z(S^{n-1})$ -algebra.

A special case of the above situation is when $Z$ is determined by an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ -algebra $A$ in $\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathrm{Sp})$ , in which case $\mathcal{B}$ is determined by an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n}}}$ - $A$ -algebra $B$ . The statement that $\mathcal{B}(S^{n-2})$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $Z(S^{n-1})$ -algebra then translates to the statement that $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-2}}}(B/A)$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}(A/\mathbf{C})$ -algebra, which is precisely Lemma 5.2.7.

Returning to the general case, the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{n-1}}}$ - $Z(S^{n-1})$ -algebra on $\mathcal{B}(S^{n-2})$ implies that there is a map $\spec\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{B}(S^{n-2})\to\spec\pi_{\ast}Z(S^{n-1})$ , at least if $n\geq 3$ . Proposition 5.2.8 (and the general discussion in Observation 5.2.11) implies that this map should be coisotropic (in an appropriate sense) for the Poisson bracket of weight $n-1$ on $\pi_{\ast}Z(S^{n-1})$ . It will be too much of a digression to discuss this here, but this coisotropicity can in fact be deduced from the secondary product structure (as discussed in [BBB+]) on local operators in extended TQFTs arising via topological descent.

### 5.3. Equivariant spectra, graded groups, and duality over $\mathrm{MU}$

Motivated by the discussion of the previous sections, we suggest that there is a generalization of the Langlands duality equivalences of Theorem 3.7.18 and Theorem 3.4.16 to “coefficients in complex cobordism”. It might be that the story suggested below is not the “correct” one, but nevertheless it leads to some interesting questions that we expect to play an important role in the future. In order to motivate our presentation, we will need to recall some results of Hausmann regarding equivariant complex cobordism.

In order to state results analogous to Theorem 3.7.18 and Theorem 3.4.16, we need to incorporate genuine equivariance into this picture. The primary motivation for this discussion is the work of Hausmann (see [Hau]).

#### Notation 5.3.1.

In what follows, we will write $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}}$ to denote the $\infty$ -category of global spectra as defined in [Sch1], so that each compact Lie group $G$ defines a symmetric monoidal restriction functor $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}}\to\mathrm{Sp}_{G}$ to the $\infty$ -category of genuine $G$ -equivariant global spectra. These functors are jointly conservative over all $G$ . Note that [Sch1] works in the model-categorical setting, but we will work with the corresponding $\infty$ -categories; the reader is referred to [LNP] for a discussion of global spectra in $\infty$ -categorical language. We will not really need this theory below, but it is useful to review the context in which global complex cobordism arose.

#### Construction 5.3.2.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the family of abelian compact Lie groups, let $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A}}$ denote the $\infty$ -category of Definition 2.2.6, and let $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ast}$ denote the (non-full) subcategory of pointed objects in $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A}}$ . Then $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ast}$ is equivalent to the (nerve of the) topological category of abelian compact Lie groups.

Let $\underline{R}$ be an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebra in $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}}$ . Then there is a natural lax symmetric monoidal functor $\underline{\tau}_{\geq\star}:\mathrm{Mod}_{\underline{R}}(\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}})\to\Fun(\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast},\mathrm{Mod}_{\tau_{\geq\star}R}^{\mathrm{fil}})$ sending $\underline{A}\in\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}}$ to the functor $T\mapsto{\tau}_{\geq\star}^{T}(A_{T})$ . This constrution can be slightly modified as follows: let $\mathrm{Lat}$ denote the $1$ -category of lattices, so that Pontryagin duality naturally gives a fully faithful functor $\mathrm{Lat}\subseteq\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast}$ . Restricting $\underline{\tau}_{\geq\star}$ along this inclusion defines a functor

$$ \mathrm{Mod}_{\underline{R}}(\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}})\to\Fun(\mathrm{Lat},\mathrm{Mod}_{\tau_{\geq\star}R}^{\mathrm{fil}}). $$

We will write $\underline{\pi}_{\ast}$ to denote the composite functor

$$ \mathrm{Mod}_{\underline{R}}(\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{glob}})\xrightarrow{{\underline{\tau}_{\geq\star}}}\Fun(\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast},\mathrm{Mod}_{\tau_{\geq\star}R}^{\mathrm{fil}})\to\Fun(\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast},\mathrm{Mod}_{\pi_{\ast}R}^{\mathrm{gr}}). $$

Let $\underline{\mathrm{MU}}$ denote the global complex cobordism spectrum, so that $\underline{\tau}_{\geq\star}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}})$ defines a functor $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast}\to\mathrm{Mod}_{\tau_{\geq\star}\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ . In fact, this refines to a functor $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast}\to\mathrm{CAlg}_{\tau_{\geq\star}\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ , which in particular defines a functor $\text{$\mathchar 525$}^{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{op}}_{\ast}\to\mathrm{CAlg}_{\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{MU}}^{\mathrm{gr}}$ . Recall that the graded ring $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU})$ classifies the universal graded ( $1$ -dimensional) formal group law by Quillen’s [Qui]. Hausmann proved a similar characterization of $\underline{\pi}_{\ast}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}})$ , too.

#### Definition 5.3.3.

A graded ( $1$ -dimensional) group law is a functor $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}:\mathrm{Lat}\to\mathrm{CAlg}^{\heartsuit,\mathrm{gr}}$ equipped with an element $x\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{Z})_{-2}$ in weight $-2$ such that for every lattice $\Lambda$ and split injective homomorphism $\chi:\mathbf{Z}\to\Lambda$ , the sequence of graded abelian groups

$$ 0\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\Lambda)_{\ast+2}\xrightarrow{{\cdot\chi^{\ast}x}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\Lambda)_{\ast}\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\Lambda/\mathbf{Z}\chi)_{\ast}\to 0 $$

is exact. Such an element $x$ will be called a coordinate. Say that an $n$ -tuple $x^{(1)},\cdots,x^{(n)}$ of coordinates on a graded group law $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}$ is strict if each $x^{(j)}$ is a multiple of $x^{(1)}$ by a unit $\lambda_{j}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{Z})_{0}$ whose restriction along the map $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{Z})\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\{0\})$ is $1$ .

#### Example 5.3.4.

Graded group laws $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}:\mathrm{Lat}\to\mathrm{CAlg}^{\heartsuit,\mathrm{gr}}$ which preserve coproducts are simply specified by $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\{0\})$ , $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{Z})$ viewed as a Hopf algebra over $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\{0\})$ , and a regular element of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{Z})_{-2}$ which generates the augmentation ideal. In particular, graded generalized groups which preserve coproducts are the same as $1$ -dimensional linear graded algebraic groups over a graded commutative ring $R$ (namely $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}}(\{0\})$ ) which are weight-connected over $R$ .

The following result then gives a universal property for $\underline{\pi}_{\ast}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}})$ , analogous to Quillen’s theorem [Qui] establishing $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU})$ as the universal ring carrying a ( $1$ -dimensional) formal group law. Note that the “global” perspective is crucial in even formulating the universal property below.

#### Theorem 5.3.5 (Hausmann, [Hau, Theorem A]; Comezaña, [Com, XXVIII Theorem 5.3]; Löffler, [Lof]).

The ring $\underline{\pi}_{\ast}\underline{\mathrm{MU}}$ is concentrated in even weights, and $(\underline{\pi}_{\ast}\underline{\mathrm{MU}})(\Lambda)$ is a free $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU})$ -module for each lattice $\Lambda$ .

Moreover, for any $n\geq 0$ , let $x_{\tau}^{(1)},\cdots,x_{\tau}^{(n)}\in\underline{\pi}_{\ast}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}}^{\otimes n})$ denote the $n$ different tautological complex orientations of $\underline{\mathrm{MU}}$ . If $(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}},x^{(1)},\cdots,x^{(n)})$ is a strict $n$ -tuple of coordinates on a graded group law, there is a unique homomorphism of graded group laws $(\underline{\pi}_{\ast}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}}^{\otimes n}),x_{\tau}^{(1)},\cdots,x_{\tau}^{(n)})\to(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}},x^{(1)},\cdots,x^{(n)})$ which sends $x_{\tau}^{(j)}\mapsto x^{(j)}$ .

#### Construction 5.3.6.

If $\Lambda$ is a lattice, let $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}(\Lambda)$ denote the graded scheme $\spec\underline{\pi}_{\ast}(\underline{\mathrm{MU}})(\Lambda)$ . If $M$ is a finite $T$ -equivariant spectrum, let $\mathcal{F}_{T,M;\mathrm{MU}}$ denote the graded quasicoherent sheaf over $\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T))$ specified by $\pi_{\ast}^{T}(M^{\vee}\otimes\mathrm{MU}_{T})$ . This defines a functor $(\mathrm{Sp}_{T}^{\mathrm{fin}})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T)))$ , which should be viewed as the analogue of the functor $\mathrm{MU}^{\ast}(-):(\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathrm{fin}})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{MU}}$ . If $M$ is the suspension spectrum of a finite $T$ -space $X$ , let $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X;\mathrm{MU})=\mathcal{F}_{T,M;\mathrm{MU}}$ . If $X$ is a $T$ -space, let $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X;\mathrm{MU})^{\vee}$ denote the $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}(\mathbb{X}^{\ast}(T))}$ -linear dual of $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X;\mathrm{MU})$ , and if $X=\colim_{i\in\mathcal{I}}X_{i}$ is an ind-finite $T$ -space, let $\mathcal{F}_{T}(X;\mathrm{MU})^{\vee}=\colim_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{F}_{T}(X_{i};\mathrm{MU})^{\vee}$ .

Since the arguments establishing Theorem 3.2.15 and Theorem 3.7.10 ultimately reduce to the case of torus-equivariant (co)homology, if one is to generalize these results to equivariant $\mathrm{MU}$ , it is first natural to ask whether equivariant $\mathrm{MU}$ admits abelian descent. Perhaps the most naïve formulation of this question is the following: if $G$ is a connected Lie group whose $\pi_{1}$ is torsion-free, $T\subseteq G$ is a maximal torus, and $W$ is its Weyl group, does restriction induce an isomorphism $\pi_{\ast}^{G}(\mathrm{MU}_{G})\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\pi_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{MU}_{T})^{W}$ ? This turns out to be false:

#### Lemma 5.3.7 ([Sch2, Remark 1.2]).

The restriction map $\pi_{\ast}^{\mathrm{U}(n)}(\mathrm{MU}_{\mathrm{U}(n)})\to\pi_{\ast}^{T}(\mathrm{MU}_{T})$ is not injective if $n>1$ .

#### Remark 5.3.8.

It is also not known whether $\pi_{\ast}^{G}(\mathrm{MU}_{G})$ is concentrated in even degrees for a general compact Lie group $G$ . This is a famous open problem in equivariant algebraic topology; see [Uri].

#### Remark 5.3.9.

Lemma 5.3.7 leads to the issue of whether an appropriate analogue of Theorem 3.2.15 and Theorem 3.7.10 should use $G$ -equivariant $\mathrm{MU}$ , or instead a more limited analogue which is built from $A$ -equivariant $\mathrm{MU}$ over all compact abelian subgroups $A$ of $G$ . The resolution of this issue in the context of Langlands duality is not entirely clear to me, although it seems that the latter analogue of equivariant $\mathrm{MU}$ should be more relevant.

Naturally, one is interested in proving a “universal” analogue of Theorem 3.2.7 and Theorem 3.7.18. We will make some speculations about the form of such an equivalence, and discuss an actual mathematical statement relating to these speculations in Section 5.4. Far too many components of this discussion do not have well-behaved foundations at the moment, and so we will label everything below as a series of expectations. It is quite likely that these expectations are too naïve, and that more refinement is needed to make them “correct”. I apologize in advance for the speculative nature of this discussion!

#### Expectation 5.3.10.

Let $G$ be a topological group, and suppose that $X$ is a stratified finite space with $G$ -action respecting the stratification. Moreover, as in Remark 4.3.4, the above equivalence of $\infty$ -categories implies (by computing endomorphisms of the skyscraper sheaf at the basepoint of $\Omega G$ ) that there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega^{2}G;\mathbf{Z}[1/|W|])\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}BZ_{e}({\check{{G}}});\mathcal{O}). $$

For instance, if $G=\mathrm{SU}(n)$ (in which case one does not need to invert $n!$ ), the centralizer $Z_{e}(\mathrm{PGL}_{n})$ is isomorphic to the group scheme $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}$ of length $n$ Witt vectors (see [Dev2, Example 4.1.8]) where the $j$ th ghost coordinate lives in weight $2j$ : indeed, both group schemes can be identified with the group of matrices of the form

$$ Z_{e}(\mathrm{PGL}_{n})\cong\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{1}&x_{2}&x_{3}&\cdots&x_{n-1}\\
&1&x_{1}&x_{2}&\cdots&x_{n-2}\\
&&\ddots&\vdots&\cdots&\vdots\\
&&&1&x_{1}&x_{2}\\
&&&&1&x_{1}\\
&&&&&1\end{pmatrix}\right\}\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}. $$

There is then an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega^{2}\mathrm{SU}(n);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}B\mathbf{W}_{n-1};\mathcal{O}); $$

moreover, this isomorphism is compatible as $n$ varies. After base-changing to $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ , this recovers [Rav, Theorem A] and the main result of [Yam]. Note, also, that when $n=\infty$ , we get the statement that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega^{2}\mathrm{SU};\mathbf{Z})$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}B\mathbf{W};\mathcal{O})$ .3030 30 This can be seen directly as follows (we will ignore gradings for simplicity). Bott periodicity gives an equivalence $\Omega^{2}\mathrm{SU}\simeq\Omega\mathrm{BU}=\mathrm{U}$ , so it suffices to compute $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{U};\mathbf{Z})$ . This in turn can be understood via the colimit over $n$ of $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{U}(n);\mathbf{Z})$ ; moreover, $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{U}(n);\mathbf{Z})$ is the cobar construction on $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BU}(n);\mathbf{Z})$ . However, it is easy to see that $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\mathrm{BU}(n);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{W}_{n}}$ ; this implies that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BU}(n);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{W}_{n}^{\vee}}$ , where $\mathbf{W}_{n}^{\vee}$ is the Cartier dual of $\mathbf{W}_{n}$ . In particular, $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{U}(n);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(B\mathbf{W}_{n}^{\vee};\mathcal{O})$ . In the limit, we find that $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\mathrm{U};\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(B\mathbf{W}^{\vee};\mathcal{O})$ ; the identification with $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(B\mathbf{W};\mathcal{O})$ now follows from the Cartier self-duality of the (graded) Witt ring scheme (see, e.g., [Dev3, Remark C.2] for a reference). One way to interpret this discussion is that the algebraic manifestation of the Bott periodicity equivalence $\Omega\mathrm{SU}\simeq\mathrm{BU}$ is that $\mathbf{W}$ is Cartier self-dual, up to reversing the grading, as a graded commutative group scheme.

#### Remark 5.4.5.

The following discussion is a digression, and can be ignored by the uninterested reader. Recall that the regular nilpotent $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ is the Chern class of the determinant line bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . It is therefore natural to wonder if there is an analogue of the determinant line bundle for arbitrary spherical varieties $X$ , which reduces to the determinant line bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ in the group case for $G$ . If $\mathrm{Gr}^{X}$ denotes the relative Grassmannian of [BZSV, Section 8.2], there is a tautological map $\mathrm{Gr}^{X}\to\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , so one can simply consider the pullback of the determinant line bundle to $\mathrm{Gr}^{X}$ .

However, this construction seems lacking in at least two ways. First, in the group case for $G$ (so $X=(G\times G)/G^{\mathrm{diag}}$ ), one recovers the tensor square of the determinant line bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , and not the determinant line bundle itself. Second, in some sense, it misses the role of the determinant line bundle: namely, it captures the first nontrivial integral cohomology class on $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ , and hence the principal nilpotent $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , but the above line bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}^{X}$ does not capture anything “new”.

In order to understand the new phenomena which appear in the relative setting, suppose $X=G/H$ with $H\subseteq G$ being a connected reductive subgroup. Throughout this article, we have emphasized that the quotient $\Omega(G/H)\simeq\mathrm{Gr}_{G}/\mathrm{Gr}_{H}$ captures the homotopically interesting content of the local relative geometric Langlands conjectures, so it is natural to ask whether $\Omega(G/H)$ carries an analogue of the determinant line bundle. The answer to this particular question is “no” for a very naïve reason: if $G/H$ is $3$ -connected, as is often the case (e.g., $\mathrm{GL}_{n}/\mathrm{GL}_{n-1}$ for $n>2$ ), then $\mathrm{H}^{2}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Z})=0$ , and so all complex line bundles over $\Omega(G/H)$ are trivial.

However, if one relaxes the notion of a line bundle by allowing for categorification, the answer seems to be “yes”. Consider, for instance, the case of $\mathrm{Spin}_{2n+2}/\mathrm{Spin}_{2n+1}\simeq S^{2n+1}$ , so that $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\Omega S^{2n+1};\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathbf{Z}\langle{x}\rangle$ with $x$ in cohomological degree $2n$ . As we have seen in Theorem 4.6.1, the class $x$ plays the role of the principal nilpotent $e\in{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{X}$ (just as in Proposition 5.4.1). In any case, $x$ may be viewed as a map $\Omega S^{2n+1}\to K(\mathbf{Z},2n)$ , and hence it classifies a nontrivial $(2n-2)$ - $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -gerbe over $\Omega S^{2n+1}$ . When $n=1$ , this is simply the determinant line bundle over $\Omega S^{3}=\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}$ .

For larger $n$ , one can wonder whether this $(2n-2)$ - $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -gerbe arises from a vector bundle over $\Omega S^{2n+1}$ , i.e., whether the map $\Omega S^{2n+1}\to K(\mathbf{Z},2n)$ factors as a composite

$$ \Omega S^{2n+1}\xrightarrow{{f}}\mathrm{BSO}(2n)\xrightarrow{{c_{n}}}K(\mathbf{Z},2n). $$

Regarding this map, we have the following result, which suggests that, in general, a geometric and representation-theoretic construction/meaning of such putative determinant $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -gerbes on $\Omega(G/H)$ seems very interesting.

#### Lemma 5.4.6.

Such a factorization 5.8 is impossible for $n\geq 2$ .

#### Proof.

Let us begin with the cases $n\neq 1,2,4$ . When restricted to the bottom cell $S^{2n}\subseteq\Omega S^{2n+1}$ , the map $S^{2n}\to\mathrm{BSO}(2n)$ will classify a vector bundle $\xi$ over $S^{2n}$ whose Euler class is a generator of $\mathbf{Z}$ . If such a $\xi$ exists, the attaching map $S^{4n-1}\to S^{2n}$ of the top cell of the Thom space of $\xi$ will be a solution to the Hopf invariant one problem; so $n$ must be $1,2,4$ , giving a contradiction.

We have already seen that the factorization 5.8 exists when $n=1$ , so let us now look at the case $n=2$ . Let $S^{4}\to\mathrm{BSU}(2)=\mathbf{H}P^{\infty}$ denote the inclusion of the bottom cell, so that the map $\mathrm{BSU}(2)\to\mathrm{BSO}(4)$ defines a map $S^{4}\to\mathrm{BSO}(4)$ which induces the map $(0,1):\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ on $\mathrm{H}^{4}(-;\mathbf{Z})$ . One can identify $\pi_{j}(\mathrm{BSO}(4))\cong\pi_{j-1}(\mathrm{SO}(3)\times S^{3})$ , and our map $S^{4}\to\mathrm{BSO}(4)$ induces the map $(0,1):\mathbf{Z}\to\pi_{3}\mathrm{SO}(3)\oplus\mathbf{Z}$ on $\pi_{4}$ . To get the desired map $f$ , we would need the attaching map of the $8$ -skeleton of $\Omega S^{5}$ to be $2\nu\in\pi_{7}(S^{4})$ . However, this is false; see [Dev1]. In brief, the attaching map of the $8$ -skeleton is given by the Whitehead bracket $[\iota_{4},\iota_{4}]\in\pi_{7}(S^{4})$ , which was computed in [Tod, Equation 5.8] to be $\pm(2\nu-\Sigma\nu^{\prime})$ . (Here, $\nu^{\prime}:S^{3}\wedge S^{3}\cong S^{6}\to S^{3}$ is the “Blakers-Massey” map which generates $\pi_{6}(S^{3})$ . It is characterized by the property that the composite $S^{3}\times S^{3}\to S^{6}\to S^{3}$ sends two unit quaternions $(x,y)$ to the commutator $xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ .) Since $\Sigma\nu^{\prime}\neq 0\in\pi_{7}(S^{4})$ , the desired factorization cannot exist.

The only remaining case is $n=4$ . Here, again, an argument similar to that of [Dev1] works to show that the desired extension does not exist. Namely, let $S^{8}\to\mathrm{BSO}(8)$ denote the vector bundle whose sphere bundle is the octonionic Hopf bundle $S^{15}\to S^{8}$ . As in [Mim, Page 133], one can identify $\pi_{j}\mathrm{SO}(8)\cong\pi_{j}(\mathrm{SO}(7)\times S^{7})$ ; and our map $S^{8}\to\mathrm{BSO}(8)$ induces the map $(0,1):\mathbf{Z}\to\pi_{7}(\mathrm{SO}(7))\oplus\mathbf{Z}$ on $\pi_{8}$ . In order to extend this to a map $\Omega S^{9}\to\mathrm{BSO}(8)$ , we would need the attaching map of the $16$ -skeleton of $\Omega S^{9}$ to be $2\sigma\in\pi_{15}S^{8}$ . However, the attaching map of the $16$ -skeleton is given by the Whitehead bracket $[\iota_{8},\iota_{8}]\in\pi_{15}(S^{8})$ , which was computed in [Tod, Equation 5.17] to be $\pm(2\sigma-\Sigma\sigma^{\prime})$ . Here, $\sigma$ is the Hopf map and $\sigma^{\prime}\in\pi_{14}(S^{7})$ is an octonionic version of the Blakers-Massey map (defined, as in the preceding paragraph, using the commutator of two unit octonions). Since $\Sigma\sigma^{\prime}\neq 0\in\pi_{15}(S^{8})$ , the desired factorization cannot exist. ∎

Our goal is to prove an analogue of Proposition 5.4.1 over the sphere spectrum in the simplest case of $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ , and (a piece) of the second part of loc. cit. when $n=2$ . Since our goal is to illustrate certain phenomena, as opposed to proving the most general statement, we will only stick to this simple case.

First, we need a construction describing a passage from homotopy theory to algebraic geometry. In previous sections, we implicitly used the construction taking in a commutative ring spectrum $R$ and producing the (graded) affine scheme $\spec\pi_{\ast}(R)$ . This construction is well-behaved if $R$ is concentrated in even degrees, but generally not so otherwise; for example, if $R$ is the sphere spectrum, the scheme $\spec\pi_{\ast}(S^{0})$ is an absolute nightmare, and so something like $\spec\pi_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)_{+})$ would be even more complicated. One important insight suggested by chromatic homotopy theory is that the algebro-geometric object associated to a ring spectrum which is not even should instead be a (graded) stack. This perspective is made precise (for ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -rings) in [HRW] and [DHRY]. Let us briefly recall the relevant construction.

#### Recollection 5.4.7.

An ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $A$ will be called even if $\pi_{\ast}(A)$ is concentrated in even weights. If $R$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring spectrum, let $\mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ denote the filtered stack

$$ \mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}:=\colim_{R\to A}\spec\tau_{\geq\star}(A), $$

where the colimit is taken over all ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring maps $R\to A$ with $A$ being even. The structure sheaf of $\mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ defines a filtered ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $\mathrm{F}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}R:=\lim_{R\to A}\tau_{\geq\star}A$ . If $M$ is an $R$ -module, let $\mathcal{F}_{M}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ denote the quasicoherent sheaf over $\mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ defined by $\lim_{R\to A}\tau_{\geq\star}(A\otimes_{R}M)$ . Of course, if $R$ is already even, $\mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}\cong\spec\tau_{\geq\star}(R)$ . The unit map $S^{0}\to R$ defines a map $\mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}\to\mathcal{M}_{S^{0}}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ .

A map $R\to A$ is called an eff cover (for “evenly faithfully flat”) if for every even ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $R$ -algebra $B$ , the base-change $A\otimes_{R}B$ is even and the map $\pi_{\ast}(A)\to\pi_{\ast}(A\otimes_{R}B)$ is faithfully flat. If $R$ admits an eff cover $R\to A$ by an even ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring $A$ , there is an equivalence

$$ \mathcal{M}_{R}^{\mathrm{fil}}\cong\colim_{\mathbf{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}}}\spec\tau_{\geq\star}(A^{\otimes_{R}\bullet+1}). $$

If $M$ is an $R$ -module, $\mathcal{F}_{M}^{\mathrm{fil}}$ can be identified with $\lim_{\mathbf{\Delta}}\tau_{\geq\star}(M\otimes_{R}A^{\otimes_{R}\bullet+1})$ . Each of these filtered stacks and quasicoherent sheaves defines graded stacks and quasicoherent sheaves, which we will simply denote by $\mathcal{M}_{R}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{M}$ . For example,

$$ \mathcal{M}_{R}=\colim_{R\to A}\spec\pi_{\bullet}(A), $$

where $\bullet$ denotes the grading.

#### Example 5.4.8.

The map $S^{0}\to\mathrm{MU}$ is an eff cover: if $B$ is an even ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring, it admits a complex orientation, and so $\mathrm{MU}\otimes B\cong B[\mathrm{BU}]$ ; but $\mathrm{BU}$ has even cells, so that $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU}\otimes B)$ is a free $\pi_{\ast}(B)$ -module on classes in even weights, and hence is itself concentrated in even weights. Furthermore, results of Quillen, Araki, Landweber, and Novikov (see [Qui, Ara, Lan, Nov]) identify $\mathcal{M}_{S^{0}}$ with the moduli stack $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ of graded ( $1$ -dimensional) spin formal groups in the sense of [Mil]. Explicitly, if $R$ is a commutative ring, an $R$ -point of $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ is the data of a line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ over $\spec(R)$ , a formal group $\hat{\mathbf{G}}$ over $\spec(R)$ , and isomorphism $\omega_{\hat{\mathbf{G}}}\cong\mathcal{L}^{\otimes 2}$ . We will write $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}$ to denote the universal spin formal group over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ , and $\omega$ to denote the line bundle over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ given by $\omega_{\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}}$ . Note that there is a canonical square root $\omega^{1/2}$ ; this plays the role of the “weight $1$ ” line bundle $\mathcal{O}(1)$ which appears throughout this article.

Any spectrum $M$ therefore defines a quasicoherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}_{M}$ on $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ . If $X$ is a space, let $\mathcal{F}(X;S^{0})$ denote the ind-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}_{(S^{0})^{X_{+}}}$ associated to the spherical cochains $(S^{0})^{X_{+}}$ , so that the pullback of $\mathcal{F}(X;S^{0})$ along the map $\spec\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{MU})\to\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ can be identified with $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{MU}^{X_{+}}$ . Note that the diagonal on $X$ equips $\mathcal{F}(X;S^{0})$ with the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -algebra in $\mathrm{IndCoh}(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}})$ . For instance, let $q:\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}\to\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ denote the universal spin formal group over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ ; then $\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};S^{0})\cong\mathcal{O}_{\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}}$ . If $X$ is a finite space, let $\mathcal{F}(X;S^{0})^{\vee}$ denote the $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}$ -linear dual of $\mathcal{F}(X;S^{0})$ .

Let us now return to the calculation at hand.

#### Construction 5.4.9.

Let $X$ be a scheme (or even a stack), let $\mathcal{L}$ be a line bundle over $X$ , and let $\mathcal{L}^{\times}$ denote the associated $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -torsor. Let $\mathbf{W}$ denote the Witt ring scheme, so that it has a $\mathbf{G}_{m}$ -action where the $n$ th ghost coordinate has weight $2n$ . Let $\mathbf{W}(\mathcal{L})=\mathbf{W}\times^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\mathcal{L}^{\times}$ denote the associated Witt group scheme over $X$ . Quotienting by the Verschiebung, one obtains the length $n$ Witt group scheme $\mathbf{W}_{n}(\mathcal{L})$ . Its Cartier dual will be denoted $\mathbf{W}_{n}^{\vee}(\mathcal{L}^{-1})$ .

Using that $\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)$ has even cells, we may identify $\mathcal{M}_{\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)_{+}}$ with $\spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})^{\vee}$ , which is described in the following result. It can be viewed as a refinement of [Dev2, Example 4.1.8], and an analogue of Proposition 5.4.1 for $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ .

#### Lemma 5.4.10.

Let $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}$ denote the universal spin formal group over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ , and let $\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}^{\vee}$ denote its Cartier dual. There is an isomorphism

$$ \spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})^{\vee}\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega) $$

of group stacks over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ , and which induces an isomorphism

$$ \spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee}(\omega^{-1})\cong\Hom(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}^{\vee},\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee}) $$

of group stacks over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ .

#### Proof.

The natural map ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1}\to\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n)$ is Bott’s generating complex from [Bot], so that there is an isomorphism

$$ \spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})^{\vee}\cong\spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\Sym_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}(\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};S^{0})^{\vee}), $$

the latter being the total space $\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};S^{0}))$ of the vector bundle $\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};S^{0})$ . It therefore suffices to observe that there is an isomorphism of group schemes

$$ \mathbf{V}(\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{n-1};S^{0}))\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega). $$

Since $\spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})^{\vee}$ is Cartier dual to $\spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);S^{0})$ , this implies that the latter is isomorphic to $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee}(\omega^{-1})$ (being Cartier dual to $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega)$ ). Lemma 3.7.6 implies that there is an isomorphism

$$ \Hom_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}^{\vee},\mathbf{W}_{n-1})\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega^{-1}), $$

since $\mathrm{Lie}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}})\cong\omega^{-1}$ ; this in turn implies that there is an isomorphism

$$ \Hom_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}}^{\vee},\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee})\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee}(\omega^{-1}), $$

as desired. ∎

#### Remark 5.4.11.

The group scheme $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega)$ over $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ can be identified with the fiber product $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\mathcal{O}(2))\times_{B\mathbf{G}_{m}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ , where the map $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}\to B\mathbf{G}_{m}$ classifies $\omega^{1/2}$ .

#### Remark 5.4.12.

The ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map $\Omega S^{3}\to{\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty}$ classifying the determinant line bundle induces a map

$$ \spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}({\mathbf{C}P}^{\infty};S^{0})^{\vee}\to\spec_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}\mathcal{F}(\Omega S^{3};S^{0})^{\vee}, $$

which, under Lemma 5.4.10 for $n=2$ can be identified with the canonical map $\hat{\mathbf{G}}^{\vee}\to\mathbf{V}(\omega)$ classifying the tautological section of $\mathrm{Lie}(\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}})\otimes\omega\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}$ . The canonical map

$$ \mathbf{W}_{1}^{\vee}(\omega^{-1})\cong\hat{\mathbf{V}}(\omega^{-1})^{\sharp}\to\hat{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathrm{univ}} $$

classifies the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle, and can be regarded as an analogue of the map $\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);\mathbf{Z})\to\mathbf{A}^{1}$ detecting the principal nilpotent element of ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}=\mathfrak{pgl}_{n}$ under Proposition 5.4.1.

According to Lemma 5.4.10, $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\omega)$ is to be understood as the analogue for the sphere of the centralizer $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(e)$ .3131 31 Note that there is an isomorphism $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(e)\cong\mathbf{W}_{n-1}(\mathcal{O}_{\spec(\mathbf{Z})})$ of group schemes over $\mathbf{Z}$ ; see [Dev2, Example 4.1.8]. Therefore, pulling back the isomorphism of Lemma 5.4.10 along the map $\spec(\mathbf{Z})\to\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ classifying the additive formal group precisely recovers the isomorphism $\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(n);\mathbf{Z})\cong Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(e)$ . In this setting, the grading on $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n}}(e)$ translates into tensor powers of the line bundle $\omega$ . As a consequence of the above discussion, $\mathbf{W}_{n-1}^{\vee}(\omega^{-1})$ is to be understood as the analogue for the sphere of the divided power enveloping algebra $U^{\sharp}(\mathfrak{pgl}_{n}^{e})$ .

Let us now illustrate an analogue of the second part of Proposition 5.4.1 for $G=\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .3232 32 To a representation theorist, this might seem like an especially trivial case, and likewise for a homotopy theorist; but perhaps for somewhat different reasons (either ${\check{{G}}}=\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is too simple, or $\Omega G=\Omega S^{3}$ is too simple). For a geometric representation theorist, this example is trivial for two reasons! In this case, we have the following (well-known) calculation.

#### Lemma 5.4.13.

Consider the dominant (co)weight $(i,j)$ of $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ , so that $i\geq j$ . Then there is a cell decomposition

$$ \mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{\leq(i,j)}\cong\begin{cases}\coprod_{0\leq k\leq(i-j)/2}\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i-k,j+k)}&i-j\text{ even},\\
\coprod_{0\leq k\leq(i-j-1)/2}\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i-k,j+k)}&i-j\text{ odd}.\end{cases} $$

If $i>j$ , there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,j)}\cong\mathrm{Map}(\spec\mathbf{C}[\epsilon]/\epsilon^{i-j},\mathbf{P}^{1}), $$

and $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,i)}=\spec(\mathbf{C})$ .

#### Proof sketch.

The only nontrivial claim is the calculation of $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,j)}$ for $i>j$ . Since there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,j)}\cong\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i-1,j-1)}$ , we may assume that $j=0$ . In this case, the $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbit of the loop $\begin{pmatrix}t^{i}&0\\ 0&t^{j}\end{pmatrix}$ consists of equivalence classes of matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}t^{i}a&b\\ t^{i}c&d\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!]$ . Note that both $b$ and $d$ cannot both be nonconstant, so $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,0)}$ is covered by the open loci where the constant term of $b$ (resp. of $d$ ) is invertible. Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}$ . Over the locus where the constant term of $b$ is invertible, we have the relation

$$ \tfrac{1}{\mathrm{det}(A)}\begin{pmatrix}t^{i}a&b\\
t^{i}c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}b&0\\
-at^{i}&adb^{-1}-c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
-t^{i}&db^{-1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Multiplying on the right by some strictly upper-triangular matrix in $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ , we can further assume that the bottom-right corner lies in $\mathbf{C}[t]/t^{i}$ . This gives an isomorphism between $\{b(0)\neq 0\}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,0)}$ and $\mathbf{C}[t]/t^{i}$ . One can similarly obtain an isomorphism between $\{d(0)\neq 0\}\subseteq\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{(i,0)}$ and $\mathbf{C}[t]/t^{i}$ via matrices of the form $\begin{pmatrix}t^{i}&bd^{-1}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ . The intersection of these two opens is precisely given by sending $db^{-1}\mapsto bd^{-1}$ , i.e., is obtained by gluing $\mathbf{C}[t]/t^{i}$ to itself along the inversion automorphism of $(\mathbf{C}[t]/t^{i})^{\times}$ . But this is precisely the mapping scheme $\mathrm{Map}(\spec\mathbf{C}[\epsilon]/\epsilon^{i-j},\mathbf{P}^{1})$ . ∎

#### Corollary 5.4.14.

Let $i\geq 0$ be an integer. If $J_{i}(S^{2})\hookrightarrow\Omega S^{3}$ denotes the partial James construction (with top cell in dimension $2i$ ), Lemma 5.4.13 gives a homotopy equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}^{\leq i}(\mathbf{C})\cong\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{GL}_{2}}^{\leq(i,-i)}(\mathbf{C})\simeq J_{2i}(S^{2}) $$

which is compatible with the homotopy equivalence $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}(\mathbf{C})\simeq\Omega S^{3}$ from Theorem 3.2.21.

Importantly, Lemma 5.4.13 implies that the Schubert varieties for $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ are rationally smooth, and so $\mathrm{IC}_{\lambda}$ is simply the pushforward of the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbf{C}}$ on $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathrm{SL}_{2}}^{\leq\lambda}$ . Therefore, if $i\geq 0$ is an integer (viewed as a dominant coweight of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ ), Corollary 5.4.14 implies that we may identify

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(2);\mathrm{IC}_{i})\cong\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(J_{2i}(S^{2});\mathbf{C}), $$

and hence Proposition 5.4.1 says (in particular) that

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}(J_{2i}(S^{2});\mathbf{C}[-2i])\cong{\check{{V}}}_{i} $$

with ${\check{{V}}}_{i}$ being the $(2i+1)$ -dimensional irreducible representation of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . To prove an analogue of the second half of Proposition 5.4.1, we therefore need to compute $\mathcal{F}(J_{2i}(S^{2});S^{0})$ as a $\mathcal{F}(\Omega S^{3};S^{0})$ -comodule (i.e., by Lemma 5.4.10, as a $\mathbf{V}(\omega)$ -representation). This is quite simple3333 33 Ha!:

#### Lemma 5.4.15.

Let $\Gamma^{j}_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}(\omega)=(\omega^{\otimes j})^{\Sigma_{j}}$ denote the $j$ th divided power of $\omega$ , and let $\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\leq 2i}(\omega)=\bigoplus_{0\leq j\leq 2i}\Gamma^{j}_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}(\omega)$ . Then there is an isomorphism

$$ \mathcal{F}(J_{2i}(S^{2});S^{0}[-2i])\cong\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\leq 2i}(\omega)\otimes\omega^{\otimes-i}, $$

and the inclusion $J_{2i}(S^{2})\to\Omega S^{3}$ induces the canonical map

$$ \mathcal{O}_{\hat{\mathbf{V}}(\omega^{-1})^{\sharp}}\cong\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\ast}(\omega)\to\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\leq 2i}(\omega). $$

Since the representation ${\check{{V}}}_{i}$ of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ (over $\mathbf{Z}$ ) can be identified with $\Gamma^{\leq 2i}(\mathbf{Z}\cdot e)$ , Lemma 5.4.15 can be viewed as an analogue of 5.9 over the sphere spectrum.

#### Remark 5.4.16.

Note that Lemma 5.4.15 (or even 5.9) only describes the action of the centralizer $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(e)$ , which is isomorphic to the unipotent radical of the upper-triangular Borel subgroup of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ , on the representation ${\check{{V}}}_{i}$ . However, it is well-known that the action of the entirety of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is completely encoded in natural structures present in this setting (this is a part of Theorem 3.2.3). Namely, in the classical setting of Proposition 5.4.1, the action of the Cartan subgroup $\mathbf{G}_{m}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is encoded by the natural grading on $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(\Omega\mathrm{SU}(2);\mathrm{IC}_{i})$ . Moreover, the action of the unipotent radical of the opposite Borel is encoded by the action of $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(e)$ under “Poincaré duality” on $J_{2i}(S^{2})$ . Although $J_{2i}(S^{2})$ is generally not a smooth manifold (and is often not even a Poincaré duality complex unless $(2i)!$ is inverted in the ring of coefficients), its integral homology and cohomology groups are dual to each other, with a shift of $4i$ .

Concretely, the abelian group underlying ${\check{{V}}}_{i}$ is $\mathbf{Z}\{v_{0},\cdots,v_{2i}\}$ , where one should understand $v_{j}$ as $\frac{e^{j}}{j!}$ placed in weight $2j-2i$ (so $v_{0}$ is in weight $-2i$ , and $v_{2i}$ is in weight $2i$ ). This specifies the action of the diagonal torus of $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ . The action of $Z_{\mathrm{PGL}_{2}}(e)\cong\begin{pmatrix}1&\ast\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ can be described through the action of $U^{\sharp}(\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}^{e})=\Gamma_{\mathbf{Z}}(e)$ : the element $\frac{e^{n}}{n!}\in U^{\sharp}(\mathfrak{pgl}_{2}^{e})$ sends $v_{j}\mapsto\binom{n+j}{n}v_{n+j}$ . Finally, the action of the strictly lower-triangular matrices ${\check{{N}}}^{-}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \ast&1\end{pmatrix}\subseteq\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ is described by “Poincaré duality”: this exchanges $v_{j}$ with $v_{2i-j}$ , and therefore $\frac{f^{n}}{n!}\in U^{\sharp}(\mathfrak{{\check{{n}}}}^{-})\cong\Gamma_{\mathbf{Z}}(f)$ sends $v_{j}\mapsto\binom{n+(2i-j)}{n}v_{j-n}$ .

The important point in the setting of Lemma 5.4.15 is that the action of the Cartan subgroup is encoded by the tensor powers of the line bundle $\omega$ appearing in $\mathcal{F}(J_{2i}(S^{2});S^{0}[-2i])$ . But as usual, the action of the unipotent radical of the opposite Borel is still encoded by “Poincaré duality” on $J_{2i}(S^{2})$ , which gives an isomorphism of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}$ -modules

$$ (\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\leq 2i}(\omega)\otimes\omega^{\otimes-i})^{\vee}\cong\Gamma_{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}}^{\leq 2i}(\omega)\otimes\omega^{\otimes i}. $$

As a first step towards Expectation 5.3.13, it would be interesting and important to prove an analogue of Proposition 5.4.1 with coefficients in the sphere spectrum for arbitrary (simply-connected and simply-laced) $G$ , and not just for $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ .

## Appendix A Sheaves on loop spaces

The proof of Theorem 3.6.4 relied on a comparison to positive characteristic. In the finite-type case, this comparison is provided by Theorem A.4, but the relevant comparison turns out to be more subtle in the infinite-type situation.

#### Notation A.1.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $X$ be an $R$ -scheme. Write $X(\!(t)\!)$ to denote the prestack sending an $R$ -algebra $S$ to $X(S(\!(t)\!))$ . Similarly, write $X[\![t]\!]$ to denote the prestack sending an $R$ -algebra $S$ to $X(S[\![t]\!])$ , and let $X[\![t]\!]/t^{n}$ denote the prestack sending an $R$ -algebra $S$ to $X(S[t]/t^{n})$ .

#### Definition A.2.

Let $X$ be an affine scheme defined over a commutative ring $R$ equipped with an action of a linear algebraic group $G$ over $R$ . The $G[\![t]\!]$ -action on $X(\!(t)\!)$ is called placid if:

- • there is a presentation $X(\!(t)\!)=\varinjlim_{j}X^{j}$ , where each $X^{j}$ is an inverse limit $\varprojlim_{n}X^{j}_{n}$ with each $X^{j}_{n}$ being a $G[\![t]\!]$ -equivariant scheme of finite type;

- • the action of $G[\![t]\!]$ on $X^{j}_{n}$ factors through $G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ for some $m_{n}\gg 0$ (compatibly in $n$ ).

- • The transition maps $X^{j}_{n}\to X^{j}_{n^{\prime}}$ are $G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ -equivariant affine smooth surjections.

Note that this is weaker than the condition that $G[\![t]\!]$ -action on $X(\!(t)\!)$ being placid in the sense of [BZSV, Section 7.3.1]: there, it is required that the transition maps $X^{j}_{n}\to X^{j}_{n-1}$ also be torsors for a unipotent group scheme.

#### Construction A.3.

In the above setup, let $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ denote the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ . Note that since the kernel of the surjection $G[\![t]\!]\twoheadrightarrow G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ is unipotent, and the action of $G[\![t]\!]$ factors through this surjection, the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ would be unchanged if we replace $m_{n}$ by any $m\geq m_{n}$ .

Let $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ denote the direct limit

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})=\varinjlim_{f_{j,n}^{!}}\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}}) $$

of the $\infty$ -categories $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ along $!$ -pullbacks. Finally, define

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X(\!(t)\!);{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})=\varinjlim_{g^{j}_{!}}\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}}) $$

to be the direct limit of the $\infty$ -categories $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X^{j};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ along the $!$ -pushforward functors associated to the maps $g^{j}:X^{j}\to X^{j+1}$ .

Suppose that there are only countably many $G[\![t]\!]$ -orbits on $X(\!(t)\!)$ . (If $X$ is affine and $G$ is reductive, Theorem 3.3.2 says that this is the case if and only if $X$ is a spherical $G$ -variety.) Then there are only finitely many $G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ -orbits on $X^{j}_{n}$ , and the maps $f_{j,n}:X^{j}_{n}\to X^{j}_{n-1}$ are $G[\![t]\!]$ -equivariant and respect the stratifications on $X^{j}_{n}$ and $X^{j}_{n-1}$ . Define $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(X(\!(t)\!);{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ to be the $\infty$ -category obtained via the above procedure, except where $\mathrm{Shv}^{\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ is replaced by the $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{et}}_{G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n};{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}})$ of $G[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ -equivariant étale sheaves on $X^{j}_{n}$ which are constructible with respect to the orbit stratification on $X^{j}_{n}$ .

#### Theorem A.4.

Let $q\gg 0$ be a large prime power. Fix a prime $\ell\neq p$ , and choose an isomorphism $\iota:{\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}}}\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathbf{C}$ . In Setup 3.2.18, suppose that the $H(R[\![t]\!])$ -action on $X(\!(t)\!)$ is placid. Then is there is a localization $R\subseteq R^{\prime}$ such that for any $k$ -point $R^{\prime}\twoheadrightarrow k$ with $k$ being a finite field, there is a natural equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{et}}_{H_{\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}}[\![t]\!]}(X(\!(t)\!)_{\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}};\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}})\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{H(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])}(X(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!));\mathbf{C}). $$

#### Proof.

By definition of the $\infty$ -categories involved, it suffices to show that for each $j$ and $n$ , there are compatible equivalences

$$ \mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{et}}_{H_{\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}}[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n,\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}};\overline{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}})\xrightarrow{{\sim}}\mathrm{Shv}^{c}_{H_{\mathbf{C}}[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}}(X^{j}_{n,\mathbf{C}};\mathbf{C}). $$

This in turn is a consequence of Theorem 3.2.19 applied to the group scheme $H[\![t]\!]/t^{m_{n}}$ over $R$ . ∎

#### Remark A.5.

Theorem A.4 implicitly uses Remark 3.2.20: it is necessary to treat the equivalence in the proof of Theorem A.4 as those of $\infty$ -categories, so that the (co)limit constructions of Construction A.3 are legal.

We will often use Theorem A.4 in the case when $X$ is an affine homogeneous spherical $H$ -variety. For this, we need:

#### Conjecture A.6.

If $X$ is an affine homogeneous $H$ -variety, the $H[\![t]\!]$ -action on $X(\!(t)\!)$ is placid (so that we can apply Theorem A.4).

However, not being a specialist in the relevant technical details, I have not been able to verify this. It is quite likely that the assumption of placidity is not necessary to prove Theorem 3.6.4, since it is only used to conclude formality of a certain $\Ext$ -algebra.

#### Remark A.7.

When $X=\mathrm{GL}_{n}/\mathrm{O}_{n}$ and $X=\mathrm{GL}_{2n}/\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ , Conjecture A.6 was verified as [CY, Proposition 22] (and the desired formality mentioned above was deduced as [CY, Theorem 23]). The stratification on $X(\!(t)\!)$ defined in [CY] induces one on the based loop space $\Omega X$ , where it has appeared previously in [CM, Discussion after Proposition 1.4].

Proposition 3.5.7 allows us to use Conjecture 3.4.12 (rather, an integral refinement of it) to give a description of the (integral) homology of the free loop space of a compact homogeneous space equipped with the Chas-Sullivan product in Langlands dual terms. #### Recollection B.2.

Fix the same localization $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ of $\mathbf{Z}$ as in Assumption B.1. If $X$ is a closed oriented $n$ -manifold, the homology $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}):=\Sigma^{n}C_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ admits the structure of an algebra via the Chas-Sullivan product. This product is given by push-pull along the span $\mathcal{L}X\times\mathcal{L}X\leftarrow\mathrm{Map}(S^{1}\vee S^{1},X)\to\mathcal{L}X$ . If $X=G/H$ , one can identify

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})=C_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})^{hH}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{{}^{\prime}hG}}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}. $$

Up to completion, $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ can be identified with the Hochschild cohomology $\mathrm{HC}(C^{\ast}(X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})/\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ ; in particular, $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ is naturally an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}$ -algebra by the Deligne conjecture. See [BR, Theorem 1.0.2]. If $X$ is simply-connected, one can also view $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z})$ as the symplectic cohomology $\mathrm{SH}(T^{\ast}X;\mathbf{Z})$ by Viterbo’s theorem (see [Abo]).

Of course, the reader only interested in string topology with rational coefficients need not use Assumption B.1 in any of this discussion.

#### Theorem B.3.

Fix a spherical subgroup $H\subseteq G$ . Let $X\simeq(G/H)(\mathbf{C})$ denote the associated compact homogeneous manifold for the maximal compact subgroup of $G(\mathbf{C})$ . Under Assumption B.1, let

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}={\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\times_{{\check{{M}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}(-2\rho)}{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}, $$

so that there is a canonical morphism ${\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ , and hence a canonical composite

$$ {\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}. $$

Then there is an equivalence

$$ \mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\Gamma\left({\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\};\mathcal{O}\right). $$

#### Proof.

It follows from Assumption B.1(b) and (an integral variant of) Theorem 3.6.4 that $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\simeq\spec C^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\times_{{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}}\{0\} \displaystyle\simeq\spec\left(C^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\otimes_{C_{G}^{\ast}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\right) \displaystyle\simeq\spec\left(C_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})^{hH}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}^{{}^{\prime}hG}}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\right), $$

whose ring of functions identifies with $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ . ∎

Note that the full strength of Assumption B.1 is not really necessary; all one needs is an integral and derived refinement of the isomorphism ${\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}\simeq\spec\mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega X;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ from Theorem 3.6.4.

#### Remark B.4.

Combined with Theorem 3.6.4, Theorem B.3 says that if $G/H$ is simply-connected, one could view

$$ \mathrm{H}^{H}_{\ast}(\Omega(G/H);\mathbf{Z})\cong\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}), $$

the latter being some appropriate version of $G$ -equivariant symplectic cohomology (i.e., a $G$ -equivariant analogue of the string topology algebra $\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}(G/H);\mathbf{Z})$ ). In particular, there should be a map of algebras

$$ \mathrm{H}^{G}_{\ast}(\Omega G;\mathbf{Z})\to\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}) $$

which is “coisotropic” as explained in Observation 5.2.11. See [GMP] for such a construction with coefficients in $\mathbf{C}$ . There should also be an equivalence (motivated by Theorem 3.6.4)

$$ \spec\mathrm{SH}_{G}^{\ast}(T^{\ast}(G/H);\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong{\check{{J}}}_{X}^{\prime}. $$

Moreover, the isomorphism B.1 should hold much more generally with ordinary homology replaced by equivariant (connective) K-theory or equivariant elliptic cohomology, and equivariant symplectic cohomology replaced by the appropriate variant.

For simplicity, we will assume $X$ is simply-connected, so $X$ is $S^{n}$ , ${\mathbf{C}P}^{n}$ , $\mathbf{H}P^{n}$ , or $\mathbf{O}P^{2}$ . These cases fall under the purview of the following lemma.

#### Lemma B.6.

Let $\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k}$ denote the graded ring with $x$ in weight $-2i$ and $b$ in weight $2j$ . Then the quotient $(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}$ has homotopy groups given by

$$ \pi_{\ast}(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}\cong\mathbf{Z}[x,b,\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})]/(x^{k+\ell},bx^{k},\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})^{2},x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})), $$

where $\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ lives in weight $2(j-(k+\ell)i)$ and degree $1$ . In particular, there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}[x,b]/bx^{k})/x^{k+\ell}\cong\mathbf{Z}[x,b,\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})]/(x^{k+\ell},bx^{k},\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})^{2},x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})), $$

where $\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ lives in weight $2(j-(k+\ell)i)+1$ .

#### Proof.

Let $n\geq k+\ell$ ; then, $bx^{n}=(bx^{k})x^{n-k}=b(x^{n})$ admits two nullhomotopies in this quotient, so we obtain a class $\sigma(bx^{n})$ which lives in weight $2(j-ni)$ and degree $1$ ; this class lies in the Massey product/Toda bracket $\langle{x^{n-k},x^{k},b}\rangle$ . Note that $\sigma(bx^{n})=x^{n-k-\ell}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})$ . The relation $x^{k+\ell}=0$ implies that $x^{n-k}=0$ for $n-k\geq k+\ell$ ; so $x^{k}\sigma(bx^{k+\ell})=0$ . ∎

#### Example B.7.

Let $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{2}]$ , let $G=\mathrm{SO}_{n+1}$ , and let $H=\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ . Using the calculations in the proof of Theorem 4.4.1 and Theorem 4.6.1 (or rather, its variant for $\mathrm{SO}_{n+1}/\mathrm{SO}_{n}$ ), we obtain isomorphisms

\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j},b]/bc_{j}&n=2j;\end{cases} $$

here, $a$ lives in weight $0$ , and $b$ lives in weight $4j-2$ . See also [Dev2, Remark B.4] for the first isomorphism. This scheme lives over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ , and we find:

- • If $n=2j+1$ , the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ is given by the map
