It follows from Theorem B.3 that $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j+1};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\left(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},(a+a^{-1})^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{p_{j}},\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}\right]\right)/(p_{1},\cdots,p_{j},c_{j+1})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\left(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[(a+a^{-1})^{2},\tfrac{(a-a^{-1})^{2}}{p_{j}},\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}\right]\right)/(p_{j},c_{j+1}).$ Though this looks complicated, the relations simplify dramatically: we find that the homotopy of this algebra is simply

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j+1};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}\left[\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}},\sigma(c_{j+1})\right]/\sigma(c_{j+1})^{2}, $$

where $\tfrac{a^{2}-a^{-2}}{p_{j}^{1/2}}$ lives in weight $2j$ and $\sigma(c_{j+1})$ (coming from the two nullhomotopies of $c_{j+1}$ ) lives in weight $-2(j+1)+1=-2j-1$ . As expected, this is precisely [CJY, Theorem 2(1)].

- • If $n=2j$ , the map ${\check{{\mathfrak{h}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{H}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ is given by the map

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j}]\to\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j}],\ p_{j}\mapsto c_{j}^{2}. $$

It follows from Theorem B.3 that $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j},b]/bc_{j})/(p_{1},\cdots,p_{j-1},c_{j}^{2})$ $\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}(\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{j},b]/bc_{j})/c_{j}^{2}.$ It follows from Lemma B.6 that there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}S^{2j};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{j},b,\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})]/(bc_{j},c_{j}^{2},\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})^{2},c_{j}\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})), $$

where $\sigma(bc_{j}^{2})$ lives in weight $-1$ . This is precisely [CJY, Theorem 2(2)], as expected.

#### Example B.8.

Let $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\frac{1}{n+1}]$ . Using the calculations in the proof of (an integral version of) Theorem 4.3.1, we obtain isomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle{\check{{J}}}_{\mathrm{PGL}_{n+1}/\mathrm{GL}_{n}} \displaystyle\cong\spec\mathrm{H}_{\ast}^{\mathrm{GL}_{n}}(\Omega{\mathbf{C}P}^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\spec\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{1},\cdots,c_{n-1},c_{n},b]/bc_{n}. $$

Here, $b$ lives in weight $2n$ . This scheme lives over ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}}$ . Taking its fiber over the origin kills the ideal $(c_{2},\cdots,c_{n-1},c_{1}^{n}-c_{n},c_{1}c_{n})$ . Note that $c_{1}c_{n}=c_{1}^{n+1}$ . It follows from Theorem B.3 and Lemma B.6 that there is a graded isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}{\mathbf{C}P}^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[c_{1},b,\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})]/(bc_{1}^{n},c_{1}^{n+1},\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})^{2},c_{1}^{n}\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})), $$

where $\sigma(bc_{1}^{n+1})$ lives in weight $-1$ . As expected, this is [CJY, Theorem 3].

#### Remark B.9.

Lemma B.6 shows that using Theorem 4.5.1 and Theorem 4.7.1, one obtains graded isomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}\mathbf{H}P^{n};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{1},b,\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})]/(bp_{1}^{n},p_{1}^{n+1},\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})^{2},p_{1}^{n}\sigma(bp_{1}^{n+1})), \displaystyle\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{C}_{\ast}(\mathcal{L}\mathbf{O}P^{2};\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}) \displaystyle\cong\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}[p_{2},b,\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})]/(bp_{2}^{2},p_{2}^{3},\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})^{2},p_{2}^{2}\sigma(bp_{2}^{3})). $$

Here, $b$ lives in weight $4n+2$ in the first line, and in weight $22$ in the second line. In the first line, one can take $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{n+1}]$ ; and in the second line, one can take $\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[\tfrac{1}{3}]$ ; see [Yan].3434 34 These denominators precisely encode the “very good primes” for ${\check{{G}}}$ ; for instance, a prime $p$ is very good for $\mathrm{PGL}_{n+1}$ if $p\nmid(n+1)$ , and is very good for $\mathrm{F}_{4}$ if $p\nmid 3$ . If a prime $p$ is very good for ${\check{{G}}}$ , it admits a quasi-logarithm ${\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ in the sense of [KV] (see [FN, Corollary 6.4]), which should imply that the usual statement of Theorem 3.2.7 holds with coefficients in $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . See Remark 3.2.8.

## Appendix C Questions/further directions

The work presented in this article is clearly far from being a complete story. There are numerous questions left open by our discussion, of varying levels of difficulty. I hope that the discussion in this article is compelling enough to motivate further study of these problems.

Let us begin with some broad questions. First, some conceptual questions about the place of this story in mathematics and physics:

- (a) Having been raised a topologist, it is inspiring to see the appearance of unstable homotopy-theoretic structures in Table 3 (such as EHP sequences and Hopf fibrations). It suggests that there might be an unstable analogue of Expectation 5.3.13 (the latter is already not well-defined!) giving a spectral decomposition for “ $G$ -equivariant sheaves of spaces on $\Omega G$ ”. There are some indications that this might be possible, and many that it might be impossible — but it is perhaps better to be optimistic! This question seems exceptionally difficult, even in the simplest case of $G$ being trivial. In this case, one can interpret the question as asking for an analogue of the theory of synthetic spectra à la [Pst] for spaces/homotopy types/anima. Considerations from the theory of power operations suggests that one should replace the fpqc stack $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{s}}_{\mathrm{FG}}$ of groupoids classifying spin formal groups and isomorphisms between them by some sort of fpqc stack of categories classifying spin formal groups and homomorphisms (in particular, including isogenies) between them.

- (b) As mentioned in [Dev2, Heuristic B.5], an unpublished conjecture of Gaiotto (which I learned about from Nakajima) says that the Coulomb branch of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory over $\mathbf{R}^{3}\times S^{1}$ with a generic choice of complex structure and gauge group $G$ can be modeled via the periodic $G$ -equivariant complex K-theory of $\Omega G$ . The calculations of this paper suggest that perhaps one can modify this proposal to use connective equivariant complex K-theory instead, and that the Bott class is related to the radius of the circle $S^{1}$ (see also Remark 5.1.15). The Bott class being sent to zero then might correspond to the degeneration of $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=2$ pure gauge theory into $3$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ pure gauge theory. For instance, in Remark 3.5.21, we find that if $T=S^{1}$ (say), going from integral to $\mathrm{ku}$ -homology has the effect of deforming the relation $[p,a]=\hbar$ in the Weyl algebra of $\mathbf{G}_{a}=\spec\mathbf{Z}[a]$ over $\mathbf{Z}$ to the relation $[p,a]=\hbar(1+\beta ap)$ over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ . (The symbol $p$ corresponds to $\tfrac{1}{a}x$ in Remark 3.5.21.) Does such a deformation have any precedence in physics? Here is a more optimistic question. Kapustin and Witten (among others) proposed viewing the derived geometric Satake equivalence of Theorem 3.2.7 as an equivalence of categories stemming from S-duality for $4$ d $\mathcal{N}=4$ gauge theory. Does Theorem 3.7.18 have any relationship to $5$ d maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory compactified on a circle of finite radius (related to the Bott class $\beta$ )?

- (c) One glaring omission in this article is the study of equivariance for loop rotation on the topological/A-side; as explained in [NS, BBB+] via the $\Omega$ -deformation and [Dev2, Remark B.2], this corresponds to deformation quantizing the spectral/B-side. From one point of view, it can be described as the study of the homology of the operad ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}\rtimes S^{1}$ associated to rotations about a line inside $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ . Is there a good theory of quantizations of $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces (and a classification thereof)? Motivated by this, and considerations involving Frobenius-constant quantizations à la Bezrukavnikov-Kaledin [BK], we are planning to discuss the $\mathrm{U}(n)$ -equivariant cohomology of the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+1}}}$ -operad with arbitrary complex-oriented coefficients in a later article [Dev5]. This discussion is heavily motivated by [DM2] (in particular, [DM2, Section 4.4] can be regarded as the simplest case of this story, namely the case of tori). Part of the reason for not discussing loop rotation equivariance in this article is our reliance on Proposition 3.5.1, which inherently breaks the natural $S^{1}$ -action on the free loop space.

- (d) Prove Conjecture 3.5.11. In every example I have studied, the construction of the relevant Kostant slice $\kappa_{{\check{{M}}}}:{\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ relies on classical invariant theory, and proving a unified statement would be very interesting and important. One interesting feature in the known examples is that the construction of such slices involves constructing a “stronger” slice ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ . However, this depends on some noncanonical choices, i.e., the map ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ is not canonical. It would therefore also be interesting to show that ${\check{{G}}}$ acts transitively on the set of all such slices ${\check{{M}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{M}}}$ (in other words, that such a slice, if it exists, is unique if we ask it to land in ${\check{{M}}}/{\check{{G}}}$ instead of ${\check{{M}}}$ ). For the usual Kostant slice ${\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}/\!\!/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{\mathfrak{g}}}}$ , this was shown in [FM].

- (e) Give an explanation for the observation in Remark 3.6.25.

- (f) Can one prove ramified versions of the local equivalences studied in this article? See Conjecture 3.4.14 for the analogue of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] with tame ramification.

- (g) In many calculations, one gets the sense that the condition of sphericity should not be crucial in relative geometric Langlands. For instance, the criteria (a) and (b) of Theorem 3.6.4 do not use sphericity of $H_{\mathbf{C}}\subseteq G_{\mathbf{C}}$ at all (and as in Remark 3.6.7, Example 3.6.13, and Conjecture 3.6.15, there should be many interesting examples of relative Langlands duality for non-spherical subgroups). One of the immediate difficulties encountered when working with non-spherical subgroups is that $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}[\![t]\!])$ -orbits on $G_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))/H_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{C}(\!(t)\!))$ are not parametrized by a discrete set; so it is hard to do “combinatorics”. Nevertheless, it would be interesting to collect other non-spherical examples satisfying conditions (a) and (b) of Theorem 3.6.4; a sufficient supply of examples might suggest a way to understand this generalization of relative Langlands duality.

- (h) In the proof (from [BF1]) of Theorem 3.2.7, many calculations can be reduced to the case of semisimple rank $1$ , essentially by localization on the affine space ${\check{{\mathfrak{t}}}}^{\ast}(2)/\!\!/W=\spec\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{G}(\ast;\mathbf{Z}^{\prime})$ . Is it possible to tackle Conjecture 3.4.12 for affine homogeneous spherical varieties of higher rank by reduction to the rank $1$ case (in which case Theorem 3.4.16 can be applied)? The technique of localization of spherical varieties, studied in [Lun, Kno3], should be crucial here.

- (i) Let $C_{2}$ be the cyclic group of order $2$ . In the case of symmetric spaces, Conjecture 3.4.12 should be closely related to $C_{2}$ -equivariant derived algebraic geometry as studied by Mike Hill and his collaborators (see, e.g., [Hil]). Let $\sigma$ denote the sign representation of $C_{2}$ on $\mathbf{R}$ , and let $\varrho=1+\sigma$ denote the regular representation of $C_{2}$ on $\mathbf{C}$ .3535 35 The notation is intended to distinguish this $C_{2}$ from the $\mathbf{Z}/2$ appearing elsewhere in this article, as well as $\varrho$ from the half-sum of positive roots (which is usually denoted $\rho$ ). On the topic of notation: it would have been great if $\varrho$ was used to denote the r(h)otation representation of $C_{2}$ (which is frequently denoted by $\lambda=2\sigma$ ), instead of the regular representation of $C_{2}$ . If $Y$ is a $C_{2}$ -space, let $\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}Y$ denote the space of maps $\mathrm{Map}(S^{\sigma},Y)$ equipped with its natural $C_{2}$ -action. Let $G$ be a connected compact Lie group, let $\theta$ be a conjugate-linear involution on $G_{\mathbf{C}}$ preserving $G$ , and let $G^{\theta}$ denote the maximal compact subgroup of the fixed subgroup $G_{\mathbf{C}}^{\theta}$ . Then, there is a $C_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy equivalence of orbispaces

$$ G\backslash\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}G/G\simeq\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}}), $$

which gives an equivalence

$$ (G\backslash\mathcal{L}^{\sigma}G/G)^{C_{2}}\simeq G\backslash\mathcal{L}(G/G^{\theta}). $$

Note that ${\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}}=S^{\varrho}$ (which one can think of as the unit sphere in $\varrho\oplus\mathbf{R}=\sigma\oplus\mathbf{R}^{2}$ ) is the standard real structure on ${\mathbf{C}P}^{1}$ . Let $R$ denote a normed algebra in genuine $C_{2}$ -spectra, and let $\Phi^{C_{2}}R$ denote its geometric fixed points (for instance, if $R=\underline{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the constant Mackey functor, $\Phi^{C_{2}}R$ is the connective cover of the Tate construction $\mathbf{F}_{2}^{tS^{1}}\simeq\mathbf{Z}^{tC_{2}}$ ). We expect that there is an $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}});R)$ of “ $C_{2}$ -equivariant sheaves of $R$ -modules on $\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}})$ ”. This $\infty$ -category should satisfy an analogue of Theorem 3.2.7. Taking geometric fixed points (in some appropriate categorical sense) of this putative spectral decomposition of $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}(\mathrm{Bun}_{(G,\theta)}({\mathbf{C}P}^{1}_{\mathbf{R}});R)$ should produce an analogue/special case of Conjecture 3.4.12 which describes $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/G^{\theta}(\!(t)\!);\Phi^{C_{2}}R)$ . For instance, one can try to access $\mathrm{Shv}^{c,\mathrm{Sat}}_{G[\![t]\!]}(G(\!(t)\!)/G^{\theta}(\!(t)\!);\Phi^{C_{2}}R)$ via an analogue of Smith theory. The case of $G=\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ equipped with the orthogonal involution, and $R=\underline{\mathbf{Z}}$ , is especially interesting, and we hope to study this question in future work. Developing this theory should lead to important interactions between geometric Langlands for symmetric spaces and $C_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy theory.

- (j) What is the underlying reason/broader context for the similarities evident in Table 3 between the dual varieties to the rank $1$ affine homogeneous varieties? In our story, these reflect the similitude between the based loop spaces of odd/even-dimensional spheres, but there are many other examples of such similarities in higher rank. We will address this question in future work; see Remark 4.1.5 for a brief comment. The recent article [Les] by Leslie is also concerned with this topic.

Some of the most important issues in this article on the topological/A-side come from defining well-behaved sheaf theories.

- (k) Verify Hypothesis 3.5.2, and more generally Conjecture A.6.

- (l) Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, and let $X$ be an (ind-)finite stratified $G$ -space. Is there a good $\mathrm{sh}^{1/2}\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\mathrm{Shv}_{G}^{c}(X;\mathrm{ku})$ which agrees with the ad hoc construction of Construction 3.7.15?

- (m) Is there a good sheaf theory of synthetic $G$ -equivariant constructible sheaves of spectra as in Expectation 5.3.10? As a first step, it seems important to study $G$ -equivariant analogues of synthetic spectra, as well as nonequivariant synthetic analogues of constructible sheaves of spectra.

The discussion in this article also suggests several (less lofty, and presumably more approachable) questions.

- (n) Can one define ${\check{{G}}}_{\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{univ}}}$ as in Expectation 5.3.11?

- (o) Is there an a priori reason that if ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}$ is an ${\check{{G}}}$ -variety over $\mathbf{Z}[\beta]$ as in Proposition 3.7.20, the map ${\check{{M}}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}\to{\check{{G}}}^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\beta}/{\check{{G}}}$ admits a Lagrangian structure? See Observation 5.2.11 for some progress in this direction.

- (p) As in Remark 3.5.19, let $W_{1}\to W_{2}$ be a homomorphism of reflection groups acting on vector spaces $V_{1}\to V_{2}$ over a field $k$ (possibly of nonzero characteristic), so that there is a map $V_{1}/\!\!/W_{1}\to V_{2}/\!\!/W_{2}$ . The Hochschild homology $\mathrm{HH}(V_{1}/\!\!/W_{1}/V_{2}/\!\!/W_{2})$ should be an interesting invariant associated to homomorphisms of reflection groups; what can one prove about it? In the case that the map of reflection groups comes from an inclusion of root data, this Hochschild homology is the content of Proposition 3.5.7, and therefore plays an important role in the relative Langlands program.

- (q) Is there an analogue of Theorem 4.6.1 for $\mathrm{ku}$ ? The difficulty lies in finding a $\beta$ -deformation of ${\check{{M}}}$ .

- (r) Can one extend Theorem 3.7.18 to the non-simply-laced case? Similarly, can one extend Proposition 5.4.1 to coefficients with the sphere spectrum? Following Lemma 5.4.10, a first step will be an understanding of $\mathrm{MU}_{\ast}(\Omega G)$ as a Hopf algebra; the cobordism groups are known by [Pet]. A description of the $\mathrm{MU}_{\ast}\mathrm{MU}$ -comodule structure would then give the desired generalization of Proposition 5.4.1.

- (s) Fix a prime $p$ . Can the results of this article (even only the ones concerning coefficients in ordinary commutative rings) be extended to the setting of $p$ -compact groups? This question was suggested by Haynes Miller. See [Gro] for a survey of the theory of $p$ -compact groups. Let us make some brief comments about this question. First, if the input into the machinery of geometric Langlands duality is the $p$ -completion of a compact torus $T$ , the “Langlands dual” appears to be the $p$ -divisible subgroup ${\check{{T}}}[p^{\infty}]$ of the Langlands dual torus ${\check{{T}}}$ . (In the rank one case, this reduces to the statement that the Cartier dual of $\Omega(S^{1})^{\wedge}_{p}=\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ , if interpreted suitably, is $\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ .) Second, the simplest exotic case of the Sullivan sphere $(S^{2n-1})^{\wedge}_{p}=\Omega(B^{2}\mathbf{Z}_{p})_{h{\mathbf{Z}/n}}$ for $n|\#\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}$ , which behaves like a compact Lie group of rank $1$ , already seems to exhibit an interesting Langlands duality: its “dual group” is built out of the $p$ -divisible torus $\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ and the Weyl group ${\mathbf{Z}/n}$ acting via ${\mathbf{Z}/n}\subseteq\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\times}\circlearrowright\mu_{p^{\infty}}$ . Third, in [Dev4, Remark 3.13], I suggest that the Dwyer-Wilkerson exotic $2$ -compact group from [DW] might act on a framed $30$ -manifold with Kervaire invariant $1$ (just as $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}$ acts on $\mathrm{PGL}_{2}^{\times 3}/\mathrm{PGL}_{2}\cong\mathbf{R}P^{3}\times\mathbf{R}P^{3}$ and $\mathrm{G}_{2}$ acts on $\mathrm{SO}_{8}/\mu_{2}\cdot\mathrm{G}_{2}\cong\mathbf{R}P^{7}\times\mathbf{R}P^{7}$ ), and that the “regular centralizer” group scheme for this action should be related to the relative Langlands program. See [Dev4] for (brief) further discussion.

- (t) Finding other examples of the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic analogue of [BZSV, Conjecture 7.5.1] is an important goal. For instance, what is the $\mathrm{ku}$ -theoretic dual of the spherical $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ -variety $\mathrm{GL}_{n}/(\mathrm{GL}_{j}\times\mathrm{GL}_{n-j})$ (which is homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{Gr}_{j}(\mathbf{C}^{n})$ )? In the arithmetic case, this was studied by Jacquet-Rallis in [JR], and is described in Conjecture 3.6.15 in the geometric case.

- (u) Is there an analogue of the theory of synthetic spectra for global homotopy theory?

- (v) Is there a structure theory for $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces? Namely, is there a well-behaved theory of “hyperspherical” $\mathrm{ku}$ -Hamiltonian spaces which generalizes the notion of hyperspherical Hamiltonian spaces introduced in [BZSV, Section 3], and an analogue of [BZSV, Theorem 3.6.1]?

- (w) Related to the preceding point, can one develop a theory of $\beta$ -deformed cotangent bundles for certain $G$ -varieties? In the case of “coisotropic subgroups” as in Remark 5.1.20, this would be a $\beta$ -deformation of [BM] (or rather, of the specialization of their results to quasi-Hamiltonian spaces).
